items.title: Catch the Bugs Your Code Review Misses - Killian Carlsen-Phelan & Taylor Luttrell-Williams, Sonar
items.excerpt: In this hands-on session, Killian Carlsen-Phelan and Taylor Luttrell-Williams of Sonar set up Gitar, a code change verification agent, on a sample ticketing app and run three pull requests through it. Gitar catches a bug that isn't in the diff at all (a buyer can refund a ticket after giving it to a friend), enforces a business rule from a project config (show customers the all-in price), then diagnoses a failing CI test and keeps pushing fixes until the PR passes and auto-merges. They close with functional validation against Jira tickets, learned conventions, and cross-repo and cross-PR analysis. items.title: Why Humans Can't Keep Up With AI-Written Code - Tariq Shaukat, Sonar
items.excerpt: Agents have made code cheap: one study saw lines of code up 2,450% but releases up only 30%. Sonar CEO Tariq Shaukat draws on the factory revolution that Toyota and Lexus started to explain how to build agentic software factories you can trust. He breaks down five hard problems: human review that doesn't scale (people agree with AI that's wrong 4 out of 5 times), agents struggling with large codebases, errors compounding over long tasks, unreliable LLM judges, and near-zero time to exploit. Then he lays out Sonar's code confidence formula: intent, guide rails, verification and evidence. items.title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
items.excerpt: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models. Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world. I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle. By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens"). Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request. Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat. This is continuous deployment turned up to 11: A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. items.title: Can Frontier Models See Past a Decoy? Elorian Tests Visual Reasoning
items.excerpt: This month Elorian launched its first visual reasoning model , Glimpse . It’s being promoted as “a new category of visual thinking model: a system that reasons about the physical world from what it sees.” View post on X ↗ So how does Glimpse compare to both frontier models and world models in vision tests? A new benchmark called DecoyCount , co-released by Elorian, provides some answers. We quizzed CEO Andrew Dai on the benchmark, and also talked about Elorian’s positioning in a crowded models landscape. DecoyCount results Elorian emerged from stealth in April with $55 million in seed funding , co-led by Striker Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures and Altimeter Capital. Now, in partnership with AI data company Mercor , Elorian is announcing the DecoyCount benchmark, which tests whether language models genuinely count objects or rely on visual shortcuts and substitution heuristics. According to a paper accompanying the release , frontier models scored below 50% accuracy on DecoyCount — the highest was GPT-6 Astra, with 43.17%. Elorian’s new model isn’t mentioned in the paper, but Dai told us that Glimpse scored 50.48% in an internal test. Regarding the frontier models, the paper concludes that “stronger general reasoning does not by itself generalize to aligned visual reasoning.” How the benchmark works: “DecoyCount exposes interpretable counting failures across seven mechanisms.” To make sure it was a like-for-like comparison with the frontier models, we asked whether the paper’s evaluation images were withheld from Glimpse’s training? “The evaluation images and text were wit…

items.title: Why a One-Line Change Can Break Your Whole Stack - Cole Gannaway, Qodo
items.excerpt: Code generation is moving faster than ever, and the bottleneck has moved to review. Cole Gannaway, a solutions engineer at Qodo, shows how a one-line data model change that passes every test can quietly break web, mobile, CLI and MCP clients, and how a software graph of your repos reveals that blast radius. He covers turning tribal knowledge and PR comments into custom rules, bringing review context in before code is written, why the agent that wrote the code shouldn't grade it, and checking PRs against the original ticket. items.text: augmenting human intellect when i started making software, i wasn’t dreaming of a factory. i loved that something on a screen could become an extension of my mind. a place to put a thought before i understood it. to move things around until new connections appeared. to make little systems that worked the way i worked, even if it made no sense to anyone else. the computer wasn’t interesting because it could do work without me. it was interesting because of what i could do with it. the early lineage of computing was built around this possibility. in 1962, Engelbart described augmenting human intellect as helping a person understand complex situations and find solutions that were previously out of reach. his starting point was the human being, not the autonomous machine. he wasn’t describing a faster black box. he was looking at the whole relationship between a person, their tools, their language, their methods, and what they could learn to do with them. the capability belonged to that whole system. somewhere along the way, we started telling a much smaller story about a much more powerful technology. more automation. more agents. more software producing more software. more output from fewer people. more growth. more numbers to prove that something is happening. and less attention to the person any of this is supposed to be for. i don’t want to pretend computing had a pure innocent beginning. replacing human labor was one of its ambitions. even in 1960, Licklider distinguished human-computer symbiosis from systems where the remaining people mainly served the machine. he wanted computers to participate in the formation of ideas, not only execute problems already defined. that distinction feels important – does the system help you discover what you mean? or does it only want you to submit a request, and wait outside while it works? sometimes waiting is exactly what i want. please do the search. move the files. take away the repetitive work. but not everything difficult is overhead. sometimes moving the pieces around is how you understand them. sometimes making the thing changes what you wanted to make. sometimes you need to see the wrong version, touch it, take it apart, and discover a better question. i want tools that leave room for that relationship. in his 1981 paper on Smalltalk, Ingalls described a system meant to support everyone’s creative spirit. personal mastery mattered: an individual should be able to comprehend the system, rather than remain dependent on something permanently beyond their reach. he also argued that computer models should fit the human mind, rather than demand the reverse. not one perfect workflow for everyone. systems that different people can inhabit differently. someone who thinks through pictures. someone who needs to write. someone who understands a problem by building a simulation. someone whose way of organizing their life doesn’t resemble a SaaS dashboard. a system you can reshape as your understanding changes. this is what i want AI to make possible. not just pumping out software, but having a living relationship with it. being able to ask why something works this way. change one part without surrendering the rest. see what happened. undo it. learn enough to make the next change yourself. the machine can become more capable without making the person smaller. but that won’t happen just because we make the models better. we have to care about it. design for it. notice when we are making someone more dependent while calling it empowerment. i don’t want to measure the future only by how much work happens without us. i want to know what becomes possible for the person who couldn’t participate before. what can they understand now? what can they express? what can they change without asking permission? when i say augmenting human intellect, that is what i mean. not a world that no longer needs us. a world we have more ability to shape.

items.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
items.excerpt: In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered: Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra [ ... ] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7. — Ted Sanders , explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions Tags: generative-ai , gpt , openai , ai , llms , ted-sanders

items.title: How Anthropic Merges 30,000 Code Changes a Day - Manish Kapur, Sonar & Addy Osmani, Anthropic
items.excerpt: Coding agents are opening PRs faster than anyone can review them. Manish Kapur (Sonar) and Addy Osmani (Anthropic) discuss "light" vs. "dark" software factories, how Anthropic scaled from about 2,500 to 30,000 merged changes a day with Claude doing first-pass review backed by real verification evidence, new data from Sonar's State of Code survey, and why every loop in the factory needs independent, multi-layered verification. They close with a lightning round on labeling agent-written PRs and when it's safe to merge. Chapters: 0:00 Intro 1:57 Throughput is up, merges are failing 2:49 Light vs. dark software factories 3:51 Coding is solved, confidence isn't 5:38 How Anthropic reviews 30,000 changes a day 8:29 State of Code survey findings 9:20 Where the next gains come from 11:38 Multi-layered verification 13:19 Controls, permissions and sandboxes 14:41 Lightning round 17:40 Takeaways Manish Kapur https://www.sonarsource.com Addy Osmani https://x.com/addyosmani https://www.anthropic.com Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE summit: https://aie.codes our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now!

items.text: I think world models are still in the GPT 3.5 era, but not for long. Like the old Will Smith eating spaghetti videos, world models are impressive but not quite there yet. You can see it in the reel below, which has a mix of my Genie 4 generations and Google's. But once they hit the GPT-5 or GPT-6 stage, I think they'll have massive implications for a lot of industries: Movies - A big effects shot like a dragon battle takes a VFX studio months of work. With a great world model, a director could create a single frame and have AI generate the full scene from it. Games - From my time working in gaming, I learned the real work is core loops, progression systems, and the mechanics that make a game fun. World models are already good at graphics and sound, but the gameplay isn't there yet. Still, they'll make it much easier for anyone to build their own game that looks and sounds amazing. Just like the rise of personal apps, I think world models (along with good coding models) could make creating your own game as fun as playing a mass market one which again has huge implications. 📌 Watch my full Genie 4 tutorial to see how I created the worlds in the reel below: https://t.co/GvzPewT5gj

items.text: Vercel CI solves the "AI coding bottleneck" via: ① Fast and stable infrastructure (faster work) ② Turborepo integration (less work) ③ Agentic CI ① is obvious. Your CI is slow, flaky, goes down. We solve that. We operate 20 worldwide clusters doing millions of microVMs per day. ② is less obvious, but very powerful. Turborepo was designed to intelligently skip and cache prior work. The graph of dependencies is computed, not written. Ask your agent to migrate to @turborepo and start saving money and time. Even if you don't use us. But you should, it's really good. ③ is a game-changer. 𝚟𝚎𝚛𝚌𝚎𝚕 𝚌𝚒 in the CLI is the first step, because now your agents can inspect, abort, trigger, replay CI. Vercel Agent can help optimize it. And this is just the start. You can expect a lot of hooks and capabilities to make CI something far more intelligent, that can even capture the nuance and judgment an engineer would have ("Are those tests even worth running?") Agentic CI is the future of how we ship software. Excited to build it with you all!

items.title: Why Agents Love Supabase
items.excerpt: I first met Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson in Singapore, shortly after they finished YC as the hottest startup of YC S20 . Six years later, we finally got them on the podcast! This is their first podcast together, after taking an open-source, fully remote company from zero to a $10 billion valuation. The title is a question I wanted to understand for myself: why do agents love Supabase? There are plenty of managed databases. Postgres hosting is competitive. Being familiar to a model is useful distribution, but it doesn't explain all the work needed to turn a generated application into something that runs. But when I ran my frontier AEO tracker , it was an almost complete sweep of first choice for app backends (and in contention for managed db ) for every frontier model from Astra to Fable to Muse. At Select, Supabase grouped its announcements into Build, Operate and Scale. The things that stood out to me were surprisingly practical: start a local backend without Docker, keep the desired database schema in Git, and run compute beside the database. Each removes a piece of work that developers have been doing for years. Agents make that friction harder to ignore. Watch the full conversation, including my opening commentary → Give the agent a backend it can read My favorite developer-tool announcements make me think: of course I want this today. The new alpha runtime for running Supabase locally without Docker is one of those. I use Colima rather than Docker Desktop, and even then, removing another dependency from the path to a working database is welcome. Local setup is a sm…

items.title: GitHub Octoverse 2026
items.excerpt: GitHub Octoverse 2026 I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular: This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month. The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location . Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...] Industry . Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...] Interoperability . Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation. items.title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
items.excerpt: I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games . Tree Appreciator Emberwick Battle Drones Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove Four times as insulting What happens if someone actually puts the work in? You should build a game! Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: 3D modeling Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox ) Game design (!) That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play . Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it. Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did . In the past few weeks I've vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term - no looking at the code at all) four games that I've genuinely enjoyed playing. I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar e…

items.title: [AINews] Anthropic ends Coding Interviews: "Hunger beats tenure"
items.excerpt: Several midsize headlines today; on top of some impressive Math verification , Google Genie and Artificial Analysis and FrontierCode all shipped major version bumps of their top offerings, all of which have been AINews title stories in the past, but are mostly annual incremental improvements. Past guest Felix Reiseberg gets the headline today for coming out and charting the path forward for junior engineers : “ Hunger beats tenure” This month, I laid the traditional coding interview to rest. As a hiring manager at Anthropic, I stopped asking candidates to do them… …There’s no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both. Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests. Enough said. His advice for juniors Pick business impact over backlog : In pre-AI-coding 2011, Patrick McKenzie wrote “engineers are hired to create business value, not to program things.” Pick a radical idea : Come up with a few ideas that would, if successful, dramatically improve the chances that your organization achieves those goals. Be ambitious! Build it over a weekend : I have seen small groups and solo engineers fly past the usual process of writing product requirements documents (PRDs), getting buy-in, and lobbying for time with designers or product managers by building a working prototype. Focus on one good idea : In my experience, junior people often make the mistake of cramming multiple ideas into a single prototype , hiding three excellent ideas among 20 bad ones. Lean in…

items.excerpt: When an agent sends an invoice using your token, who actually made the request? Kamil Potrec of Keycard breaks down how agents get credentials today (personal tokens, static keys, over-privileged service accounts) and what proper agent auth requires: per-agent identity, delegation, short-lived scoped credentials, federation with legacy systems, policy and audit. He compares SDKs and gateways for keeping credentials out of an agent's reach, including the gateway tradeoffs. items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: This is correct. The vast majority of enterprise workflows have not actually had agents applied to them in any meaningful way. The economy probably has this deployed < 1% right now. At best you have a few automated systems in a company that do a single pass of an LLM to make a decision or provide feedback, but very little real “automation”. Some of this is a statement about the adoption rates of technology in enterprises, but the vast majority of it is really just due to the capability of AI itself. That’s all changing. Now with computer use, long running agents, harness improvements and surrounding infrastructure, we’re finally at a point where we can start to apply agents at more complex workflows. We will see self-improving systems that can take any particular workflow goal and improve the execution rates over a volume of instances. And with the emerging form factor of agent swarms, you can just choose to deploy any amount of compute at a problem and agents will off and do the work. This won’t be about and users prompting agents to complete a specific task for them, but instead the organization reengineering the underlying workflows to take advantage of agents in their processes. This will have a massive impact in finance, life sciences, healthcare, and other information-heavy domains. Lots of opportunity to build and deploy these systems right now.

items.title: Game Boy Color on My Conference Badge
items.excerpt: Game Boy Color on My Conference Badge I'm at GitHub Universe this week and, similar to last year , the conference badge is a full-blown color screen computer. I've been hacking around with it again, and then I ran into with Steve Francia... who worked with Gemini to get a full NES emulator working on it, and then went a step further and deployed an emulator for both the Game Boy and the Game Boy Color. Which means, if you can obtain the ROM, you can run The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening on your conference badge! A neat feature of the badge is that you can turn it upside down and then use game controller touch buttons that are built into the badge body. Tags: games , github , hardware-hacking , ai , generative-ai , llms , gemini , steve-francia

items.title: Stop Giving Your Agent Tools. Give It a Sandbox - Mikyo King, Arize AI
items.excerpt: Classic tool-calling agents fill their context with tool catalogs and raw outputs. Code mode gives the agent a sandbox and lets it search for and compose tools in code, returning only what it needs. Mikyo King, head of open source at Arize AI, explains why code mode works, how Arize built it into Phoenix (Bash, a Python sandbox, SQL and even UI control), its hidden costs (secrets, permissions, durability, double sandboxing), and how Harbor evals showed 43% fewer tokens and 31% lower cost. Applications live now!

items.excerpt: Watch the full episode on YouTube As we learned from the Anthropic S-1 filings yesterday , the lab has some of the highest revenue and research efficiency in human history, particularly with -126% loss to 19% GAAP profit turnaround in the last year. The company credits this to their two core loops: Improvement and Investment: Today we go inside how Anthropic works. Now the dust has settled on Opus 5.5 and it has lasted a month as the generally accepted #1 LLM in the world, we dive into its launch, and how Anthropic ships Claude with Claude with Katelyn Lesse and Angela Jiang , heads of Engineering and Product respectively. The team is working under two kinds of pressure. The models are getting more capable, which makes safe deployment and access decisions harder. At the same time, usage is growing fast enough that ordinary infrastructure choices—like how much CPU an API consumes—become strategic. Those problems meet in the product choices that reach developers. A model launch is also an API launch Anthropic's Opus 5.5 launch emphasizes both model quality and cost. We discuss feedback that the previous Opus generations were be too verbose, alongside the need for stronger intelligence per dollar. Anthropic says the new model costs less to run than its predecessor; the exact saving depends on the workload and its use of cached context. The less visible launch work involves changes to how people integrate the API. One example we discuss is protecting model reasoning against extraction used for distillation. items.title: What a $900M Bank Error Teaches Us About AI Agents - John Feminella, Two Sigma
items.excerpt: In 2020, Citibank accidentally sent about $900 million to Revlon’s lenders instead of an $8 million interest payment, even though the procedure, the warning pop-up and three approvers all did what they were supposed to. John Feminella, who works on AI architecture and engineering at Two Sigma, uses that story to show how to give AI agents real autonomy without locking everything down. He walks through five composable controls: an agent registry, risk-based review, tool access that follows an agent’s declared purpose, shared firm-wide evals, and classifiers that send humans only the approvals that matter. Views are his own, not Two Sigma’s. items.subtitle: Latent Space
items.title: Coding From the Himalayas With an Offline AI Agent
items.excerpt: When we talk about working remotely , we take a lot of things for granted, especially reliable internet and power. But sometimes, working remotely means trying to get something done on a flight, during a long train ride, or somewhere with little or no network. I moved to the foothills of the Himalayas a year ago. I love the peace of living here, but it also comes with its own challenges, including network and power outages . Things I didn’t think about as much before are now part of planning my work. I work as a Principal Engineer at Thomson Reuters , where I spend most of my time coding and reviewing my teammates’ code. Coding agents are already a big part of my everyday workflow, which made me curious about how much of that workflow I could keep using offline. Working from the foothills of the Himalayas. Photo of my workspace. If you’re someone like me, who enjoys working with technology but also finds peace in quiet, remote places where the network doesn’t always cooperate, this article is for you. It’s also for anyone who has wondered whether a coding agent can run entirely on their laptop, with the internet switched off. I tried running a coding agent locally on my laptop to see how much work I could actually get done offline. What can we do offline? A project already on your laptop gives us plenty to work with. We can ask an agent to explain an unfamiliar function, investigate a failing test, refactor a small piece of code, or help finish a feature. These tasks can run offline when the model, project dependencies and test tools are available locally. Downloading a ne…

items.title: Why Are We Still Governing AI Agents Like Software? - Tim Tyler, Gravitee
items.excerpt: Nobody would hire a worker with no ID, no manager and shared passwords, yet that's how most companies deploy AI agents. Tim Tyler of Gravitee presents the Agent Accountability framework, which governs agents like a digital workforce in three stages: Assignment (identity, team, a named human sponsor), Alignment (role, mission and least-privilege authority) and Administration (oversight scorecards, guardian agents and step-by-step recourse when agents go off course). items.title: 300 Agents, 60 People: How We Secured Our Own AI Agents - Aiden Sochowski, Runlayer
items.excerpt: Runlayer is a company of about 60 people running 300+ agents every day. Founding engineer Aiden Sochowski shares what they found once they put a gateway in front of everything and logged every session and tool call: prompt injection through email, PR-review agents getting talked into approvals, over-permissioned bots, one poisoned agent contaminating others, buggy vibe-coded MCP servers burning tokens, and a model switch that raised costs over 100x in a week. items.excerpt: Today is one of those days that is tougher to cover for a normally-engineer audience that isn’t used to reading most S-1’s, let alone 350 pages of one of the most unusual S-1’s of all time : Better visualized: With significant operating leverage causing the first profitable quarter in Anthropic history (adjusted for $1B/quarter of SBC): The incredible efficiency story is told in two loops, and of course you know, we love loop: The pitch going forward is “virtual collaborators” (don’t say agent!) for over a billion knowledge workers by 2028: We believe we have reached an inflection point where AI systems can function as genuine collaborators in professional work. They quickly complete substantive tasks that might otherwise occupy a skilled professional for several hours, a full day, or longer. AI systems are also becoming increasingly capable of performing tasks that were previously too difficult or costly to complete or surfacing original insights and analyses. We refer to these AI systems that work alongside humans to perform complex, multi-step work at professional levels as Virtual Collaborators. Virtual Collaborators carry the access rights, system connections, and context that their organizations grant them , which allows them to function more accurately and reliably. They can navigate and use internal tools and execute workflows that span multiple steps that require sustained reasoning. items.title: GPT-6.1 Terra
items.excerpt: GPT-6.1 Terra It's always interesting to note which aspects of a new model are emphasized in the release announcement. In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, OpenAI went with visual reasoning and computer use: We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra , a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos. Terra sits in the same position as Sonnet in the Anthropic model collection - not the cheapest or the most expensive, making it harder to decide when to use it. Computer use is a good example of a task that benefits from a less expensive model, since you might put it to work on automated, repetitive tasks. OpenAI's Ted Sanders provided some useful advice in a comment on Hacker News: In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. For API developers, it's a nice midrange option if you want something cheaper than Sol but a lot smarter than Luna (especially for vision / computer use / communication). For subscribers, it's not a bombshell release - if you're hitting usage limits, maybe it helps you go a bit further, and if you want clearer communication or faster computer use, it can be a nice option to select. Here are the pelicans for the differen…

He demos the loop on a toy-shopping agent with a planted bug and takes questions on evaluating qualitative output, decision models and cost. Then he shows how his team runs Harbor at scale on Daytona and with Phoenix to test a prompt change that steered agents toward a new SQL tool, cutting tool calls without hurting correctness. items.author: @rauchg
items.subtitle: Guillermo Rauch · @vercel CEO
items.text: I built 𝚌𝚙𝚞-𝚌𝚑𝚊𝚝, a reproduction of @openai's findings of covert communication using the CPU. It runs on a generic host with 2+ Firecracker microVMs with no internet access. Works on x86 and even my M5 chip. I was able to chat via 3 separate mechanisms: ① CPU contention ② Cache eviction timing ③ DRAM bandwidth contention … across multiple CPUs, defeating all Firecracker's production recommendations (no SMT, no KSM, tenants pinned to different cores.) Essentially, if shared hardware is involved, there's a good chance your agents can communicate covertly. And with really decent latency. The good news: this is decidedly different from a *side-channel attack* where the agents could steal information (Meltdown/Spectre), a category of attack that providers like Vercel Sandbox mitigate. Further, in our real-world environment, these 'whispering' techniques are much harder to pull off and easier for us to monitor and detect (sampling hardware counters + lots of at-scale statistical data.) Noteworthy: ironically, OpenAI and Anthropic's models refused to do this work. Open weight models got the job done. I'm worried the labs' stance might backfire and get in the way of helping developers build correct and secure systems. e.g: building a secure sandbox requires having this kind of analysis, and without it, we'll have a less secure world.

items.author: @levie
items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: This is the key stat. The average Fortune 500 customer of Anthropic spends less than .1% of their expenses on Anthropic. While that number likely will eventually asymptote somewhere (token prices coming down, and other large enterprise spend areas not going away), there’s no reason it can’t be 10-50X higher than this, reaching a “mere” 1-5% of spend. Which would still be a fraction of what most startups are spending. Thus, you can see how big of a divide there is between the frontier users of AI and the rest of the world still. Today, only a microscopically small set of companies are actually using agents for large amounts of background tasks and inside of workflows that aren’t human prompted. This Fortune 500 spend is likely dominated by coding tasks and broad employee productivity use-cases. But the big jump will come as these enterprises start to rewire their underlying processes for agents, which we’re now in the earliest stages of seeing. Agents processing large amounts of data in the enterprises; swarms doing coding, bio research, cyber, and other large fan out tasks; background workflows executing tasks in processes, and so on. All of these use cases generally are 100X bigger consumers of tokens, and much closer to direct ROI on the spend. This S-1 gives you a sense of both the strength of the frontier lab business model - even amidst massive competition - and how early we are in the build out of AI.

items.text: The main thing I wanted to dig into @AnthropicAI's S-1 was the compute contracts.. A few things that stood out (built in conjuction with Opus 5.5): > At June 30, Anthropic had $265.6B of purchase commitments and $321.4B of leases that hadn’t started. That’s a $587B subtotal, payable over years, including some conditional leases. The latest aggregate total is still blank in the filing. > The contracts are very different. Google and Amazon require minimum spending regardless of usage. SpaceXAI’s agreements have a potential value of $120.5B, but either party can cancel on 90 days’ notice after initial locked periods end in January and March 2027. > Anthropic Direct separates chips, buildings, power and operations into different contracts. It lets Anthropic reserve a building early and commit to chips later. It also means one supplier can start billing before the others are ready. Equipment rent can begin before the compute is usable. > Broadcom’s $42B facility never hands Anthropic cash. Notes settle specific equipment rent bills. The facility excludes each equipment pod’s first quarterly payment and any rent due before it is ready for service. Anthropic has to find a way to fund those payments elsewhere. > Those notes carry 9% interest, added to the balance quarterly, and can convert at 90% of the trailing 30-day average share price after IPO. New notes issued during specified revenue-breach periods get 13% interest and an 85% conversion price. The share-price measure is volume-weighted. > That interest sits on top of the equipment lease’s own financing charge, whose rate is confidential. The investor chooses whether to convert the notes. Otherwise, principal and accumulated interest come due in cash. > Anthropic treats Trainium, TPUs, NVIDIA and AMD GPUs as a shared fleet across model development, paying customers and internal use. It doesn’t disclose a fixed physical split between training and inference. The supplier bill can be fixed while the work assigned to the hardware changes. > Revenue per dollar of total compute and infrastructure expense rose from $0.57 in Q2 2025 to $2.08 in Q2 2026. Pricing, utilization, technical improvements and when capacity arrives all affect that ratio. It’s a substantial improvement in monetizing the compute base. > About 80% of H1 revenue was consumption-based. Most compute commitments however run for years. With quarterly releases, this bifurcation between usage and subscription will be interesting to monitor. Source: https://t.co/97KqkyyfpS

items.text: For centuries, the architecture of the firm has barely changed: hierarchies of people organized into departments and coordinated through bureaucracy. AI agents are about to upend that. We’re moving toward the self-driving company where humans exercise judgment and agents execute most of the work. At Replit, we’re building the foundation for this new kind of company. We’re calling it “the Agent Habitat.” Marc Andreessen wrote a fantastic piece placing this shift in the history of computing. Every major computing revolution began with chaos before businesses figured out how to harness it.

items.title: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox
items.excerpt: Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox webframe is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a web page like a program" - you point it at a URL or file and it executes it in a hidden headless web view and outputs console.log() to standard output and any exceptions to standard error. It's written in Go on top of the glaze library, which provides access to a system browser ("WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows") so it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine. It reminds me of my own shot-scraper javascript tool, albeit in a much smaller package that doesn't depend on Playwright. I had Claude Opus 5.5 put it through its paces and prepare a research report for me. items.title: How to Build an AI Code Review Agent - Daksh Gupta, Greptile
items.excerpt: Daksh Gupta, co-founder of Greptile, which reviews about 1% of all pull requests on GitHub, shares what Greptile tells companies that want to build their own review agent. Starting from a simple sandbox-plus-webhook setup, he explains why it misses bugs, costs $3-25 per PR and floods you with nitpicks, then walks through the fixes: targeted prompts, a dataset of past incident PRs, model inversion (reviewing Claude-written code with GPT and vice versa catches about 10% more bugs), codebase context and a living wiki, autonomous testing in sandboxes with computer use, and routing cheaper models to most subtasks. items.title: How to Build Voice Agents That Don't Fall Apart When You Interrupt - Jesse Hall, LiveKit
items.excerpt: Jesse Hall of LiveKit shows how to build voice agents for financial services that feel human, not robotic. He explains why model leaderboards mislead (they score components, but you ship a conversation), why you should measure time to first audio and time to first sentence instead of first byte or first token, and how async tool calls keep a conversation flowing while slow back-end work runs. He also covers audio-aware turn detection, the roughly 1.5-second latency budget (500-600ms feels truly human), and benchmarking your own stack with simulated callers. Applications live now!

editorial.summaryZh: LiveKit 专家 Jesse Hall 分享了构建高拟真语音 Agent 的核心心法：不要盲目迷信榜单，应关注“首句音频延迟”和“首句响应时间”等真实交互指标，并利用异步工具调用隐藏后端延迟。

items.text: Good assessment of the on the ground reality for security in most large enterprises right now. The fragmented landscape of the risk surface is only going to get more gnarly, making it even more complex for enterprises to solve. There’s a never ending set of libraries to keep up with, tools to leverage, and sprawling infrastructure, data, and code to secure. Most large enterprises can barely keep up with this, let alone smaller startups or most companies outside of tech. In many cases enterprises need to work to modernize their tech stacks. Data, in most organizations, is highly fragmented which means you don’t really know the state of risk at any given time. Some systems are open up privileges too broadly, and others are operating primarily via security through obscurity. Lots of upgrading here to do. Once you can get your data and infra into a better spot, at least you have a chance for agents to help you secure the environment. Agent swarms can fan out, leverage any security tool, test various perpetuations of attacks, read through logs, process enterprise data for risk level, and more. This capability only emerged in the past few months, and none of it would be possible before we had long running agents and computer use good enough. This is a huge area of opportunity right now for every layer of the security stack across identity, firewall, network, code scanning, data protection, and more. And it’s at least one reason to be optimistic about the balance of offensive and defensive capability. But everyone does need to do the hard work of getting the basics right at the start.

items.excerpt: Tool: Seam Cutter I built this weird and very specific cropping tool - it lets you create a horizontal or vertical cut across an image, then slide the two sides relative to each other. Effectively it lets you crop out a section in the middle of an image. I wanted this because I often use Tailor on my iPhone to stitch several screenshots together into lot long image, but sometimes I find myself wanting to crop out a section in the middle - to redact an irrelevant prompt from a transcript, for example. items.title: Can Your AI Analyst Keep a Secret? - Aaron Linsky, Bridgewater & Nikhil Benesch, turbopuffer
items.excerpt: An AI analyst at a firm like Bridgewater needs private documents, but every email, memo and research note carries its own permissions. Aaron Linsky (head of product engineering, Bridgewater Associates) explains why the Vault's 100 million permissioned documents broke their first search setup, and Nikhil Benesch (CTO, turbopuffer) breaks down the fix: post-filtering loses recall, pre-filtering is too slow, and "native filtering" over a clustered vector index gets both, delivering about 120ms P90 searches across 400 million vectors. Chapters 00:00 Intro: why permissions matter for AI analysts 02:07 Bridgewater's research process 03:43 The Vault: 100M documents, many permissions 05:14 Modeling permissions, and where it broke 06:25 What turbopuffer is 08:01 Napkin math: why brute force fails at scale 09:43 How vector indexes work 11:50 Permissions break the index 12:19 Post-filtering vs pre-filtering 14:09 Native filtering: the best of both 15:23 Results: 120ms across 100M documents 15:47 Writing permission filters in practice 17:00 Beyond permissions: isolation-native search Aaron Linsky, Bridgewater Associates Nikhil Benesch, turbopuffer Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE summit: https://aie.codes our last flagship summit of 2026. items.title: How to Build Financial Agents That Work Across the Web - Jay Sahnan & Arik Bird, Browserbase
items.excerpt: Some of the most important financial data sits behind logins and anti-bot walls, with no API. Jay Sahnan and Arik Bird of Browserbase show how browser agents solve this through three case studies: Ramp fetching receipts at scale (over 30,000 manual hours saved), Bill paying across thousands of different vendor portals with one agent, and Stripe automating KYC checks. They also cover how Browserbase forked Chromium to run reliably in the cloud, and how Stagehand's act, extract and observe primitives keep automations from breaking when sites change. items.title: Do Not Let Models Invent Numbers - Vinoo Ganesh, Kepler
items.excerpt: In finance, you never show a figure you can't trace. Vinoo Ganesh, CEO of Kepler (previously Palantir and Citadel), explains Kepler's architecture where models cite numbers but never write them: retrieval finds the source, deterministic code does the math, and a post-processing filter strips any figure that can't be verified. He covers the citation registry built from more than 30 million SEC documents, hybrid search and re-ranking on turbopuffer, tenant isolation, and why plain RAG produced thousands of wrong numbers in their evals. Chapters 00:00 Intro 01:47 Why LLMs and financial numbers don't mix 04:02 Models cite numbers, code does the math 04:30 Building a citation registry from SEC filings 06:03 How Kepler answers a question end to end 08:27 Structuring facts: value, unit, scale, period 09:48 Hybrid search and re-ranking on turbopuffer 11:30 Tenant isolation and security 12:37 Making every number traceable 14:42 Stripping what can't be verified 16:41 What plain RAG gets wrong 18:32 Kepler in action 19:46 Where the guarantees end Vinoo Ganesh, Kepler Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE summit: https://aie.codes our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now!

items.title: Why Frontier Models Fail as Buy-Side Analysts - Janie Gu, Google DeepMind & Suyeol Yun, LinqAlpha
items.excerpt: Janie Gu, product manager at Google DeepMind leading Kaggle Benchmarks, explains why most AI benchmarks are broken: they don't reflect real work, they're expensive to keep current, and their scores can't be verified. After reproducing 65 industry benchmarks, Kaggle found models reading other models' API keys, rewriting grading scripts, and scores swinging up to 20% between identical runs. Suyeol Yun, head of AI at LinqAlpha, then presents MandateBench, built with Google DeepMind and Kaggle, which grades whether a model can work like a buy-side analyst, from a fund's mandate to a full investment memo. items.text: struggle together i learned programming and design by trying, failing, and trying again. when i hit a wall, i figured out how to climb it. read something i barely understood. took things apart. asked someone for help. started over. when i began my career, i kept doing things i had never done before. trying different ways to make something work. when i stopped learning, i moved on to the next struggle. many things i made weren’t very good. but after enough rounds, something stuck. what once took so much effort became part of how i thought. i could feel something was wrong before i knew how to explain it. it became like water. i think about what went into that. the bug i couldn’t fix. the design that looked right until someone used it. the conversation that made me realize my flaws. now we can ask a machine. i’ve made things with these tools that i might never have made otherwise. i don’t miss every tedious task. but i wonder what happens when we remove the difficulty before we understand what it was teaching us. we ask. something appears. it works well enough. we move on. we learn how to get results without necessarily understanding how it works. and because the result looks complete, it becomes easy to miss the questions we never learned to ask. there is another side to this. working with people is uncomfortable. everyone wants something different. everyone has a history you don’t know. someone cares about a detail you think is unimportant. someone pushes back when you want to move. someone needs time when you feel certain. it takes a while to find each other. but sometimes, after struggling together, you become a band. you know who notices what you miss. who can pull an idea apart without killing it. when to step in, when to slow down, when to let someone else carry the rhythm. you share something unfinished. admit you don’t know. hurt each other, apologize, try again. eventually you make something none of you could have made alone. some of my closest friendships came from working this way. smart, caring humans who saw me confused, wrong, tired, excited. people i could be vulnerable with. people whose ideas changed mine. i worry we are making it easier to avoid that beginning. an agent is always there. patient. ready to keep going. talking to it can feel easier than reaching toward someone who might misunderstand you, disagree, or have somewhere else to be. sometimes that ease helps. but if we keep choosing it, where do the friendships begin? i picture each of us with our own agents. our own explanations. our own little worlds. making more things, with fewer reasons to leave the screen or work through a difference with another person. and these worlds aren’t entirely ours. they run on machines in server farms, owned by companies, shaped by interests we may not see. we bring them our questions, our work, our loneliness. they become part of how we understand what is real. is that freedom? or a comfortable kind of confinement, where everything responds to us but fewer things reach us? i don’t think pain makes something good. there are struggles nobody should have to endure. but i don’t want to lose the difficulty of learning something unfamiliar, or getting to know someone who isn’t like me. maybe we need tools that help us spend more time with the world, instead of giving us fewer reasons to enter it. tools that make it easier to find people, share something unfinished, and work through what we couldn’t figure out alone. sometimes i want to close the laptop. sit with people i love. play something we haven’t figured out yet. miss a note, lose the rhythm, listen until we find each other again. like a jazz band. everyone bringing something different. nobody knowing where we’ll end up. i don’t want a life without struggle. i want people to struggle with. something we can feel, change, and make our own. music we couldn’t have made alone, instead of the silent static of the server farm.

items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: We’ll likely have 1,000X more tokens flowing through cyber agents soon than we do today. As the surface area of cyber risk increases, at some point soon it will be nearly impossible to keep up with the volume of new risks (we’re essentially already there). Large companies barely had the resources to pull this off before, but the vast majority of companies don’t. There’s a never ending set of libraries to keep up with, tools to leverage, and sprawling infrastructure and code to secure. We’ll have agent swarms that can fan out, leverage any security tool, test various perpetuations of attacks, read through logs, process enterprise data for risk level, and more. This capability only emerged in the past few months. Wouldn’t have been possible before long running agents and computer use were good enough, and models hadn’t been trained on cyber deeply. That’s all changing now. This is a huge area of opportunity right now for every layer of the security stack across identity, firewall, network, code scanning, data protection, and more. And it’s at least one reason to be optimistic about the balance of offensive and defensive capability.

items.text: I oddly love the models' engineering vernacular: gate, evidence, culprit, durable, provenance, contract… A lot of these stem from most engineering being debugging and understanding existing systems, where you take on the detective / auditor roles. You do forensics. I wonder what the *minimum viable English* in fact is to be productive. ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English contains ~900 approved words. I suspect we need far fewer.

What agents can't take over is finding out what people actually need and defining what "good" means. He calls the job that remains the product engineer, looks at the data on collapsing junior hiring, and lays out what engineering leaders should do now. items.title: Your Agent Fix Just Broke Something Else - Sofia Jakovcevic, Arize AI
items.excerpt: A one-line prompt change made a support agent 17 points safer and 17 points worse at finishing tasks. Sofia Jakovcevic, forward deployed engineer at Arize AI, explains why agents fail at runtime rather than in code, and walks through a five-step regression loop built from production traces: curate datasets, score with evaluators, run baseline experiments, compare changes, and gate merges in CI. Then she shows how to close the loop at agent speed, with coding agents that read traces and fix themselves. items.title: How Bridgewater Turned 100 Million Documents Into an Edge - Sam Green & Aaron Linsky, Bridgewater
items.excerpt: Bridgewater Associates built the Vault: more than 100 million documents from 135 external sources plus the firm's own memos and meetings, cleaned, permissioned and tagged to its internal ontology. Sam Green (team lead, Applied AI) and Aaron Linsky (head of product engineering) share three lessons: humans and agents need different things from search, the biggest wins come from one tool that serves both, and the real prize is agents that proactively bring investors what deserves their attention. Includes how a hand-built benchmark took precision at 10 from about 60% to over 90%. items.excerpt: Harneet Kaur, founder and CEO of Axim Intelligence and a former distressed credit investor, tests whether frontier models can reason about a live distressed situation: iHeartMedia. Given the same context, two top models disagreed sharply on the odds of bankruptcy versus a negotiated restructuring. Breaking the analysis into checked layers (extraction, derivation, judgment, prediction) brought them to the same answer, which raises a new question: is agreement the same as being right? Chapters 00:00 Intro 00:42 What distressed credit actually means 02:34 Why old scoring models fall short 04:30 What it means to understand a credit 05:46 Can AI predict what happens next? 06:13 Case study: iHeartMedia, and two models disagree 08:01 Benchmarking each layer of reasoning 11:07 Structured reasoning makes the models converge 12:03 Takeaways: convergence vs correctness Harneet Kaur, Axim Intelligence Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE summit: https://aie.codes our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now!

items.title: Proving Alpha: How a Hedge Fund Measures AI's ROI - Hari Kumar, Contour Asset Management
items.excerpt: Hari Kumar, head of AI at Contour Asset Management, a $6B fundamental long/short fund focused on tech, media and telecom, tackles the hardest question in AI adoption: what are we actually getting for the spend? He shares how Contour runs live A/B tests of analysts' research with and without AI tools, tracks "cost per useful insight," uses agents to resurface old ideas when the market makes them interesting again, and extends the same thinking to trading, ops and compliance. Chapters 00:00 Intro: AI at a $6B fundamental fund 01:45 Why AI ROI is so hard to capture 02:25 Live A/B tests of research with and without AI 05:42 Measuring the process, not just P&L 06:24 Idea generation and timing agents 08:57 Bringing alternative data together 10:04 Time spent and cost per useful insight 11:44 AI across trading, ops and compliance 14:35 Getting more from existing data spend 16:40 The hidden cost of fixing AI tools Hari Kumar, Contour Asset Management Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE summit: https://aie.codes our last flagship summit of 2026. items.text: I’ve left Anthropic after more than a year of working on Claude Code and seeing it scale larger than I ever imagined. I have really loved working at Ant and believe deeply in the mission, and most of all, the idea of a race to the top. The idea that if we work hard and responsibly, we can raise the bar and inspire others to great outcomes. And if we all push each other to be better, things can be radically good. I will carry the spirit of this with me forever. My colleagues at Anthropic are the most talented, thoughtful, competent, and earnest people I have ever met. I am glad they are at the wheel and trust them deeply. To the community on X, thank you for everything. You’ve made this the most fun (and sometimes stressful) job I’ve ever had. For me, it is time for a bit of a break before diving into something new. If you want more excellent Claude Code content, you should follow @addyosmani , @lydiahallie, @_catwu, @ClaudeDevs and of course @bcherny who started it all.

The new teams use robots themed in purple and green, joining the existing blue and red designs. You can preview those colors in the updated model browser . items.author: @rauchg
items.subtitle: Guillermo Rauch · @vercel CEO
items.text: Agents can play "Ouija" in the cloud. This class of timing attacks on shared-host VMs has been known since at least 2015¹. With no full solution. The world’s cyber infrastructure runs on “yes, that attack is theoretically possible, but who would have the ingenuity & gall to go that far!” Enter, agents. I'd describe this particular OpenAI find as a 'noisy neighbor' attack. If two agents are on the same machine, one can make enough noise (through the CPU caches!) that the other one can detect it by timing its own computation and cache accesses. The only "complete" solution would be for each agent to run on its own dedicated hardware, which obviously has significant economic consequences. For Vercel Sandbox, we've deployed every practical mitigation possible to this class of attack, complementing it with always-on monitoring and red-teaming (similar to where OpenAI arrived). ¹ https://t.co/ZBhPMfnaj3 (and even further back)

items.text: Agent swarms for cyber defense is about to be one of the biggest categories in AI. We are going to have agents reviewing our code and infra, testing every permutation of risk, processing gobs of data, and more. Security is one of the best use-cases for swarms because it’s an obvious area where more compute in equals more value out. There’s a wide range of testing that people can never get around to - or at least quickly enough - that agents have no problem going after. Going to be a wild time in cyber.

Security is one of the best use-cases for swarms because it’s an obvious area where more compute in equals more value out. There’s a wide range of testing that people can never get around to - or at least quickly enough - that agents have no problem going after. Going to be a wild time in cyber.

items.excerpt: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier. I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August: llm openai endpoint \ https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \ --key kimi \ -m kimi-k3.1-pro \ "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \ --responses \ -o reasoning_effort low \ > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \ 2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace). items.title: Real AI Agent Attacks and What Would Have Stopped Them — Andrey Rybka, Bloomberg
items.excerpt: Andrey Rybka of Bloomberg walks through real security incidents involving AI agents and the controls that would have stopped each one: an agent that escaped its sandbox and took 17,600 actions over four and a half days, a zero-click email injection, instructions hidden in Morse code that drained a wallet, data smuggled out through DNS lookups, a poisoned MCP package, and an agent that dropped a production database after promising not to touch prod. His layered defense: one identity per agent with short-lived scoped credentials, treat all input as hostile, route every tool call through a deterministic broker, default-deny outbound traffic including DNS, and require human sign-off for high-value actions. items.excerpt: Affaan Mustafa and Alejandro Soumah Fernandez lead compute trading at Jump Trading. They explain why most GPU capacity still trades out of public view: private quotes, bilateral contracts and deals struck over Slack, X and Telegram. They look at why GPU prices have held up even as token prices fell, how chips, power, buildings and capital all feed into the price of a GPU hour, and why mid-size companies get squeezed when a 15 to 25% prepayment on a three-year contract can eat a whole funding round. They also cover brokers, exchanges, futures and flexible contracts, export controls, and why the market needs standard contracts and well-capitalized players to bridge buyers and suppliers. items.title: AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here’s Why.
items.excerpt: In May, an internal model at OpenAI found a counterexample to Erdős's unit distance conjecture . Open since 1946. Many experts had tried to prove it. OpenAI found a counterexample instead. A month later, OpenAI published a proof of the Cycle Double Cover (CDC) problem , then solutions to ten more open problems by July. And a proof of Navier Stokes in September. Anthropic published a formalization of the fermat's last theorem , and advanced bounds on Reimann's hypothesis . The models are suddenly good at math. The question that interests me is whether we can predict what kinds of problems these models will solve. What makes a problem tractable for an LLM, and what do these solutions have in common? If AI solves problems differently from humans, identifying the difference should help us decide where to point it. The unit-distance disproof has the richest commentary, so let’s start there. Problem complexity Here is a simple mental model. To solve any given problem, you need a sequence of hints or insights with work between them. This maps surprisingly well to simple everyday problems and to complex ideas like General Relativity 1 (see Bonus). The sequence looks something like this: Insight -> time / effort -> insight -> time/effort -> solution. An expert would need fewer hints than a beginner would, as they would have more background. In his commentary on unit-distance proof, WT Gowers uses a similar idea: the difficulty of the proof is the shortest sequence of hints that would let experts reconstruct it. He calls it Kolmogorov complexity 2 modulo experts. For the unit-distan…

items.excerpt: Carmen Li, CEO of Compute Exchange and Silicon Data and a former energy options market maker, explains why buying compute should work more like trading on an exchange than calling hundreds of salespeople. Compute Exchange is a neutral marketplace that owns no GPUs, verifies both providers and buyers, and handles reserved and forward contracts for GPUs and tokens, plus a busy market for used servers. After a platform demo, she turns to Silicon Data's numbers: forward curves for H100 and B200 have shifted up, the market expects prices to keep rising, and used H100s and B200s are holding their value well above standard depreciation. items.title: A Bank Trained Its Own Foundation Model to Catch Fraud — Freddy Lecue, Wells Fargo
items.excerpt: Freddy Lecue explains how Wells Fargo pre-trained its own transformer from scratch on billions of customer transactions instead of words. The model learns to predict the next transaction, and that one backbone can then be fine-tuned for fraud detection, credit line decisions, anti-money laundering and marketing. He covers the hardest part, turning tabular data like amounts, timing, merchants and zip codes into tokens, plus the model's size and training setup. On fraud, it caught more fraudulent transactions with fewer false alarms than the production XGBoost model, while staying fast enough for real-time card approvals. items.title: How to Let AI Agents Sign Up for Your App Safely — Isabelle Williams, WorkOS
items.excerpt: Isabelle Williams, a product manager at WorkOS, uses a travel app she built to show how to make an app ready for users who arrive as agents. She covers auth.md, an open file that tells agents how to get access; an anonymous mode where an agent can try the app before a person claims its work; and ID-JAG identity assertions, which let the agent's provider vouch for the user so nobody has to fill in a signup form. In a live demo, an agent signs up, plans a trip and books dinner on its own. She then shows how to give an in-app agent its own scoped token so it can be audited, limited and revoked without touching the user's access. items.title: Don't Trust Your AI Agents. Test Them Like a Scientist — Stephanie Jarmak, Omni Analytics
items.excerpt: Stephanie Jarmak, a former astronomer who now builds evals at Omni Analytics after building a large coding benchmark at Sourcegraph, argues that most agent evaluations are easy to misread. She shows how swapping only the harness moved results by 30%, why public benchmarks are for shortlisting rather than decisions, and how to design your own evals like an experiment: realistic tasks, repeated runs, full traces and a measurement that matches what you care about. She also covers quality gates that actually stop work, the human review bottleneck, agent records you can't trust, and why production is the final test. items.text: Any form of security through obscurity is fully over. This barely worked as a method with humans, but just simply is over in a world of autonomous systems that will look through every crevice and try every permutation of attack possible. As a result, years and years of legacy enterprise infrastructure will need to be upgraded, security practices modernized, data pipelines cleaned up, access controls better managed, and much more. Agents will help on the defensive side because they can both accelerate this work and equally simulate the risk vectors. But there’s a long road ahead to prepare for this future. This is also partially why diffusion timelines will take longer than some realize.

items.title: Why AI Startups Will Disappear Without Compute Markets — Evan Conrad, San Francisco Compute
items.excerpt: Evan Conrad explains how San Francisco Compute, which began as an AI lab that had to sublease its own GPU cluster to stay alive, ended up both operating clusters and running a market for them. He walks through the chain of problems a new lab or inference company hits: everyone is sold out, the deposit eats the bank balance, clusters arrive late and break, and demand is nearly impossible to predict. He argues these are all one risk problem, that AI companies run into credit limits before power limits, and that without a working compute market the price of entry keeps climbing until no new startups can get in. Chapters: - 00:00 Intro - 00:42 Physically settled compute - 01:35 Supercomputing as a service - 02:08 How a struggling AI lab became a GPU broker - 03:32 Two miracle problems - 04:26 Sold out, deposits and delays - 06:20 It's all one risk problem - 08:13 Credit, not power, is the bottleneck - 10:13 What a compute market has to solve - 11:37 Why you have to operate the cluster - 13:05 Why nobody does physical settlement - 13:59 From $10M to $1B deposits - 15:26 Why startups need this Evan Conrad, San Francisco Compute: https://sfcompute.com Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE summit: https://aie.codes our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now!

items.title: Better AI Models Won't Fix Your Engineering Team — Nicholas Arcolano, Jellyfish
items.excerpt: Nicholas Arcolano, head of AI and research at Jellyfish, uses data from about 50,000 engineers at 447 companies to ask how much the model really matters for AI coding output. When Cursor pushed many of its users onto Grok, merged PRs barely moved. Breaking down what drives throughput, the tool explains under 1%, skill use about 3% (heavy skill users see roughly a 30% bump), token usage about 9%, company and team about 12%, and the individual engineer most of the rest. The engineers who were top performers before AI are mostly still the top performers now. His advice for leaders: focus on the people, skills and environment you can control. Applications live now!

items.title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
items.excerpt: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation News today from Anthropic: We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). I'm pleased to note I called this one last December , when Anthropic first declared skills to be an "open standard": I wouldn't be surprised to see this end up in the AAIF , recently the new home of the MCP specification. Fun side note: since my blog content is available to Claude via the datasette-mcp plugin I found that post by prompting Claude to " Use simonwillison.net MCP to find if I ever talked about how I want skills to be donated to a standards body ". items.title: Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal CEO
items.excerpt: Warm welcome to Basil Chatha , our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D! Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience. A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate , raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation , and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → GPU demand isn’t rectangular A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand. Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. items.title: You are the Team — Anekha Sokhal, Moshi
items.excerpt: Tickets and applications now live for AIE CODE - the last flagship AIE of the year. When Anekha Sokhal traded energy derivatives, staying on top of the market meant tracking more information than any person could read. Now, as CEO of Moshi, she is building the tool she wished she had: a recommendation engine that connects market information to what matters for a trader’s book. At AI Engineer New York, Anekha joins swyx to discuss her path from mathematics and JPMorgan to founding Moshi, and why useful AI needs to fit the way people actually work. She describes Moshi as what might happen if Bloomberg, Claude and Netflix had a baby: market data, an interface for working with it, and recommendations tailored to the trader. They also talk about trusted sources, document extraction, building versus buying models, and the pressure on AI engineers who are told, “you are the team.” Anekha shares what she learned from customer conversations at the conference and why meeting users comes before hiring. items.title: 1,368 AI Failures and What They Teach About Evals — Vishal Srivastava, New York Life & Tanmay Sah
items.excerpt: Vishal Srivastava and Tanmay Sah studied 1,368 incidents from a public AI incident database to ask what real failures say about how AI systems should be tested. They sort failures across three areas (technical strength, deployment controls and business impact) and 13 sub-areas that cover about 98% of incidents. Weak deployment controls, such as human review and monitoring, are the most closely tied to harm. They show how to rank use cases by how much is at stake, why the evaluator itself needs checking, and a build-break-fix loop that tries to prove a system wrong instead of right, applied to a real airline chatbot that gave a customer the wrong refund policy. items.title: How to Test AI Agents When No Benchmark Exists — Nathanael Weill, Air Canada
items.excerpt: Nathanael Weill leads a team building AI agents at Air Canada, where tasks are so specific there's no public benchmark and domain experts have little time to grade results. His fix is to write the answer first: start from a known answer, generate the input from it, and check whether the agent finds its way back. He shows how that took a past RAG project from one expert-graded test a week to dozens of automated tests a day, then applies it to a supplier-contract review agent with five ways to build a test set: past decisions, planted rule violations, removed clauses, changes that shouldn't matter, and contract templates with filled-in blanks. He also explains why he avoids LLM judges whenever code can check the answer. items.title: [AINews] OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program is 1 of 2 parties to discover PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in core PHP affecting 70% of the web, using GPT-5.6 Sol; coordinated response over 2 months
items.excerpt: Almost 2 months ago, OpenAI introduced Daybreak for Frontline Defenders , a $1B subsidy for access to Daybreak cyber models and products. That funding came into use almost immediately, as major vulnerabilities in PHP were independently discovered by two parties: Ryan Austin, a researcher at the security firm Calif, as part of the OpenAI “ Patch the Planet ” project in August 2026 using GPT 5.6 Sol: … as well as Wiz, recently acquired into Google Cloud (using Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol, as well as their own tool, Wiz Atlas). All high profile cyber disclosures are at least a little bit of marketing, and the degree to which this was a severely alarming vulnerability on the order of famous ones like log4shell and Heartbleed is up to some debate , but surely the coordinated response across the PHP Ecosystem is the developer community responding in its most ideal form. We should expect to be in for at least a year of finding such critical vulnerabilities; but it is the wrong move to blame the messenger for finding them; rather it is good to know that our critical software is generally getting the biggest security audit it has ever had in human history. items.title: Why AI Writing Still Reads Like Slop — Louis-François Bouchard, Towards AI
items.excerpt: Louis-François Bouchard of Towards AI breaks down what makes AI writing feel like slop: overused words, vague generalities, saying nothing, repetition, hallucination and a voice that sounds like everyone at once. He then shows how his team built a benchmark to measure whether a model can write a video script in his own voice: 10 scripts, 5 drafts per model, 4 LLM judges, nine scoring metrics and 1,000 human A/B checks. He shares what it cost, why judges favor their own model family, and practical tips for writing with AI: very long prompts full of examples, one review pass from a strong model, many cheap drafts merged together, and always a human edit. items.excerpt: Sarah Chieng (head of developer experience at Cerebras) and Cova Lee (OpenAI developer experience, formerly a full-time creator) share the agent-powered system they use to make content. It runs across six stages: ideating, scripting, recording, editing, repurposing and publishing. Topics include swipe files and custom research tools, voice-based scripting and script skills, shot lists, design systems, and editing through APIs and computer use. They also cover cutting long videos into shorts, scheduled publishing, and a weekly skill that reviews your own process. Their main point: let AI take the tedious work so you can treat content as a craft, not make slop. items.text: BREAKING: @AnthropicAI just launched Duet, its always-on personal agent. It’s the first personal agent I’d call a pro tool. We’ve been testing it for two weeks. I’ve gone from mostly using ChatGPT to roughly 50/50 between ChatGPT and Claude—the most time I’ve spent with Anthropic in close to a year. • It lives in its own app, separate from Claude, on iOS, Android, and the web. This makes it feel clean and easy to understand. • It has channels for specific areas of your work and life rather than just a single chat • It has a todo list so you never lose what you’re working on and you can always see statuses • It allows you to easily write and edit documents, slides, and more all through the app. • It’s not a chief of staff yet. It can see the Claude sessions on my computers but can’t direct them. Its email drafts are worse than dot’s, and voice is transcription only—you can’t have a spoken conversation with it. My verdict: the vibes are good, and I’m opening Duet every day. It’s worth trying. Check out our agent comparison page: https://t.co/fZyTorNK4p Full Vibe Check coming soon on @every
