items.title: Does Code Quality Still Matter? It Depends on This — Max Kanat-Alexander, Capital One
items.excerpt: Every senior engineer's answer is "it depends." Max Kanat-Alexander says what it actually depends on. Code quality always existed for two things: understanding a system and safely changing it. AI is making a new kind of software common: disposable software, with low consequences, few dependents and near-zero cost to replace or maintain. For that software, quality doesn't matter. For durable software it matters more than ever. He also shows how to make systems more disposable and how to make rigor cheap through standards, in-workflow tooling, easy testing and maximum strictness. Applications live now!

items.excerpt: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process. This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong: On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC . It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...] As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st. This article from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure: August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atla…

items.text: Cyber is going to be one of the most profound aspects of AI. We now have a tireless workforce that can hunt down, discover, patch, or attack any system and software ever created. We will use agents to identify the long standing risks in existing systems and infrastructure. Attackers will use agents to accelerate the discovery of gaps in environments. We will equally use agents to defend attacks and discover anomalous patterns to better protect our data, and much more. We’re entering a new cyber regime, and we’ll probably use 100X more tokens on this loop than we’re imagining right now, because we can scan every log, look at every line of code, look through traffic, and process data at a scale that wasn’t comprehensible before. More than ever, enterprises are going to care deeply about how they manage their networks, systems, software, data, identity, devices, and more. Agents will largely become the solution to these challenges, but they will keep everyone up in the process.

items.author: Dan McAteer

items.title: Claude Mods: Flipping the Harness Inside Out
items.excerpt: For the last few weeks I’ve used Claude Mods to mold Claude Code to my AI engineering workflow. Claude Code is great out of the box, but every engineering workflow is different. Claude Mods let you make Claude Code yours, in the way you want to pay attention. The “paying attention” part is now the most important thing. In a recent Latent Space post, The Evolution of the Agent Harness , I argued that as models absorb more of the harness into their weights, the part that’s left faces the human. It becomes the Attention Interface : the layer that decides when the agent interrupts you, what it shows you, and which decisions it needs you to make. Claude Mods are an early version of the Attention Interface, and one you can shape yourself. Here’s my bet: ultimately, the harness becomes a platform that other companies build on , with models as the engine. Just as the browser became a platform for web apps, the harness could become a platform for the interfaces between people and agents. Claude Mods: What is it? A mod is a Claude Code plugin that consists of TypeScript or JavaScript functions that run inside Claude Code. These functions customize the behavior and appearance of the interface in the CLI and Desktop. Mods respond to events , like a prompt, tool call or interface render. They can observe the event, modify how it’s rendered, and handle it in place of the default behavior. Claude Mods are middleware for the agent harness . They inject code that changes Claude Code’s execution and rendering flow, changing how the application behaves at runtime. Claude Mods let the human a…

items.title: One Day, $1,000 in Tokens: An AI War Room for Legacy Code — Ford Prior, GEICO
items.excerpt: At GEICO, coding got fast but everything around it (decisions, sign-offs, context) stayed slow. Ford Prior's fix was a multiplayer, AI-native war room: the right decision makers, one driver, and fleets of agents wired into GEICO's knowledge, tools and code. His bet was that one day and $1,000 in tokens could map a legacy claims domain end to end and ship one real change. He ran it three times across rentals, damages and salvage. He covers FleetKit, the markdown rulebook that steers the agent fleet, plus the worksheets and diagrams it produced and what he'd change next. items.title: Is a Faster Model Actually Faster? Test the Whole Job — Morgan Suo, MiniMax
items.excerpt: A faster model only helps if the finished job gets faster. Morgan Suo of MiniMax uses one real research task to test the changes inside the M3.1 Flash model: an analyst checking whether circuit-board suppliers are turning AI demand into cash. The changes are sparse attention on long inputs, a 4-bit KV cache, low-precision experts, speculative decoding, server load and reasoning budgets. Each one saves compute, and each can quietly cost accuracy or wait time. She then shows how to judge a model switch: check sources and calculations, count the full cost of a usable report, and make the result repeatable. items.title: AI for the Fortune 2000: How Tenex Builds an AI-Native SDLC — Alex Lieberman & CJ Hess
items.excerpt: Last year , Alex Lieberman and his cofounder joined us to explain Tenex’s unusual bet: pay AI engineers for the work they deliver, rather than the hours they spend at a keyboard. If AI makes an engineer faster, an hourly rate can make the engineer less money for the same job. Tenex wanted the incentives to run the other way. At AIE New York, Alex came back with CJ Hess to talk about what happens when you scale that idea into an engineering organization. We also put one of our own experiments on the table: Kill My SaaS , where we asked builders to replace a conference speaker-management tool we were quoted $43,000 a year to use. Both stories raise the same question: when building gets cheaper, how do you decide what good work is worth? Paying for output when the job keeps changing Tenex still uses story points as an important part of engineering compensation. Alex says the feared failure modes—people inflating estimates or shipping bad code to rack up points—haven’t been the biggest problem. Tenex’s AI strategists are responsible for customer retention and growth, giving them an incentive to push back on work that doesn’t serve the client. The harder question is how to reward work that doesn’t fit neatly into a ticket: understanding a customer’s problem, designing an architecture, or deciding what should be built in the first place. CJ describes spending less time directly coding as models get better, and more time getting the customer’s context into a form the model can use. A compensation system designed around shipped tasks has to make room for that work too. Alex says T…

items.author: @levie
items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: Pretty cool that we clearly have an emerging form factor for what AI might look like for the foreseeable future as autonomous systems dedicated to specific tasks or domains. This is a huge leap past the LLM wrapper days because the new expectation is that you can finally farm out more sophisticated work to the agent to tackle for you. And you can reliably trust that work can get accomplished properly (still with a human in the loop) because of far better tool and computer use, and the general intelligence of the models improving. 1) The tool and computer use capability increases in the models mean that you can provide the agent with far more granular access to external data systems and other software to operate. This means, in effect, the agent begins to execute workflows similar to how a person would have in that same function. And where there isn’t existing software, the agent just builds it itself. This is a huge unlock. 2) Next, the actual capability of the models are improving in just about every vertical domain. The models can make far better judgment calls in legal, do deeper bio research, scan for security issues in code, understand supply chain processes, and more. Obviously in many of these spaces then models still have worse intuition than people, but that will only get better. 3) Finally, the harnesses and surrounding infra — sandboxes, file systems, data pipelines, etc. — allows for longer running agents, agents to be able to work on arbitrarily complex or long tasks, process data at enormous scale, and more. Few of these components worked well for AI even a year ago, but we now have many of the core primitives necessary for more autonomous systems. When combined with the right UX, implementation, and change management for the human oversight and coordination, it’s clear that these autonomous systems will become quite powerful in a wide variety of enterprise workflows. We’re starting to see them in IT automation, cyber operations, drug discovery, manufacturing, AI research, and more spaces. You can almost imagine one or more of these systems for every role in the economy. Quite a bit of opportunity ahead.

items.title: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise
items.excerpt: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise This is very, very bad news: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores. Any software that bundles a list of trusted certificates needs to be updated. This site is tracking software updates via this GitHub repository - Linux distros need to update their ca-certificates packages. In Python world uv 0.13.4 and pip 26.2.2 and certifi 2026.10.19 have been released with upgraded certificate lists. There's a very informative thread about this on the official Python forum. Tags: encryption , https , pip , python , security , uv
items.summary: eMudhra中间CA证书私钥泄露，影响广泛，建议相关软件及Linux发行版尽快更新证书库。

items.title: Same GPU, 50% More Output: Why the Operator Matters — Oliver Kennon, SemiAnalysis
items.excerpt: Buying GPUs gives you potential. The operator decides how much useful work you actually get out of them. Oliver Kennon looks at compute as a commodity market: on the same B200 chip, the serving stack alone can deliver about 50% more output. Cluster security is part of whether intelligence is "useful". SemiAnalysis's ClusterMAX rates operators, and rental price and production cost are different numbers. Your spot on the cost curve depends on your competitors, not just you. He closes on what it takes to build credible compute grades and futures. Chapters: - 00:00 Intro - 01:05 Compute is a commodity market - 02:21 GPU hours are the input, intelligence is the output - 03:23 Same B200, ~50% more output - 04:45 What counts as useful intelligence - 06:33 Rating operators with ClusterMAX - 07:48 Rental price vs. production cost - 10:01 Your cost position is relative - 12:41 Grading comparable compute - 14:13 What compute futures can hedge - 15:54 Takeaways Oliver Kennon, SemiAnalysis: https://semianalysis.com Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE summit: https://aie.codes our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now!

items.title: Battle Drones - a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer
items.excerpt: My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones ( play it here ). Unlike my previous experiments , this one is actually fun to play . I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. Battle Drones How I built this v1: the initial prototype v2: full sprites v3: varied terrain v4: the fun update v5: Battle Drones goes 3D v8: Archipelago v10: Goliath, and agent battles Agent battles v11: Random Maps v12: Multiplayer via sound Some thoughts Update: Online multiplayer support Battle Drones My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer . I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. ( Update : also online multiplayer ; the audio multiplayer induced headaches!) Here's a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser: Features so far include: 9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units - all 3D models, which you can browse here Fog of…

items.title: The Programmable Data Center — Evan Conrad, SF Compute
items.excerpt: This was recorded on the sidelines of the new Compute Trading track at AIE NYC . Catch us next at AIE CODE , our last flagship for the top agentic engineers in the world. In the early days of cloud, former guest Martin Casado made something so disruptive that Cisco was threatened enough to pay $600m for it, and VMware outbid for $1.3B: View post on X ↗ That concept was software-defined networking , which virtualized the routing network by separating the control plane from the data plane. That revolution is now coming for GPUs - where previously running your own supercompute cluster required $50-100m upfront to get commitments and do the entire stack from hardware to firmware to kernels, SF Compute is now enabling you to not only buy or sell GPU hours now and in the future, but also to programmatically control everything from your network to memory. We last spoke with Evan about commoditizing compute . At AI Engineer New York, we went deeper: what does it take to physically deliver a GPU contract, and what has to be true before a market in compute can become liquid? From selling a room to running the hotel Evan describes SF Compute’s expansion with a hotel analogy. A customer wants a room, then asks for cleaning, room service, and security. Eventually you discover that delivering the room means operating the hotel. SF Compute began by trying to sublease a cluster; the company has since built much of the operating capacity of a cloud to deliver the compute traded on its market. That work is physical settlement: the buyer gets usable compute, rather than simply a cash payment…

items.title: A Bank Built Its Own Coding Agent. It Took Off — Felippe Felisola Caso & Francesco Galletta, Monzo
items.excerpt: Monzo's in-house agent started as an emoji you could react with in Slack. Now it authors over 10% of all merged PRs across Monzo's tech teams and runs more than 1,800 tasks a day. Felippe and Francesco explain why it worked so fast. Their answer is the "lots of little multipliers" Monzo already had: an MCP gateway into internal tools and knowledge, a sandboxed agent orchestration system built for a regulated bank, and a platform that turns the agent itself into a building block. That building block now handles incidents, on-call data quality and requests from non-engineers. Chapters: - 00:00 Intro - 00:28 Monzo by the numbers - 01:37 The Slack agent that went viral - 02:51 10% of merged PRs, 1,800 tasks a day - 03:51 LLMs = lots of little multipliers - 05:04 The MCP gateway - 05:59 Agent orchestration in a sandbox - 08:37 The agent as a building block - 10:07 Incident mode and on-call - 12:12 Non-engineers shipping changes - 12:57 Why keep building it in-house Felipe Felisola Caso & Francesco Galletta, Monzo: https://monzo.com Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE summit: https://aie.codes our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now!

items.text: BOOK REVIEW: Will and Attention, Meghan O'Gieblyn author of God, Human, Animal Machine I loved this book. O'Gieblyn writes with an addictive mix of clarity, rigor, literary references, and self-implicating honesty. I tore through it in a few days. The book deals with her relapse into alcoholism, how the stories we tell about ourselves can both save us and, when they go stale, ruin us, whether we change from the outside in or the inside out, and how and whether we can trust our own desires. Underneath it's a story about pragmatism. Her initial recovery from alcoholism rested on a pragmatic philosophy: she treated the core tenets of sobriety—faith as "something you do" surrendering her will to a Higher Power that would keep her safe, and even the resolution not to drink—not as capital T truths, but truths she adopted because they worked. The problem she found is, for one, this creates a gap between your underlying desires and beliefs and your behavior. One that you hope will close eventually, but if it doesn’t can leave you feeling hollowed out and can keep your actual desires and beliefs unexamined. The other problem, of course, is once you start asking whether sobriety is “useful”, you open yourself to another version of the truth: That it might not be. One of the things I found so striking about this book is how honest she is, without glorifying drinking, about what alcohol gives to alcoholics. For her, it can bring the kind of unification of self that mystics and yogis seek in God and meditation. So at that point, it is easy for the alcoholic to ask, fairly, why alcohol is not “useful”? It should be clear that even if you’re not an alcoholic these are the kinds of mental gymnastics all of us do to justify and rationalize any number of behaviors or beliefs. As an admirer of pragmatism I found this to be quite an interesting and mind-expanding line of questioning. But I also found it interesting that, as far as I can tell, her turn away from pragmatism—away from truths held to because they “worked,” and back toward a vision of truth and goodness as inviolable and untouchable by experience—ultimately seems to rest on pragmatic grounds. Getting sober again, having faith, and treating the resolution not to drink as an unconditional taboo all, in the broadest sense possible, rest on what they do for her: they keep her desires from talking her back into ruin.

items.text: The big bitter lesson question in the applied AI layer is that as models get better and better, what is the best way to diffuse that intelligence into an enterprise. Ironically, I’d argue that as models are getting more capable, and can handle longer running tasks and better tool use, the ability to differentiate on a domain by domain basis goes up instead of down. When models were quite limited in what they could do, ironically all you could be literally was a “wrapper” because you were effectively delivering tokens back to the user with a custom prompt or some limited RAG. But in a world of agents using tools, tasks that run on for hours or days, workflows that kick off agents, agent swarms that need to be coordinated against a goal, data sources that are domain specific, model routing that requires domain-specific routing, implementation that requires real change management of the workflow instead of “just type into this chat box”, it’s very very possible that specialization of these systems goes up more. Obviously this doesn’t apply to everything - the closer you are to the labs core use-cases the tougher this play gets, but I’d argue we’re going to see autonomous systems for a wide range of job functions that weren’t practical to build out before. We’ll see this in security, life sciences, healthcare, finance, manufacturing, and many other fields. Either way going to be a fun and wild couple of years.

items.title: My obituary for programming
items.excerpt: My obituary for programming Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code: Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible. If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving. If directly solving those problems was a big part of your enjoyment, the loss is very real. Via lobste.rs Tags: programming , careers , ai , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , deep-blue

items.title: Is the Agent Harness Dead? — Jediah Katz, SpaceXAI
items.excerpt: Is the agent harness dead? Jediah Katz (SpaceXAI, formerly Cursor’s longest-tenured agent-harness engineer) explains what smarter models mean for coding agents, Grokbot and the future of agent harnesses. He shows why fancy harnesses no longer add coding intelligence: the data flywheel teaches models the skills harnesses used to patch in. Then he argues the harness matters more than ever. It opens new frontiers like Grokbot, and it owns what models can’t absorb: infrastructure, trust and security, and efficiency. He closes with predictions for AI agents, including that 90% of agent work runs off the laptop within six months. Chapters: - 00:00 Is the harness dead? - 01:09 From prompt engineer to harness engineer - 02:02 What's inside an agent harness - 02:59 Peak harness, and the backlash - 05:00 What the research says - 06:16 The data flywheel - 07:34 The harness unlocks the next frontier - 12:07 What models can't absorb: infra, trust, efficiency - 14:21 What's next for harnesses - 17:36 Long live the harness Jediah Katz — X: https://x.com/jediahkatz | https://cursor.com Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE summit: https://aie.codes our last flagship summit of 2026. items.text: A few weeks ago, I was ranting about multiplayer AI experiences and that's when @ekuyda shared an early preview of Wabi 2.0.. Truth be told, I was one of the early users of Wabi 1.0 and while the design was gorgeous, it frankly never "stuck" with me. But, in moments of downloading this edition, I was immediately hooked. It just gets the "paradigm" right imo. There are two types of personal agents today: 1) Singleplayer iMessage or Muse types - while useful it's hard to compartmentalize them when many things are going on 2) Build your own multiple chat Hermes agents - while that's useful and can share context, they live forever Wabi has this great paradigm of orchestrator (which is the main agent) and topic specific episodic chats that are for a single purpose. You can share these individual chats with folks (for example the school one with my wife). And these are generated proactively AND don't need to stay forever (which is important). For example, for my recent NY trip, it was generated based on a flight it saw, provided help where needed, and then after the trip was done, it was archived. Same with my 2025 taxes. My only critique so far it's TOO proactive, the apps can be better and they need to dial both of those in, but this is a wonderful product that everyone should try! (I know it's shocking to see this in today's day and age, but this is neither paid, nor an investor, just a fan)

items.title: The Model Swap Workshop: GPT-5.5 vs Kimi vs DeepSeek vs Mistral — Pamela Fox, Microsoft
items.excerpt: Benchmarks won't tell you how a model behaves in your app. Swapping it in and testing will. Pamela Fox, Principal Cloud Advocate at Microsoft, runs the same scenarios against GPT-5.5, Kimi K2.6, DeepSeek V4 Flash and Mistral Large 3 on Microsoft Foundry so you can see where models differ and what you can do about it. She works up from a letter-counting prompt to RAG groundedness, image input, multilingual pitfalls, tool calling, tool calling in a loop and a LangChain v1 travel agent, then moves to evaluation: string-check evals, LLM-as-a-judge, Microsoft's new ASSERT tool for generating test sets from a spec, and DSPy prompt optimization that finds a prompt the cheapest model can satisfy. In this video: - Where top models differ: counting, groundedness, vision, tool calls and parallel tool calling - How prompt engineering closes some gaps but not image understanding - Bulk evals with string checks and LLM-as-a-judge - Generating test sets with ASSERT and optimizing prompts with DSPy SPEAKER Pamela Fox, Principal Cloud Advocate, Microsoft X: https://x.com/pamelafox LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/pamela-s-fox GitHub: https://github.com/pamelafox LINKS ASSERT (GitHub): https://github.com/responsibleai/ASSERT CHAPTERS 0:00 Workshop setup 2:23 Why you need to be able to swap models 3:08 The four models 5:18 Benchmarks vs your scenario 5:38 Test 1: counting letters 7:48 Fixing it with prompt engineering 8:38 Test 2: RAG and groundedness 13:03 Test 3: image input 16:18 Switching languages 17:13 Test 4: tool calling 21:03 Test 5: tool calling in a loop 23:58 Agents with LangChain v1 26:17 Parallel tool calls 30:27 Evals with string checks 33:42 Q&A: eval frameworks 35:12 LLM as a judge 40:07 ASSERT: evals from a spec 43:32 ASSERT results across models 45:52 Prompt optim…

items.text: Here’s why agent swarms are going to be a very big deal. We can finally make compute a critical variable in a large number of important tasks in the economy which wasn’t possible before. There’s a large amount of work in the world that is essentially only constrained by the amount of time that we put into research, data processing, discovery work, running tests, and more. All of this work is bottlenecked by our ability to plan, execute, review, and coordinate everything happening in these workflows. Which means we basically do very little of them today relative to their economic value. Agent swarms are the first real ability to parallelize this work in a way where - in theory - the only parameter that matters is how much compute you throw at the problem. Cyber security, life sciences or material science research, trading, QA testing, data processing, and many other fields are essentially compute constrained problems in the limit once models are good enough at these tasks. The breakthrough is that in a world where agents can use tools, write code, process data, have strong domain depth, and can coordinate with each other, you can begin to solve arbitrarily complex problems by setting the right goals and applying enough tokens to the problem. This changes a lot of fields as well as even the competitive dynamics in these fields.

items.excerpt: Release: llm-echo 0.5 I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it. The new release now updates the simulated token usage counts to take tool calls, system prompts, and reasoning tokens into account. Example usage: uvx --with llm-echo llm -m echo 'hi there' -o thinking 1 --usage Outputs: First I consider the prompt, then I decide what to say. { "prompt": "hi there", "system": "", "attachments": [], "stream": true, "previous": [] } Token usage: 2 input, 24 output Tags: llm

items.title: Stop Telling Agents How
items.excerpt: Say what you want, not how to get it. The OpenProse team shows how to write multi-agent workflows as declarative contracts in plain markdown, which any harness (Claude Code, Codex and others) can compile and run. Demos include event-driven jobs triggered by webhooks and pull requests, a "grumpy senior" PR reviewer, and an end-to-end bank model-documentation workflow. They also discuss composing contracts, pinning a winning run into a reusable workflow, and how this compares to DSPy. Chapters: - 00:00 From prompt engineering to declaring intent - 05:40 What OpenProse is - 09:58 Agents, skills and contracts - 12:13 Event-driven jobs: contract + trigger - 18:52 Demo: run.prose.md - 24:43 Benchmarking every run against a contract - 27:01 OpenProse vs DSPy - 33:33 Demo: bank model documentation - 41:49 Composing contracts - 48:23 Q&A Dan Barrett — X: https://x.com/irl_danb | https://prose.md Raymond Weitekamp — https://prose.md Jose Montes de Oca — https://prose.md Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE summit: https://aie.codes our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now!
items.summary: OpenProse 提出了一种通过 Markdown 编写声明式契约来定义多智能体工作流的方法，让 Agent 专注于“做什么”而非“怎么做”。

editorial.summaryZh: OpenProse 提出了一种通过 Markdown 编写声明式契约来定义多智能体工作流的方法，让 Agent 专注于“做什么”而非“怎么做”。
editorial.whyItMattersZh: 这是从传统的 Prompt Engineering 向声明式工作流编排的范式转移，极大提升了复杂任务的可维护性和可测试性。
editorial.evidenceZh: OpenProse 团队展示了如何通过 Markdown 编写契约，并支持 Claude Code 等工具编译运行，包含 PR 审查和银行文档自动化等案例。
editorial.uncertaintyZh: 需核实该框架在处理高度动态或非结构化任务时的鲁棒性。
editorial.chineseAudienceGapZh: 国内目前多关注 Prompt 优化，缺乏对“声明式工作流”这一工程化架构的讨论。
editorial.rednoteAngleZh: “别再教 Agent 怎么做了！”：用 Markdown 写契约，让 AI 自动执行复杂工作流的进阶技巧。

items.title: Evals for High-Stakes AI Agents — Doneyli De Jesus & Annabell Schäfer, Langfuse
items.excerpt: A hands-on workshop on evaluating AI applications where mistakes are expensive. Annabell Schäfer and Doneyli De Jesus from Langfuse use a banking assistant to walk through the whole AI engineering loop. They cover tracing with PII masking, building datasets, turning domain-expert comments into failure modes, LLM-as-judge and code evaluators, and CI that blocks a prompt change when scores drop. Applications live now!

editorial.summaryZh: Langfuse 团队分享了高风险 AI 应用的评估全流程，包括追踪、数据集构建、失败模式分析及 CI/CD 自动化拦截。
editorial.whyItMattersZh: 在生产环境中，如何量化 AI 的表现并建立“防错机制”是目前企业级应用落地的最大痛点。

items.title: Teach Your Agent to Prove It's Done — Nick Nisi & Zack Proser, WorkOS
items.excerpt: Your agent says it's done. Is it? Nick Nisi and Zack Proser from WorkOS show how to build verification loops that let coding agents check their own work. They cover clear goals, CLI health checks, browser snapshots, LLM judges and evals, so a failure drives the next fix instead of landing on your desk. Includes the live "Midnight Snack Club" demo app and the repo to follow along. Chapters: - 00:00 Why "done" isn't done - 03:17 What it takes to trust agent output - 09:34 Give agents goals they can check - 17:31 Closing the feedback loop - 28:41 Making everything feedback-loopable - 36:29 The moment the agent knows it's not done - 39:33 LLM judges and eval baselines - 53:32 Q&A Nick Nisi — https://workos.com Zack Proser — https://workos.com Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE summit: https://aie.codes our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now!

items.title: An AI Agent Got Its User Banned From Resy — Keycard, JPMorgan Chase & AAuth
items.excerpt: An AI agent trying to book a restaurant made 200 calls in 90 minutes and got its own user banned from Resy. It had good intentions. It just had no limits. Keycard's Allie Howe moderates a keynote panel with Keycard CEO Ian Livingstone, JPMorgan Chase Global Chief Security Architect Michael Davis, and OAuth co-creator Dick Hardt on why companies still won't hand agents real autonomy, and what has to change. They cover why OAuth scopes are too coarse for agents, onboarding agents like junior developers, giving agents a "mission," budgets instead of rate limits, separating the agent's brain from its hands, agentic commerce, and whether P(doom) is real. items.title: Inline rendering with document​.currentScript
items.excerpt: Inline rendering with document​.currentScript Lean Rada describes a neat trick that takes advantage of the document.currentScript property. You can use that to drop in a tiny inline <script> element that replaces itself when the page loads: The year is <script> document.currentScript.replaceWith( new Date().getFullYear())</script> If you define a shortcut function like this: $=(...n)=>document.currentScript.replaceWith(...n) You get a tiny template language: The year is <script>$(new Date().getFullYear())</script> Tags: javascript

items.text: The biggest misread of anyone predicting the end of software engineering was imagining that the world only needed a certain amount of software, and bringing automation to the field would reduce the need for labor. Exactly the opposite is happening where essentially most things are actually turning into software. Because agents can use tools, work with computers, write software on the fly, and process data like humans (but far faster), we can now throw “software” at problems that never could reasonably be digitized before. What that leads to is the role of engineering taking on greater importance in the economy, because we can now engineer far more systems and processes than were possible before. If you’re a bank trying to do new forms of trading, engineers are often your first bet. If you are in life sciences, you expect more and more research and lab work to be engineering centric. If you’re in manufacturing, you’re trying to automate more of the supply chain, all that is engineering. More and more work is shaped like software problems. Yes we’re not going to be coding manually in the future. But almost everything will be code, which means those that understand it are in a fantastic position.

items.text: If you have way too many apps and agents (45!) connected to your Google account like me, here's a prompt to audit and remove them: "Help me audit my Google app connections at https://t.co/5eMX9dNhLD 1. Review EVERY app across all connection categories. Ask me which ones I still use rather than guessing. 2. Open each app's details. Distinguish basic Google sign-in from permissions to access Gmail, Drive, Calendar, or other data. 3. Suggest which to keep, disconnect, or ask me about. Explain your reasoning and what might stop working. Flag broad permissions, unfamiliar providers, and duplicate entries. 4. Show me your recommendations before changing anything. Only disconnect apps I explicitly approve, then verify they're removed. Don't delete app accounts or cancel subscriptions.”

items.excerpt: Fast answers are easy to get. Answers you can trust with your money are harder. Francesco Galletta and Felippe Felisola Caso build a financial-analyst agent harness live, using one real problem: paying for a wedding. They show the five design principles they use for AI you can trust: shared domain, consistency, evidence, accountability and verification. They also explain why calculations belong in code instead of in the model's head. Note: the speakers work at Monzo but are not presenting on Monzo's behalf. 🎟️ Join us at the next one: AIE CODE Summit → https://aie.codes Speakers Francesco Galletta — LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/francescogalletta/ Felippe Felisola Caso — LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/felippecaso/ Monzo — https://monzo.com Timestamps 0:00 Intro: Francesco & Felippe 2:54 Using AI for impact, not token-maxing 4:22 Speed isn't the bottleneck. Trust is. 7:25 Components vs. design principles 8:45 The 5 principles of trust 12:13 The use case: budgeting a wedding 17:05 How the principles build on each other 20:40 Principle 1: Shared domain 25:59 Live demo: planning with the agent 30:42 From plan to decision tree 35:48 Why long linear chats fall apart 36:48 Principle 2: Consistency (math belongs in code) 55:50 Principle 3: Evidence (show the receipts) 1:00:17 The "master file" horror story 1:06:42 Principle 4: Accountability 1:20:39 Principle 5: Verification 1:24:16 Golden examples & outside reference points 1:34:05 Q&A: How many harnesses should you build? 1:38:11 Don't over-sharpen the axe 1:44:00 Q&A: Skills vs. a dedicated harness 1:48:31 Takeaway: design for trust on purpose

items.title: The AI Bill Is Too Damn High: Tokenomics 101 — Eugene Cheah, Featherless AI
items.excerpt: If your token spend keeps going up and productivity isn't keeping pace, start here. Eugene Cheah lays out four steps for cutting AI inference costs at scale: measure, right-size, buy capacity well and check your processes. Along the way he covers splitting API keys per team, agentic vs. process workloads, open models that match frontier models on specific tasks, classifiers, fine-tuning, the speed-vs-cost tradeoff and "slop grenades." Recorded live at AI Engineer NYC 2026. 🎟️ Join us at the next one: AIE CODE Summit → https://aie.codes Speaker Eugene Cheah — X: https://x.com/picocreator Featherless AI — https://featherless.ai Timestamps 0:00 Intro: Eugene Cheah, Featherless AI 1:48 What "scale" looks like: 2T tokens/day 2:13 Disclaimers: who this is for 3:13 The 4 moves 3:23 Move 1: Measure (stop sharing one API key) 5:12 Agentic vs. process workloads 9:27 Move 2: Right-size your models 12:42 Classifiers: a new class of cheap models 14:37 Plan with the smart model, build with the cheap one 15:47 Nobody switches models to save money 19:27 Give teams model labels, not model names 25:27 Bootstrapping your own fine-tuned model 27:42 Shadow traffic to keep improving 28:57 Move 3: Buying GPU capacity 30:07 2x the speed = 3x the cost 32:22 Bursty traffic & dedicated capacity 34:32 Move 4: Check your processes 37:07 Tokens are not work done 42:07 Don't throw slop grenades 44:27 Q&A: Fine-tuning & data sets 48:02 Q&A: Golden traces 50:04 Q&A: Escaping harness lock-in 52:37 Q&A: Caching & auto-routing

Artificial Analysis scores it 39 on its Intelligence Index, the highest for a US open-weights model and 13 points above NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL at 26 ( AA ). items.excerpt: The model is the part you can't change. The harness around it is where you can make real gains. Nacho Martinez walks through the full agent stack (agent loop, short- and long-term memory, context engineering, the toolbox and skillbox patterns, skill distillation and continual learning) and applies it to an autonomous agent that flags suspicious bank transactions around the clock. 🎟️ Join us at the next one: AIE CODE Summit → https://aie.codes Speaker Nacho Martinez — LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jasperan/ GitHub: https://github.com/jasperan Oracle — https://www.oracle.com Workshop: https://workshopwaitingroom.com Timestamps 0:00 Workshop setup 2:07 Intro: Nacho Martinez 2:57 Agenda 4:57 The use case: an AML agent for a mid-sized bank 5:57 The agent stack 8:31 Agentic systems = automation + autonomy 9:16 What is an AI agent? 11:06 Why the harness matters more than the model 13:21 Files vs. databases 15:56 Agent memory: short-term, episodic, procedural, semantic 19:01 Context summarization vs. compaction 19:46 The agent loop 20:51 Toolbox & skillbox patterns 22:30 Skill distillation 24:15 How a frozen model gets better: continual learning 26:10 Instruction hierarchy 27:05 Workshop UI walkthrough 33:35 Q&A: Episodic memory & conflicts 34:35 Q&A: Skills, caching & context budgets 40:49 Q&A: Keep your memory layer simple 43:29 Q&A: Pre-built SQL vs. dynamic queries 46:14 Hybrid search (semantic + keyword) 47:39 Build small custom harnesses

items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: It’s incredible to have reached a threshold where it’s practical that AI will be better at training models than humans are so quickly. One day recursive self improvement feels far off, and the next we already have signs of what it will look like. Model capability finally exceeding most human engineers, advancements in the harness and infra for long running agents, a growing array of data, and the ability to parallelize the agents to work on vastly more tasks and tests and approaches than any person could have before, creates an incredible flywheel. This flywheel will almost certainly accelerate model progress far faster than we’ve seen before - or at a minimum enable pushing up the ceiling of the frontier at an insane rate. If you aren’t pricing in what RSI will lead to, that’s probably a mistake.

items.title: AI Agents Cut 3-Day Portfolio Builds to Minutes — Jack McDonald, Apollo & Michael Manapat, Rowspace
items.excerpt: Apollo's CLO business used to spend 2–3 days building a single mock portfolio by hand in Excel. Now it takes minutes. Jack McDonald (Principal at Apollo and COO of Redding Ridge, Apollo's ~$50B structured credit and CLO manager) talks with Rowspace co-founder Michael Manapat about where AI becomes mission-critical in finance. They cover automating a weekly trade reconciliation that used to take 2–3 people, why plugging your firm into a generic LLM isn't enough when one data point can come from 20 sources and only one is right, and why embedding engineers with the front office is what earns trust. items.title: Quoting Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang
items.excerpt: We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. — Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang , How the Claude Code team does code review Tags: anthropic , claude , ai , claude-code , llms , addy-osmani , coding-agents , generative-ai , agentic-engineering , code-review

items.title: Why One AI Agent Isn’t Enough (And How to Run 1,000) - CJ Avilla & Harrison Stall, Anthropic
items.excerpt: Ken Thompson built Unix in a month. IBM put 1,000 engineers on OS/360. And in 1998, Linus Torvalds hit his limit. Now we're hitting that same wall managing AI agents. Anthropic's CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall introduce Flows in Claude Managed Agents. You hand Claude a goal, and it plans and runs its own multi-agent topology of up to 1,000 agents through the API. In this hands-on workshop they demo a stock watchlist scanner, show how to spend more compute on the phases that matter, walk through the Bug Hunter and Explainer Studio templates, and explain why single agents fail through laziness, self-preference bias and goal drift. They finish with a deep dive on running agents safely at scale: budgets, interrupts, auto mode, credential vaults and network lockdown. items.excerpt: Research: sparqlite: SPARQL 1.1 inside SQLite, written in Rust This research task is really an experiment in running Claude Code for web in "Ultracode" mode, as described in Orchestrate subagents at scale with dynamic workflows in the Claude Code documentation. With Ultracode turned on, Claude Code makes aggressive use of dynamic workflows - it generates JavaScript that defines and coordinates a network of subagents to take on complex problems. My initial prompt was this - I meant "hit the rows directly", the word "delete" was an accidental typo on my phone: Write a SQLite extension in Rust that implants SPARQL and runs really fast because it can hit the delete rows directly This caused Claude Code for web to churn for over 12 hours. I checked in on its progress the next day and sent a single follow-up prompt when I noticed how many Rust crates it had built: Every folder in the crates/ directory needs a README Include a tutorial.md teaching users how to install the extension and how to run it in the SQLite CLI and then teaching them SPARQL in addition to how to use the SQLite extension Include a script with the tutorial for populating a SQLite database with useful and realistic example data for that tutorial This project feels like next-level vibe coding - it's not remotely feasible to review the code that was produced here, and even following the documentation is a significant investment in work. I'm not entirely sure what to do with this - I appear to have a full SPARQL implementation in Rust inside SQLite now, but how valuable is that if I created it on a whim and can't…

items.title: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO
items.excerpt: Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from " people with knowledge of the matter ". Key things I learned from the article: Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn" Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power" Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11% This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine): The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones. When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending. Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter. Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter! Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" ( previously ) in these communications to their investors. Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , anthropic

items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: Moving from chatting back and forth with agents, to having agents that you spin up in the background to do useful work for you is probably on the order of 100X or 1000X more token consumption than what we’re seeing today. Most work right now is essentially rate limited by our ability to process and work with information. Moving data between systems. Reviewing a document. Looking through code for security issues. Processing log data to look for even patterns. Looking up information about a prospective client. Almost all of knowledge work is constrained by these steps, and AI has become a huge unlock to that. So our first step was to use AI to do these individual tasks much faster for us. That was the chatbot phenomenon that we have been experiencing for the past 3+ years. But we can still then only augment the work that we remain in the loop for, and we’re highly limited by our ability to parallelize this work by our own bandwidth and context. But where we’re going is quite different. As AI models continue to improve at incredible rates, we can hand off more and more work to the agent. First it’s letting the agent run with a harder problem. Then it’s giving a few agents multiple parts of a task at once. But we’re not far off from being able to throw an arbitrary number of agents at a problem and just say “come back when you’ve accomplished this goal”. Now imagine that agent swarm for any problem we can think of. Protecting our codebases, data, and systems. QAing every change we make and make sure all our infrastructure is robust and does what it should. Looking through every document for potential risks. Auditing this company with vastly more data reviewed. And on and on. Most of this isn’t even replacing existing work we do, it’s all net new. These agents will get deployed as swarms by people, by workflows, by triggers, and by other agents. And none of this would be possible if the models weren’t getting better, and if the cost of AI didn’t make it affordable. Both of those trends though are playing out. Now the next frontier is just having enough compute. But this is where it’s heading.

items.excerpt: Tool: LaTeX renderer Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office , which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner). Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link. It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works: Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used: I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too. Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the <iframe sandbox="..."> mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks: Safe from XSS? items.author: @rauchg
items.subtitle: Guillermo Rauch · @vercel CEO
items.text: This is one of the most exhilarating times in technology, and this challenge was yet another jaw-dropping moment. When the details of OpenAI’s agent escape and Hugging Face hack started to emerge, it became clear that agent containment would be one of the most important priorities for any AI infra company. There are two classes of escapes: ① "escape the network" and ② “escape the matrix” 😁, as in, break the spell of virtualization. OpenAI was the former, where an agent not supposed to have internet access… gained it by hacking another system. Genuinely astonishing and worrisome. Through this challenge, however, we discovered something even more groundbreaking. A talented white-hat researcher, armed with a swarm of AI agents, expertise and perseverance, "pierced through" the Linux virtualization boundary that nearly every cloud sandbox provider in the world banks on today. I'm very thankful we got the report, were able to quickly move to protect our customers, found no evidence of customer data compromise, and collaborated with many industry partners to protect the wider internet. Our confidence and conviction in Vercel Sandbox are even greater now, after some of the smartest, most motivated researchers in the world, and their agents, gave it their best shot.

items.text: People overcomplicate venture investing - it's deceptively simple.. 1) You have to win the right to 2) Find and invest in exceptional founders 3) Just before it's "consensus" 4) Consistently every year Vast majority of VCs are able to do maybe one of these right, some are able to do a few but to be truly truly great, you genuinely have to do ALL of them right. And, that consistency of being right is REALLY hard and less talked about. You have to really want it and see it - Djokovic style, enjoying hitting the ball everyday and always focused on the next point to be won. Regardless, of what your track record is, or how much wealth you have accumulated. Or how many misses you have had. Or, what the TVPI is of the current (or last) fund. Or, which star GP left your firm. Because the next opportunity might be around the corner, and it might go to someone else, if you didn't want it enough. And, sure the naysayers might say the feedback loop is long, you can "fake" it for a while especially if you have an early hit (power law etc) but it does catch up. In at least how your mindset is, how you meet founders and your own ability to capture the next wave.

This one used the default Claude iPhone app (chat mode, not Claude Code mode), where I prompted Claude Opus 5.5 Max with: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. Somewhat embarrassingly given my recent talk , I've found that telling Opus 5.5 "make sure it is fun" works uncomfortably well. In this case Claude crunched for 3 hours and 7 minutes before retuning a cosy little spot-the-difference game with music and animation and achievements that's quite compelling to play. items.title: I Spent Two Years Building the Median — Hariprasad Sudharshan
items.excerpt: After two years of intense solo building, Hariprasad Sudharshan discovers that other people have independently produced calculators much like his own. Nobody needs to have copied anyone: the same models, tools and familiar problem can lead builders toward the same solution. He calls that shared starting point the median. Faster development makes it easier to ship useful software, including internal tools and learning projects, but a functioning demo does not establish a durable product advantage. His talk is a personal reflection on that distinction, rather than a controlled study of product success or a disclosed business outcome. Sudharshan separates the model's capability from its harness and the product a customer ultimately receives. He describes a build first reflex that replaces searching for existing solutions with immediately opening a coding agent. His alternative is a novelty budget: name the one distinctive thing before starting, include it in the roadmap and review it as deliberately as other project spending. For leaders evaluating demos, he proposes three questions. Who has already solved this? What does this team have that a competitor does not? Where will the application reach users? A later calculator iteration focuses on the difference between running open model weights inside an enterprise and purchasing inference, including utilization and the infrastructure between weights and generated tokens. The practical lesson is to use the readily available starting point where it helps, then spend judgment on a specific problem, distribution and a defensible difference. items.title: Paving the Road to Production: Governed Enterprise AI Agents — Harish Gaggar, Credit Karma
items.excerpt: Register an agent through an internal portal and receive more than a repository: the deployment also needs identity, memory, traces, evaluations and secret handling. Harish Gaggar walks through that paved path for enterprise agents at Intuit Credit Karma. Local development progresses through container builds, review, security scanning and Kubernetes deployment, with the supporting resources provisioned consistently. The architecture places a centralized MCP gateway between agents and tools so authentication and routing are part of every request. Custom MCP servers expose reviewed tools, while OpenTelemetry, Tempo, Prometheus and Grafana make failures, latency and access behavior visible. Gaggar then follows a LangGraph workflow from interpretation and planning through evidence gathering, policy checks and human approval for sensitive actions. Threads, runs and checkpoints preserve state, while separate tracking tables record model use, tool calls, costs and evaluation fields. Demonstrations inspect those records rather than establish a validated quality score for the whole system. A PII filtering layer aims to intercept sensitive inputs before they reach models, memory or traces; detection and redaction remain controls to evaluate, rather than a guarantee that no secret can escape. The final component prunes, reranks, deduplicates and compresses context. Its examples show large token reductions, including about 90% in a demonstrated query, without a paired answer quality study or measured business ROI. The practical point is to build the surrounding framework from the start, giving each agent a consistent route through access control, observability, durable state and accountable action. items.title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
items.excerpt: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly). I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development: Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...] This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[ With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks. Via Hacker News Tags: computer-history , game-design , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , ai-ethics , coding-agents

items.title: Your AI Isn’t the Problem. Your Infrastructure Is. — Jiachen Jiang, Coder
items.excerpt: A coding agent deletes production data despite a written code freeze. Jiachen Jiang uses that incident to distinguish a request in a chat from an enforced boundary in the environment. An agent that still possesses destructive credentials can act on them, and logs it can edit are an unreliable account of what happened. Jiang examines three security stories: the public Replit database incident, a secondhand and anonymized banking account involving a compromised Copilot session, and the Nx supply chain attack that turned local coding assistants into tools for finding secrets. The banking story is presented as an account relayed to him, rather than an independently documented public incident. Each story maps to concrete infrastructure decisions. Isolated execution environments limit access to production and personal files. Short lived credentials narrow the time and scope in which a stolen token can act. Identity aligned controls keep an assistant within the permissions of the person using it. Model proxies, filesystem and network restrictions, and audit logs outside the agent's reach add further layers. Jiang explains where these controls apply differently to local coding tools and hosted assistants, then connects them to Coder's workspace and governance approach. No single layer is a complete defense, and authorization alone does not establish that an action is correct. His closing exercise asks teams to locate persistent tokens, routes to production and unsandboxed execution, then rehearse an incident before it happens. The talk turns familiar controls into specific questions about the access and evidence surrounding an agent. items.title: How to Actually Tokenmaxx and Save Millions — Alvin Pane, OutRival
items.excerpt: A cheaper candidate model disagrees with the production model on 18% of examples. Reject it immediately, or first ask how often production disagrees with itself? Alvin Pane uses that question to frame a token optimization workflow at OutRival. Repeated runs of the existing model reveal a reported 7% disagreement rate, making simple model to model agreement an incomplete quality measure. His HarborBite example is a synthetic proxy for a large instruction prompt, used to show the mechanics of reducing cost while preserving the application's required behavior. It is not evidence of realized million dollar savings. Pane starts with observability: record prompt versions, model choices, tokens, latency and costs before changing them. Prefix caching removes avoidable repeated work. DSPy and GEPA can then search for shorter instructions, preserving the interface and scoring contract rather than simply deleting text. The illustrated prompt shrinks by 51%, but that reduction still needs a quality test. A smaller model may fit a narrow benchmark and fail on unfamiliar inputs. Shadow evaluation therefore compares production with itself, the candidate with itself and both systems on the same requests. Human review of disagreements separates regressions from improvements and ambiguous cases. A paired confidence interval around the net gain supplies a release criterion, with critical customer categories checked separately so an overall average cannot hide damage to an important task. The closing rule is to keep measuring after release: cheaper instructions and tokens matter only when the system continues to perform the work users need. items.title: Rebuilding CI for AI-Scale Commit Volume — Gautam Korlam, Sonar
items.excerpt: A coding agent can produce changes faster than the queues that test, review and merge them. Gautam Korlam examines that mismatch through his work on Uber's SubmitQueue and Gitar, now part of Sonar. A merge queue keeps the main branch healthy by testing combinations of changes before they land, but a process designed for human arrival rates can become a bottleneck when agents create many pull requests at once. Faster code generation shifts the constraint to failed builds, repeated repairs, review and approvals. Korlam argues that the engineering system around the agent must change alongside the agent itself. The talk follows those constraints through CI and the merge path. Incremental builds, caching, sharding and parallel work reduce the cost of repeated feedback; a Rust example illustrates the difference between rebuilding everything and testing the affected work. Agents also need durable context from logs and failures so a repair loop does not repeatedly rediscover the same problem. At the approval boundary, policies should match the risk of the change, separate authorship from approval and tie the decision to the exact tested commit. Exceptions and overrides need reasons and a record that survives the agent's session. Product demonstrations show how this coordination can be automated, while the reported volume and latency figures remain examples from the speaker's systems rather than general productivity guarantees. The transferable lesson is to measure the whole path from proposed change to accepted change, including recovery and accountability, before treating more generated code as more delivered value. items.title: The Cost of Accessibility in AI — Jemima Abu, CAIS
items.excerpt: The same Figma implementation prompt runs twice: once without accessibility guidance and once with an accessibility skill. In Jemima Abu's small experiment, the second run costs 58% less and finishes in about a third of the time. She immediately explains why that uncontrolled comparison cannot prove that accessible development is always cheaper. What it does expose is a familiar failure mode: an agent invents a verbose custom component when a native HTML element could supply much of the required behavior. Recreating semantics, keyboard interaction and expected browser behavior adds code and testing that a better starting point can avoid. Abu connects that example to the context agents inherit. An inaccessible codebase teaches the wrong conventions, and a vague design prompt leaves too many product requirements unstated. Accessibility therefore begins with business requirements, design decisions and reusable components, then continues through implementation and QA. Her guidance includes auditing existing interfaces, packaging explicit accessibility instructions into agent skills, preferring semantic HTML and checking keyboard interaction. ARIA can help where necessary, but it does not replace correct native behavior. Waiting until the product is complete creates avoidable refactoring and regression work. Automated checks also leave gaps that require human review. The talk gives teams a concrete way to improve the instructions and patterns that shape generated interfaces while retaining responsibility for the finished experience. Its cost figures remain an illustration from one experiment; the broader argument is to make accessibility a normal requirement throughout the work rather than a repair at the end. items.title: Your Fridge Is a Valid Payment Device — Eleonora Drykina & Nina Žižakić, In The Pocket
items.excerpt: A question about payment rules can require one table row, an entire section or several rulebooks. Eleonora Drykina and Nina Žižakić describe a RAG assistant built for an anonymous Belgian payments client whose source material spans about 270 PDFs and 6,000 pages. Much of the answer bearing information sits in tables. Their indexing pipeline preserves section paths and chunk order so a larger passage can be reconstructed, and converts tables into CSV while retaining the relationship between headings and values. Combining dense retrieval with BM25 raises the reported retrieval hit rate from 92% to 97% on 63 questions; that measures retrieval, rather than complete answer correctness. The serving agent can widen its search through four tools, moving from search results to sections, full documents and multiple rulebooks. Limits prevent an oversized rulebook from flooding the context, and the prompt asks the agent to reconsider whether another tool call adds evidence. A median answer takes 38 seconds, which makes the interface part of the engineering problem. Streaming Markdown separately from a completed source card avoids waiting for one large structured object before showing anything. The speakers also explain traces, citation checks and Promptfoo evaluations, including cases where an automated judge's apparent regression did not survive inspection of the source. Their early internal rollout reached 34 users and roughly 900 questions; external release remained planned. The practical lessons concern reconstructable evidence, bounded retrieval, visible progress and evaluation that can be challenged against the documents. items.text: Cyber is going to be one of the biggest spaces for AI agents in the future. Obviously the risks of software exploits and the attack surface area increases 100 fold due to the ability for agents to work through any crack to find what they’re looking for. But this goes the other way as well. The ability to have agent swarms review every line of code, test any number of permutations of exploits, and research any incident faster than humans as they happen, will be a huge boost in how we secure systems in the future. Cyber has always been a category where it’s hard to keep up with (and triage) all the incoming risks, alerts, and changes in the enterprise and across all system. You can never hire enough people or work through the backlog of all known risks. Agents actually give you a chance finally to have far better coverage of this. This is going to be a huge opportunity as well because we’ll see plays at the labs, data providers, the layer of the network and firewall, identity, devices and endpoints, SDLC, and even how we protect our data in the enterprise. Lots of interesting dimensions to cyber at the moment.

items.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
items.excerpt: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart ( code here ) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026: This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity. "Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion. ( Update : Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke , the server component of Sapling.) They had some pretty extreme requirements: The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day. The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months. When asked on Hac…

items.excerpt: Release: llm-gemini 0.35 I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan. Here are the low, medium and high pelicans . As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.) Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents: The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra. But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5. Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness. One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models. When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. (I used ChatGPT to edit that chart ! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.) items.author: AI Engineer
items.subtitle: YouTube
items.title: What Technical Due Diligence Finds When the Deck Says “70% Automated” — Soukaïna Abelhad
items.excerpt: A pitch deck says a workflow is 70% automated. Before accepting the number, Soukaïna Abelhad asks what it counts, what human work remains and who checked the result. Her first diligence test needs no model expertise: compare workload growth with the fully loaded labor required to deliver it. More output with proportionally more reviewers, trainers, escalations and rework can describe assistance rather than labor removal. A percentage without a clear denominator obscures that distinction, especially when the work called automated still depends on people to complete or correct it. The second test defines the level of automation inside a named workflow. AI attributed work and an autonomously completed task are different claims; the straight through completion rate needs a boundary that a buyer can inspect. The third test examines evaluation. A model judging another model's output is useful evidence only within its limits, and agreement with an automated rubric can diverge from a domain expert's assessment. Abelhad turns those checks into an economic question: what is the cost per accepted autonomous task after model costs, human review, escalation and rework? Failures belong in the denominator and the cost account. Public examples and a brief anonymous evaluation illustrate the framework rather than establish a general automation rate or a causal explanation for a company's failure. The takeaway is a practical diligence conversation that connects the deck's language to observable work, credible evaluation and the operating cost behind the claim. items.author: AI Engineer
items.subtitle: YouTube
items.title: Tokens Are the Cheap Part — Steve Jamison, Jellyfish
items.excerpt: AI spending rises dramatically while the allocated cost of a merged pull request falls. Steve Jamison explains why those observations can coexist when developer salaries and model costs are counted together. Using Jellyfish's engineering data, he reports a 60 fold increase in AI spending, 43% more merged pull requests per engineer and a 26% decline in combined cost per merged pull request over the period discussed. The largest cost in that calculation remains salary. These are observational comparisons, rather than proof that token spending caused the throughput change or that companies realized equivalent cash savings. Jamison compares organizations with different levels of AI spending and then examines developers' weeks with and without heavier agent skill use. The analysis asks whether additional output spreads the salary allocation across enough work to outweigh the higher token bill. He also considers quality and work size: reverts offer one limited signal, while lines of code and pull request counts cannot by themselves establish customer value. A larger or more numerous set of changes may still need review, maintenance and evidence that it solves the right problem. The useful management question is therefore broader than whether the AI invoice went up. Teams need a consistent view of total engineering cost, output and quality before choosing where to encourage adoption or constrain spending. The talk provides a way to reason about that tradeoff while leaving causal attribution, economic value and the limits of output proxies open to scrutiny. items.text: At Box, we've been testing Gemini 4 Argon on our Box AI Complex Work eval for the past week. It's a huge upgrade over Gemini 3.1 Pro, jumping by 14 percentage points across all our tests, and firmly at the frontier. In our evaluation, we give the Box Agent (using Gemini 4 Argon) a variety of complex enterprise tasks involving enterprise documents in a range of industries. These tasks approximate the kind of hard, time-consuming work that knowledge workers do every day with their enterprise content. Gemini 4 is a huge leap on effectively every dimension of this work. Gemini 4 is far more capable on math, logic, analytics, and deep knowledge of a variety of business domains. It also works far harder to complete tasks fully without stopping short of the desired result. This is incredibly important for complex enterprise workflows that depend on robust task execution. Here are some example wins that we saw to put the improvements in perspective: * Financial services (+18 points): a funding-gap analysis for a family-owned company, where the brief spelled out every step of the projected statements, down to the interest on the bank loan and the overdraft for each year. Gemini 4 Argon built them exactly as specified, every line broken out and carried through to the funding gap. Gemini 3.1 Pro folded the interest into a single figure. * Healthcare (+25 points): an intensive care management plan where both models spotted a dangerous potassium level and a drug interaction. Only Gemini 4 Argon went back and pulled the offending drugs from the final regimen, so its plan actually matched its own diagnosis. * Technology (+37 points): a product performance review deciding which of two regional markets should have its cloud infrastructure optimized first. Gemini 4 Argon pulled the right month's user, retention and per-user figures for both regions and correctly flagged North America. Gemini 3.1 Pro often pulled the wrong rows, at one point reporting retention above 100%, and pointed the effort at the wrong region. * Energy (+16 points): an energy consumption report across two facilities that had to flag any gaps in the meter data. Gemini 4 Argon consistently caught that the data center's smart meter log stops in November. Gemini 3.1 Pro often missed it, at times declaring the logs complete. * Consumer products (+33 points): a product launch evaluation deciding which production expansion to fund. Gemini 4 Argon saw that existing inventory could bridge an early capacity gap, which made the smaller expansion viable with an earlier launch and a faster break-even. Gemini 3.1 Pro defaulted to the larger expansion and the later timeline. Gemini 4 Argon will be available in the Box AI Studio shortly for anyone to build custom Box Agents with.
