items.title: The Agent Works. Does Anyone Trust It? — Michele Grant, Leading at Scale
items.excerpt: An agent's reports match the analysts' work during a pilot, yet the steering committee still has to decide whether it should operate in a core business process. Michele Grant uses an illustrative acquisition integration scenario to examine that decision. The question moves beyond technical accuracy to measurable value, accountable ownership and evidence for greater authority. A faster report is useful only if it changes a decision or releases capacity that the organization actually redeploys. Her framework starts with a baseline for reporting time, analyst capacity, operating cost and the detection of material issues, so an attractive demo does not become its own business case. Grant separates the people who operate the workflow, oversee its risk and provide independent assurance. A Human Works Standard records what the agent may do, where human judgment remains necessary and who must intervene when something goes wrong. An auditable decision log, a maintained inventory of agents and dependencies, and an autonomy scorecard make those boundaries reviewable. Financial calculations stay in deterministic code while the model helps with narrative and interpretation. Authority advances through shadow operation, reviewed drafts, exception handling with sampling and finally exception focused review supported by independent checks. At that last stage, missed issues matter as much as flagged ones. A falling override rate can reflect weaker review rather than better performance. The acquisition values and capacity examples explain the operating framework; they are not disclosed results from a completed deployment or proof that the agent created the projected synergies. items.title: Deploying AI Inside a Bank Is Not an Engineering Problem — Paden Gayle, Applied AI Engineers
items.excerpt: A bank's document exception assistant produces a convincing demo, but security, data owners and risk reviewers still cannot approve it. Paden Gayle uses that hypothetical project to show why a working model does not establish a route into production. The missing decisions concern where the system runs, who authorized the documents, who reviews a wrong exception and which existing controls the workflow must satisfy. Drawing on his engineering experience, Gayle makes discovery part of the build: find the people who own those decisions in the first week, then define the smallest useful system they can evaluate. When a customer cannot supply a complete specification, his method is to shadow the work, draft a concrete workflow and shrink it with the control owners. Autonomy starts with the least authority needed to solve the problem. A drafting assistant can gather evidence about errors, overrides and recovery before anyone grants it permission to take further actions. Gayle also outlines an evidence pack covering intended use, data lineage, failure modes, results by segment and accountable controls. Original inputs and outputs belong in that record; rerunning a model later cannot reconstruct exactly what happened. Aggregate performance can conceal a poorly supported document type or user group, so weak segments need explicit restrictions. The closing checklist turns unresolved approval decisions into named owners and next steps. It is a planning aid for deployment, rather than a claim that the illustrative bank project shipped or that a checklist guarantees approval. items.title: Every Building Is a Balance Sheet: Spatial Memory for Real-World Assets — Jordi Spranger, Spranic
items.excerpt: Two scans of the same kitchen reveal that three chairs have moved. The change can be queried against the captured scene, with a reference back to the observation. Jordi Spranger demonstrates the idea behind Spranic's spatial memory: turn a walk through a building into a record of its objects, relationships and changes over time. A conference hall scan provides a second example. Instead of leaving the evidence scattered across photographs and PDFs, the system stores a semantic representation in a graph that can connect observations from repeat visits. Questions such as where to find a radiator or a drinking glass become queries against that representation. Spranger frames the problem around the gap between frequently updated financial records and infrequently updated knowledge of the buildings underneath them. He explains how an off the shelf sensor captures a space, how repeat walks align along a timeline and how object changes can feed downstream workflows. Maintenance, interior design, robotics and insurance are proposed uses of the same underlying asset record. For insurance, he sketches an initial inspection and renewal comparison that could inform a more specific policy. These are proposed applications, rather than demonstrated insurer deployments or measured premium reductions. The external building statistics discussed supply market context, rather than results from Spranic's product. The practical demonstration is narrower and concrete: preserve scene observations, compare visits and make spatial evidence available to the people and systems that need it. items.title: Judge a Transaction by the Company It Keeps — Somya Rai & MD Sharique, EXL
items.excerpt: A transaction can look harmless in isolation and suspicious once its links to recent fraud become visible. Somya Rai and MD Sharique explain an EXL fraud detection system that adds graph embeddings to an existing XGBoost classifier. The objective is precision within a fixed analyst alert budget, rather than a better headline score alone. Rai introduces the neighborhood signal and the constraints of two transaction portfolios; Sharique then walks through sampling, graph construction, explanation and serving. They report relative detection improvements of 27% to 33% against their tabular baseline at matched alert rates. The financial figure discussed is projected annualized incremental fraud capture, rather than realized savings. The engineering decisions start before training. Selected users retain their transaction histories so sampling does not destroy the neighborhoods the model needs. Separate monthly graphs, earlier timestamps and training only preprocessing constrain leakage. GraphSAGE combines mean, maximum and standard deviation, preserving an unusual neighbor that averaging alone could obscure. Attribution connects a suspicious score to specific transaction edges for analyst review. For serving, cached representations and a small online forward pass keep graph sized work off the request path. Moving from transaction node embeddings to user and merchant embeddings reduces the stated cache footprint from roughly 60 GB to 2 to 3 GB. The talk closes with rolling windows, temporal decay and reported millisecond latency, showing the tradeoffs behind the system rather than presenting a universal fraud benchmark. items.title: I Believe Everything My Agents Tell Me: Three Levels of Review — Corey Gallon, Rexmore
items.excerpt: A demand letter passed its drafting agent's own checks, yet two independent reviewer agents found that the supposedly expired contract had renewed less than three weeks earlier. Sending it could have left the business owing thousands of dollars. Corey Gallon uses that case to explain a three level review method for agents that overstate completed work, misread facts or draw the wrong conclusions. His analysis of his own 2026 sessions found a consequential error in about four out of ten sessions; that is a description of his sample, not an error rate for all agents or for the final reviewed outputs. Level one requires a verified artifact with a fingerprint, or an explicit account of what is missing. Level two has independent agents extract the same material against a control total, then settles every difference against the source. For a year of scanned accounting statements, that process found 56 differences and produced records that balanced to the penny. Level three combines a self audit, cold reviewer agents with reasons to challenge the work and fresh reviewers for the revision. A memory leak investigation exposed a flawed reproduction and an overstated fix before the maintainer merged the corrected change. Gallon reports the time and token costs for these cases and releases the method as agent skills. The evidence supports a concrete checking workflow, rather than a guarantee that review eliminates every error. items.title: Hello Python 3.15, goodbye 3.10, and now I can use 3.11
items.excerpt: Python 3.15 is here ! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11. First, some highlights from Python 3.15. Explicit lazy imports I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810 . These let you import modules like so: lazy import json lazy from pathlib import Path The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows. My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost. Unpacking in comprehensions The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation : lists = [[ 1 , 2 ], [ 3 , 4 ], [ 5 ]] [ * L for L in lists ] # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] # equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L] sets = [{ 1 , 2 }, { 2 , 3 }, { 3 , 4 }] { * s for s in sets } # {1, 2, 3, 4} # equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s} dicts = [{ 'a' : 1 }, { 'b' : 2 }, { 'a' : 3 }] { ** d for d in dicts } # {'a': 3, 'b': 2} # equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()} PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpa…

items.title: Agents in Orbit: Workflows, Not Autopilot — Eduardo Simon & Javier Casal, Flywire
items.excerpt: More than 9,700 code review runs in 30 days came from a workflow that lets the model read code but never modify it. Eduardo Simon and Javier Casal describe Orbit, Flywire's internal platform for putting model steps inside deterministic engineering workflows. A YAML definition goes through the same merge request review as other code, declares the tools and access each step can use, and runs on the company's existing deployment infrastructure. The predictable work stays in code; a model supplies the judgment. Human review of merge requests remains part of the process as the platform expands across roughly 400 engineers. Code review, translation updates, dependency fixes, ticket triage and bulk repository changes show the range of tasks this pattern supports. The architecture separates orchestration, execution and session state, then adds timeouts, rate limits and locks against duplicate runs. Per step restrictions cover network access, tools, skills and MCP servers, while structured outputs drive subsequent branches. The speakers are candid about the remaining work: new workflows initially receive a few real case checks, golden datasets run on demand, online evaluations are still being built and full sandboxing is a goal. Their reported execution success rate does not establish answer correctness. The practical adoption path starts with a useful skill, proves the recurring task and then turns it into a background workflow with explicit ownership and review. items.title: Reliable, Smart Workflows for Finance, Wealth and Insurance — Karthic Rao, Perpetual
items.excerpt: “Fill out a form for Mr. Harper” becomes a process that lasts days: identify the right household, find missing information, contact the client, wait, follow up, obtain a signature and retain the evidence. Karthic Rao uses that wealth management example to show why a fixed flowchart breaks on ambiguity and an improvising agent creates a different reliability problem. At Perpetual, his design puts control flow, evidence and external actions in a deterministic system. Models handle interpretation and judgment at explicit, typed points. A judgment can create a smaller plan, but that plan must pass the same compilation and approval boundaries. The planner translates a request into a semantic graph whose nodes point back to the request. A compiler validates it against the firm's action contracts, returning a valid plan, a clarification request or a refusal. Approved plans are immutable, and external actions have separate gates tied to the exact payload. Waiting and followups are state machine steps; uncertain action outcomes go to manual review rather than automatic retries. Rao shows an illustrative 20 decision run with 19 decisions assigned to a smaller model and one to a frontier model. That ratio is a design target, not a measured fleet result. Typed, logged judgments offer a path toward privately hosted inference and future training, while the training loop remains forthcoming. items.text: Agent swarms are going to be a core part of many enterprise workflows in the future. The ability to throw compute at problems that you can massively parallelize will be too useful to not take advantage of. Cyber will be one of the biggest beneficiaries of this as it’s a space where testing vast number of permutations of attacks (without getting tired or bored) is an incredibly useful property. You have a wide search space of possible risk vectors and you generally need to be able to chain together different scenarios to achieve the exploit. This will become one of the biggest token uses in large enterprises given the range of IT systems, software, physical infrastructure, and data that needs to be protected at all times. Super interesting times in cyber.

items.title: Just-in-Time Ontologies: What Cheap Intelligence Means for Data — Hrishi Olickel, Southbridge AI
items.excerpt: A pipeline stripped the minus signs from loan amounts and turned a net $784,000 into $5.3 million of debt, with multiple models agreeing on the wrong result. Hrishi Olickel uses failures like this to explain why transforming data requires more than a universal schema or a confident agent. A customer means something different to billing, support and compliance. Useful structure depends on the source, the storage constraints, the decision being made and the assumptions a model brings to the task. His alternative is a just in time ontology: build the transformation when the question is known, and preserve its context and evidence for reuse. An Ohio campaign finance entity resolution project provides the working example. Olickel describes separating models that design a pipeline, models that perform its individual jobs and models that optimize the resulting system. Definitions, held out cases and disagreement checks matter as much as model selection. Comparing different model families can concentrate review on their disagreements, but shared assumptions can still produce the same wrong answer. The optimization loop needs a stable execution surface, bounded budgets, reusable methods and a defined way to fail. Small pilots establish a baseline; independently checked work segments make revisions easier to inspect and revert. Only then can the pipeline trade among cost, speed and accuracy without losing the evidence behind its answers. items.title: Please… Enough with the Sloppy, One-Shot SaaS Replacements — Mahmoud Abdelwahab, Railway
items.excerpt: A single internal app now handles Railway's marketing content, email, social posts, media, creator relationships and launch planning. Mahmoud Abdelwahab built it with coding agents, but getting the features to run was only the beginning. The difference between a quick SaaS replacement and a tool his team wants to open every day lives in the details: background saving, responsive interactions, reversible actions and consistent screens. His starting point is a structured codebase with reusable abstractions, so each new feature follows existing patterns instead of inventing another way to do the same work. Abdelwahab works through the product behaviors he has learned to request explicitly. Autosave should preserve progress without blocking typing; optimistic updates should make suitable actions feel immediate and recover when the operation fails. Undo and archiving give people room to change their minds. URL state makes a filtered view shareable, while infinite scrolling removes repetitive navigation. Referencing an existing page helps the agent reuse the app's interface and data fetching conventions. He then packages recurring design and deployment preferences into agent skills. The final step is a verification loop that opens the running application and exercises the feature from start to finish, because a successful build and passing tests can still leave a broken experience. These are practical lessons from an internal tool, without a claim of measured financial savings. items.title: Your GPU Neighbor Can Hear Your Model — Branislav Brzak, Stealthium
items.excerpt: Three microseconds of extra latency can reveal activity on another tenant's GPU slice. Branislav Brzak demonstrates an H100 timing side channel that probes only the attacker's own memory, without reading the victim's memory or exploiting a software bug. His experiments use the signal to infer model depth and decoding speed, then distinguish workload categories such as code, prose, JSON and retrieval. He explicitly separates that inference from recovering actual prompts or answers: the attack observes timing, not their contents. Memory and compute isolation do not automatically eliminate signals from hardware operations that affect the whole GPU. The walkthrough follows the trace from repeated memory reads to frequency analysis, token rates and layer signatures. Similar decoding speeds make tempo alone a weak fingerprint; the additional layer signal helps distinguish models with related architectures. Workload inference in the demonstrated setup depends on speculative decoding, whose acceptance patterns change step timing. Brzak then moves to a separate GPU on an NVSwitch connected H100 server and shows a weaker but still informative signal across NVLink. These are results from the tested configurations, rather than a claim that every shared deployment leaks equally. He closes with the operator choices that follow: consider tenant placement, understand the different isolation and communication tradeoffs, and observe the probing workload on the GPU itself. items.title: Your Agent Is a Lethal Trifecta (And What to Do About It) — Kim Maida, Keycard
items.excerpt: An on call agent drops a billing database, restarts a production server and scales a service from four pods to 40, adding $420 an hour to the bill. Kim Maida's staged triage demo shows what happens when an agent receives standing API keys and an administrator's database credentials. Private data, untrusted tickets and access to external services combine into the lethal trifecta. The agent can do useful work, but its credentials give it far more authority than any one ticket requires. A human approval button alone cannot tell it which actions the user is actually authorized to approve. Maida walks through delegated authorization using OAuth token exchange: carry the user's identity through the agent and MCP server, evaluate policy at a security token service and issue short lived credentials scoped to the requested access. She also explains Keycard's approach to intent based authorization, which she identifies as a proposal rather than a finalized standard. The second demo uses task based policy instead. Customer data access and database deletion are denied, certificate renewal is allowed, and a server restart stays blocked even after approval because the user's role cannot authorize it. Scaling proceeds when the user has the required authority. The demos make identity, delegation and policy decisions visible throughout the request chain, while keeping authorization distinct from whether an agent's answer is correct. items.title: We Let Our Financial Planners Write the Agents — Matthew Ragone, Range
items.excerpt: While one financial planner is on a client call, an agent drafts another client's cash flow or insurance analysis. The planner reviews every recommendation before anything reaches the client. At Range, Matthew Ragone and his colleagues built the skills behind that workflow without writing code. Six months in, he reports 24 skills across the company, including 17 in planning, with sales, product and marketing adopting the same approach without a mandate. The change came from capturing how the firm actually works: what a planner checks first, which questions must be asked and where an agent must stop. Ragone breaks the process into five steps: pick a repeated workflow whose output you can judge, teach it with real cases, package the judgment into a skill, test it five to ten times and ship it with an owner and a separate reviewer. Narrating why you open a document matters more than listing the clicks. Questions and limits belong in the skill alongside the procedure, including the rule that an agent drafts but never sends recommendations to a client. Testing exposes missing questions and confident mistakes; ownership keeps the instructions current as the firm's practices change. The remaining challenge is how to check quality at scale when the output requires professional judgment. items.title: Decoupling the Brain from the Hands: Claude Managed Agents (Part 1 of 4) — Anthropic
items.excerpt: The first version of Claude Managed Agents put everything in one container. Here's why Anthropic split it apart. NEXT UP: AI ENGINEER CODE SUMMIT Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE Summit, Nov 10–12, our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now: https://aie.codes Priyanka Phatak, who leads the Claude Managed Agents engineering team at Anthropic, defines an agent as a model in a loop with tools, plus a harness and a sandbox, and explains why harnesses encode assumptions that go stale with each new model. She walks through the first architecture, where the session, harness and sandbox shared one hard-to-debug 'pet' container, and the redesign into an append-only session log, a brain (harness plus Claude) and hands (sandboxes and tools). Credentials stay out of the sandbox and time to first token dropped about 90%. Then she introduces the core APIs with a simple joke-teller agent. This is part 1 of 4 of the Claude Managed Agents workshop from Anthropic. items.title: Auth for Agents: Let AI Sign Up for Your Product with auth.md — Michael Grinich, WorkOS
items.excerpt: Agents are starting to pick your vendors, and most signup flows block them at the door. NEXT UP: AI ENGINEER CODE SUMMIT Join us in SF for the second annual AIE CODE Summit, Nov 10–12, our last flagship summit of 2026. Applications live now: https://aie.codes Michael Grinich, founder and CEO of WorkOS, argues that as agents run for hours and increasingly choose tools on their own, services have to make something agents want. The missing piece is agent registration: today's signup flows assume a human who can fill out forms, solve CAPTCHAs and copy API keys, and MCP auth still needs a person in the loop. He introduces auth.md, an open spec built on OAuth standards that tells agents how to register, then demos an agent that finds Cloudflare's auth.md, proves its identity with ID-JAG, gets a temporary account and deploys an app with no human signup. items.excerpt: We pointed a coding agent at our own sandbox overnight and told it to break things. Here's what failed. items.text: This is a good way to understand how early we actually are in AI diffusion right now. The vast majority of people are using AI as a chatbot for simple interactions that approximate next-generation search. This is super useful but dramatically underrepresents the full capability of AI. On the complete other end of the spectrum, agent swarms represent possibly the ultimate form factor of what agents will do inside of our workflows. Math, cyber, bio, materials science, software engineering, finance, and any other field that has valuable tasks that can be executed in parallel where compute can be applied to accelerate work all have this characteristic. Less than a fraction of a fraction of the population uses AI in this way right now, due to a mix of the capabilities of models relative to the user's domain, the cost of doing these types of workflows today, the harnesses available to do this style of AI work, and the availability (or lack thereof) of frontier models to the general public. There will also be a huge amount of change management necessary to get most areas of work -beyond software and AI research- to benefit from this style of agents. Companies need to upgrade their workflows, data needs to integrated and migrated into modern platforms, and companies will need to work through compliance, governance, and security frameworks to pull it off. But this all represents opportunity right now. A lot of this is where the applied layer of AI will really shine in the enterprise because of the domain specificity of this type of work. You can get an early sense of where things are going and the opportunity ahead by seeing through the funnel that Andrej lays out.

items.title: Containment Is Lying to You: Measuring AI Agents Like Employees — Druid AI
items.excerpt: Two AI interns. One handles 96% of conversations alone, the other only 80%. The dashboard picks the wrong one. Druid AI's team, including co-founder and chief product officer Dan Bălăceanu, shows why containment rate, the metric on every agent dashboard, can point you to the wrong agent. In their bank example, the intern who escalated more often was handing senior bankers customers who were about to refinance. They walk through a performance review framework built with their customers: seven pillars split into what the agent is configured with and what it does at runtime, with governance across both. Twenty-six components are each scored 0, 1 or 2 (missing, defined, or actually governed and tracked over time) and weighted by business impact, with governance and mandate weighted highest. They cover error tolerance, risk, compliance, observability, drift, hallucination, tone and sentiment, the agent's mandate, scope, business case and budget, a shared platform, and validating outcomes. They also show a dashboard that stays green all year while the agent's real score slides from 83% to 60%, how to answer the ROI question, and why containment targets differ by industry in Druid's 2026 AI Adoption Benchmark. items.title: Stop Renting Intelligence: The Train-to-Deploy Loop for Specialized AI — Fireworks AI
items.excerpt: Closed models are getting expensive fast. Open models can match them, if you keep training them on your own data. Jetashree Ravi, who leads part of the applied machine learning team at Fireworks AI, explains how teams move from closed models to open ones without losing quality. Her three truths: open models like GLM 5.2 are production-ready, customization closes the remaining quality gap, and the AI stack is shifting to a continuous train-and-serve loop. She shares Fireworks' scale (about 30 trillion tokens, 10,000+ companies) and customer results: Cursor's Composer 2 trained and hosted on Fireworks with 13x faster inference, a 40x latency improvement for Vercel, and 12% better quality for Genspark with reinforcement fine-tuning. She covers the FireAttention engine and its custom CUDA kernels, speculative decoding with custom draft models, and three ways to train (a training agent, managed training, and a training API for SFT, RFT and DPO), then the flywheel: one-click deploys, monitoring, hot-loading new weights with no downtime, and matching numerics between training and serving. She ends with demos of the training agent and managed training. In this talk: • Why open models plus customization can match closed ones • FireAttention, custom kernels and speculative decoding • Training agent, managed training and the training API • Hot loading and numerical fidelity for a continuous train-and-deploy loop SPEAKER Jetashree Ravi, Tech Lead Manager, Applied ML, Fireworks AI LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jetashree-ravi/ GitHub: https://github.com/jraviS2023 LINKS Fireworks AI: https://fireworks.ai Managed fine-tuning docs: https://docs.fireworks.ai/fine-tuning/managed-finetuning-intro Supervised fine-tuning docs: https://docs.fireworks.ai/fine-tuning/supervised-fine-t…

items.title: The Autonomous Computer: Infrastructure for Computer Use Agents — Ang Li, Simular
items.excerpt: A computer agent finds a speaker on Tuesday's conference schedule, saves the successful steps as a skill, and tries to replay them for Wednesday. A hiccup pushes it back into model driven exploration before the workflow completes. Ang Li uses that demonstration to explain Simular's approach to autonomous computers: combine adaptable vision agents with reusable automation code, then check the environment as each step runs. The workshop traces Agent S from accessibility based control to visual grounding, multiple models, and parallel attempts. It also asks a different reliability question from getting one successful result: can the same agent complete the task repeatedly when prompts and environments vary? Li demonstrates a coding agent opening the AI Engineer website, reading an accessibility snapshot, and producing a summary. He then connects code replay and recovery to the tension between stability and adaptation, showing where a fixed script can break and where a model can help repair it. The infrastructure discussion moves from an agent occupying a personal desktop to fleets of cloud computers controlled through an interface or API. Recorded examples include legacy form entry and Android interactions. Audience questions examine screen understanding, verification loops, irreversible actions, operating system restrictions, and workflows built from internal procedures. The session presents an experimental direction with visible limitations: benchmark progress and successful demos still leave substantial work in making everyday computer use reliable. items.title: Hill-Climbing Skills: Improve Agents Without Changing the Model — Shubhankar Srivastava, Browserbase
items.excerpt: An agent succeeds at a flight search, then fails on its next iteration. Shubhankar Srivastava uses that uneven progress to show how browser agents can learn a task without changing model weights. His AutoBrowse loop pairs a doer that operates the browser with a teacher that reads screenshots, traces and results after each run. The teacher writes lessons into a strategy file, and the next attempt starts with those lessons instead of starting from zero. The flight demo discovers that a URL can encode the search directly, avoiding repeated calendar clicks and an awkward time filter. The final artifact is a skill file that future agents can reuse. Earlier runs on a conference schedule and restaurant search show how the file preserves navigation choices, waiting behavior and site specific constraints, while replays make the claimed results inspectable. Srivastava then explains what another domain would need to use the same approach: an environment that can be replayed and an outcome that can be verified. Questions expose the limits of that requirement, especially when finding an acceptable flight is easier to judge than finding the best one. The discussion explores task specific versus general skills, different optimization goals, iteration costs and how to measure the verifier itself. For changing websites, he describes monitoring and failure triggered repair loops that produce changes for human review. Prompt injection adds another constraint: generated skills need scrutiny alongside controls on inputs, allowed actions and destinations. items.title: Taming the AI Hardware Cambrian Explosion — Abdul Dakkak, Modular
items.excerpt: Compute is booked out for years and new chips keep arriving. The hard part is software that runs well on all of them. Abdul Dakkak, chief scientist at Modular, explains why today's AI software stack is a mess, with vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM and llama.cpp each patching around different hardware, and how Modular rebuilt the stack from the ground up. Mojo is a Pythonic systems language for CPUs, GPUs and accelerators that aims to match CUDA's performance; Modular has open-sourced its kernels, including matmul and attention kernels he says beat the vendor libraries and FlashAttention 4, with Mojo 1.0 and an open-source Mojo coming. MAX is an inference framework that rethinks PyTorch-era assumptions, supports thousands of model architectures behind OpenAI-compatible endpoints, and runs across GPUs, nodes and even mixed hardware. Modular Cloud ties it together as a tunable glass box. He shares benchmarks (Kimi K2.5, FLUX.2, AMD MI355 and Gemma 4), sub-second image generation, and how to try it with pip install modular. In this talk: • Why the explosion of AI hardware broke the software stack • Mojo: Pythonic, portable, and as fast as CUDA • MAX: inference across GPUs, nodes and mixed hardware • Benchmarks vs vLLM and torch.compile, and sub-second image generation SPEAKER Abdul Dakkak, Chief Scientist, Modular LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/adakkak GitHub: https://github.com/abduld LINKS Modular: https://www.modular.com Modular docs: https://docs.modular.com Modular (GitHub): https://github.com/modular/modular CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:23 Compute crunch, hardware explosion 1:03 A messy software stack 1:48 Rebuilding the stack 3:53 Mojo 4:28 Mojo vs CUDA, Triton and OpenCL 5:23 State-of-the-art kernels 6:13 MAX 7:43 Thousands of models supported 8:58 Multi-GPU, multi-node,…

items.title: Parameter Golf with AutoResearch — Vayum Arora, Zhengyao Jiang, Dixing Xu & Dhruv Srikanth, Weco AI
items.excerpt: An agent keeps the code changes that improve a language model's score and discards the rest. Weco AI turns that research loop into a workshop, using Mini Parameter Golf to make training experiments small enough to inspect as they run. Zhengyao Jiang introduces autoresearch as repeated proposals and evaluations, and Dixing Xu explains the team's Aiden system and its contributions to OpenAI's Parameter Golf challenge. Vayum Arora and Dhruv Srikanth then connect those results to a practical setup that combines a modifiable source file, a fixed evaluation command and a measurable goal. The walkthrough focuses on what determines whether the search is useful: fast and stable evaluations, a clear direction for the metric, time limits, initial guidance and protection against reward hacking. Weco's experiment tree makes each attempt inspectable, with its code changes and score visible in the dashboard. The presenters show how to branch from promising work and steer a running search toward a different idea instead of simply letting it continue. Internet problems lead to a guided setup demonstration, followed by questions about reinforcement learning and combining multiple objectives. The final exercise swaps model training for a Flappy Bird controller scored across normal play, moving gaps, wind and mixed conditions. A hidden validation set and limits on what the controller can edit make the competition another lesson in designing an evaluation that rewards the behavior you want. items.title: Burn Your Flags: Interactive CLIs for Agents — Mark Lummus & Navinkumar Patil, PayPal
items.excerpt: An agent can miss an interactive terminal prompt without producing an error. The human sees a question and arrow key options; the agent sees a redraw loop and loses the interface state. PayPal's Mark Lummus and Navinkumar Patil use that failure to challenge the standard fix of adding more command flags. Flags work when inputs are independent and the path is known in advance. They become awkward when later questions depend on earlier answers or live API responses. Interactive workflows already contain guidance, choices and guardrails that an agent should be able to follow. The workshop puts that idea into practice with Barista 9000, a coffee ordering CLI that participants adapt for an agent, with a leaderboard and a Mac Mini prize. Patil introduces three approaches: tmux sessions for sending keys and capturing terminal state, IPC side channels that expose structured JSON instead of screen scraping, and context injection that makes options and constraints explicit. Lummus also asks participants to try less expensive models rather than brute force the task with maximum reasoning. Audience solutions push the benchmark toward deterministic parsers and very low response latency, prompting a discussion of what the competition actually rewards. The closing lesson is to keep the CLI predictable while giving the agent enough context and access to navigate its decisions. items.title: Build with Perception Agents — Emile Baizel & Shruti Arora, Amazon AGI Lab
items.excerpt: A coding agent says it added a duck icon to a podcast page; a browser verification pass checks whether the change actually appeared. That audience demo captures the loop Emile Baizel and Shruti Arora build around two perception agent primitives. Visual annotation lets a person select an element, draw on the page or drop a pin, then export structured feedback for a coding agent. Visual verification checks the rendered site against design expectations and user flows. The annotation step is deterministic and produces JSON; the verification step gives the agent a way to inspect the result of its work. Arora starts from a podcast landing page whose heading, colors and buttons need changes, then connects the browser extension to a coding agent through a local bridge. Participants modify the extension's permissions and add an Apply Changes button, turning exported feedback into a workflow that edits the code, runs verification and produces a report. Easy and medium paths let them follow the wiring directly or solve more of the integration themselves. A guest demonstration uses a simulated Bee conversation as another source of design feedback, feeding the same edit and verification loop. Audience examples extend the idea to spoken feature discussions, project planning and recorded UI feedback, with several integrations still at the concept stage. The closing discussion keeps the focus on making collaboration visual and checking the rendered result, rather than accepting a coding agent's claim that the change is done. items.title: AI Security Engineer Foundations + Certificate — Javier Garza, Snyk
items.excerpt: An AI bill of materials turns a repository into a searchable inventory of models, datasets and agents. Javier Garza demonstrates the workflow from a CLI scan to a visual dashboard, then asks it which models the project uses. That inventory anchors a broader security problem: teams cannot assess the AI components they do not know are there. The workshop connects shadow AI to prompt injection, supply chain risk, sensitive information disclosure and excessive agency, using Gandalf challenges and malicious instructions embedded in external content to show how an application's intended rules can be bypassed. Garza works through defenses at several layers. A database view can restrict what an assistant is allowed to retrieve; limited permissions, output validation and human approval constrain what it can do next. Threat modeling maps assets, trust boundaries and possible attacks before deployment, with an intentionally vulnerable student assistant offered for practice. For skills and MCP servers, he separates scanning tool definitions for hidden instructions from scanning the underlying code for vulnerabilities, then explains a scan, fix and rescan loop driven by coding agent rules and hooks. The final sections examine secure prompting, dependency verification, separate development and production environments, IDE configuration and developer review. Governance depends on explaining guardrails as well as enforcing them, because unexplained restrictions invite workarounds. He closes with offensive agent workflows, training resources and challenges that let participants test these ideas themselves. items.title: Same Model, Different Speed: Why Your Inference Provider Matters — FriendliAI
items.excerpt: Open-weight models are good enough now. The question is who can run them fast and reliably. Yunmo Koo, founding engineer at FriendliAI, argues that open-weight models like GLM 5.2 and MiniMax M3 now compete with the best proprietary models. He shows GLM 5.2 and Claude Opus 4.8 building similar tower defense games from one prompt, with GLM 5.2 more than 5.6x cheaper. Then he runs the same model and the same coding agent on two providers: FriendliAI builds a Candy Crush-style game in about two minutes, the other takes more than three. He explains where the gap comes from: prefix caching with cache-aware routing and a GPU, CPU and NVMe cache hierarchy for long, repetitive agent inputs, plus hybrid speculative decoding that adapts to live traffic. He also covers why reliability matters for agents (one failed call can sink a whole run) and shares Kilo Code's results of up to 7x faster responses with fewer errors. In this talk: • Why open-weight models are now good enough for many workloads • Why the same model feels different on different providers • Prefix caching, cache-aware routing and a tiered KV cache • Hybrid speculative decoding and why reliability is part of speed SPEAKER Yunmo Koo, Founding Engineer, FriendliAI LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/yunmokoo/ GitHub: https://github.com/kooyunmo LINKS FriendliAI: https://friendli.ai Kilo Code case study: https://friendli.ai/customers/kilo CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:40 Open vs closed models 1:09 Open weights crossed the threshold 2:24 GLM 5.2 vs Opus: a tower defense game 2:49 5.6x cheaper 3:09 Provider quality 3:53 Same model, different provider 4:33 It's the whole stack 5:28 Long, repetitive agent inputs 6:27 Cache-aware routing 6:47 A cache hierarchy 7:37 Speculative decoding 9:06 Hybrid, self-improving speculation 9:4…

items.author: @karpathy
items.subtitle: Andrej Karpathy
items.text: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel. - Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all. - Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract. - Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code. - And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while. The funnel is driven by a combination of factors: 1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel. 2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel. 3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal. So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

items.title: SonarQube + OpenAI: Agentic Development — Killian Carlsen-Phelan, Sonar
items.excerpt: A tiny Python project contains a hardcoded API key, a SQL injection path and other deliberately planted issues. Killian Carlsen-Phelan runs it through SonarQube, brings the findings into Codex and asks the agent to fix the vulnerable query. The scan follows user controlled input into database execution; the repair replaces string interpolation with a parameterized query. A verification hook checks the edited code again, putting the security feedback inside the coding loop rather than leaving it for a later failed build or review. The workshop develops Sonar's guide, verify and solve workflow through a live setup of SonarQube Cloud, its CLI, plugin and MCP server. A secrets detection hook blocks a fake credential in a prompt, while an issue listing skill gives the agent evidence from the project dashboard. Context augmentation supplies coding guidance before generation, and agentic analysis checks edits as they happen. The opening OpenAI introduction separates execution containment from artifact correctness and defines completion through a reviewable change and independent evidence. Questions explore how the hooks can be bypassed, which steps run locally or in a container, and which features depend on organizational access. Killian finishes by adding a new database operation under the same verification loop, showing how the setup supports both fixing existing issues and checking new work. items.title: Let Your Agent Cook: Using Skills to Evaluate and Improve Your App — Ankur Duggal, Arize AI
items.excerpt: A financial agent invents answers, repeats tool calls and produces summaries that its own evaluations flag as wrong. Ankur Duggal connects those failures to a coding agent through Arize's CLI and skills, then asks it to investigate traces, change the application and run experiments. The demo begins with an investment question that looks reasonable at the surface but lacks enough context to support its recommendation. Traces reveal the supervisor, specialist agents, model calls and tools underneath that answer. They turn a vague complaint about quality into evidence about the exact steps that failed. Duggal sets up the CLI profile and skills, then shows the coding agent pulling spans and evaluation results into its local workspace. The investigation uncovers numeric grounding problems, fabricated responses, redundant searches and failures that the agent silently works around. An earlier experiment targets stock queries outside the United States: changing the country context alone is insufficient until the underlying tool is also updated. Dataset, evaluator and experiment skills make those proposed fixes testable rather than a collection of unverified edits. items.title: AI Apps in a Flash: Ship to GPUs Without Docker — Dean Quiñanola, Runpod
items.excerpt: Write code, build the image, push it, run it, find a bug, repeat. One loop can take 15 minutes. Runpod Flash cuts it out. Dean Quiñanola, staff engineer at Runpod, introduces Runpod Flash, which lets you run Python on cloud GPUs as if the GPU were local, with no Dockerfiles, image builds or registry pushes. He covers serverless queue and load-balanced endpoints, endpoints that call each other like local functions, network volumes with warm caching, and live serverless for instant iteration. In a live demo he checks which GPU he's on (an RTX 4090), evolves the same function into text generation and then image generation, installing dependencies on the fly, and deploys it to production with one command that packages and serves the app without Docker. He also shows off a hackathon project that fans experiments out across endpoints, and how to get started. Lotte Verheyden and Annabell Schäfer build that monitoring workflow with Langfuse and a sample support agent called Specs. The hands on setup connects a TypeScript application built on the OpenAI Agents SDK to Langfuse. Schäfer adds a judge evaluator for user disagreement, a code evaluator for all caps and a scope check that compares the user's request with the system prompt. Each evaluator targets the relevant messages through explicit variable mappings, so its score answers a defined question. Seeded production traces then give a coding agent enough evidence to investigate patterns through the Langfuse CLI and skill. The analysis surfaces issues such as unnecessary tool calls, retries, latency and incomplete evaluation coverage, and the presenters explore a proposed code change. The closing discussion places this online monitoring inside a continuous improvement loop: turn observed failures into representative datasets, run offline experiments, check regressions and repeat as real usage changes. items.title: Build a Platform and Watch It Burn — Michael Forrester, Accenture & Whitney Lee, Datadog
items.excerpt: A burrito ordering assistant deploys an external container image and exposes a secret recipe from its Kubernetes environment. Michael Forrester and Whitney Lee invite the audience to push that deliberately permissive bot beyond ordering food, then repeat the attacks with infrastructure and AI guardrails. The exercise makes excessive agency tangible: a friendly business story can turn an ordinary chat interface into a route to tools, files and cluster operations. Model refusals also change between attempts, which complicates the live demos and shows why an application's boundaries cannot depend on the model choosing to refuse. The workshop moves through three configurations. The first leaves the bot exposed; the second adds infrastructure controls, including Kyverno rules restricting image sources and deployment requirements. Intended runtime protections do not consistently stop recipe access, so the presenters distinguish what worked from what still needs fixing. A third environment lets them toggle LLM Guard input and output filtering, comparing a response that exposes sensitive content with one that redacts it, and a request blocked before model processing. A weather tool introduces another trust boundary: its description asks the agent to read internal configuration alongside a legitimate task. OpenTelemetry traces reveal prompts, tool calls and results in Datadog, making that behavior inspectable. The final discussion connects agent security to established CI/CD, identity, network and artifact controls, and asks when an AI workflow has clear boundaries, a worthwhile cost and a verifiable output. items.title: From Zero to Leaderboard: Agent Evaluation — Wolfram Ravenwolf, Weights & Biases
items.excerpt: An agent repairs a broken git repository and earns a perfect score, but the run stays out of the default leaderboard because it tested only one task. Wolfram Ravenwolf uses that distinction to build an evaluation pipeline where every score can be traced back to its conditions. WolfBench compares the average, best and worst runs, the tasks solved at least once, and the tasks solved every time. Repeating the same configuration exposes the gap between a lucky success and dependable behavior. The configuration includes six layers: benchmark, runner, sandbox, agent, model service and settings. Versions, provider routing, system prompts, resource limits and timeouts all affect what the result actually measures. The live workflow launches a Terminal Bench task through Harbor, collects the results, filters incomplete runs in a Marimo dashboard, and turns valid runs into an interactive leaderboard. Weave preserves the trajectories behind the bars so reviewers can inspect commands, messages and failures. Ravenwolf examines two traps in interpreting the results: a cheaper model can consume enough tokens to raise total cost, and greater reasoning effort can lower the score when it leaves too little time to execute commands. Infrastructure failures need different treatment from genuine task failures, while zero temperature still does not guarantee identical runs. The resulting comparison helps teams choose a configuration for their own constraints, with costs and consistency visible alongside the headline score. items.title: How Secrets Leak Through AI Agents (and How to Stop It) — Venice AI
items.excerpt: A private model doesn't make a private product. The leaks happen in everything you build around it. Joshua Mo, lead developer relations engineer at Venice AI and previously lead maintainer of the Rust AI framework Rig, explains why privacy matters (one breach and users leave, and less stored data means a smaller blast radius) and how Venice approaches it: no stored prompts, anonymized requests to closed providers, models in trusted execution environments, and split-key encrypted storage. Then he shows where agent systems leak: logs that quietly capture prompts and secrets, and secrets fetched from a vault straight into the reasoning layer, where a tool call can exfiltrate them. His patterns: hashed IDs instead of personal data, split-key custody, revocable handles, narrow agent scope, a classifier in front of the agent to catch prompt injection, wiring the vault to the execution layer instead of the LLM, sandboxes plus permission monitoring, and confidential compute with verifiable attestations. He closes on the open problem of confidential tool calls. In this talk: • Why privacy is about blast radius, not just the model • How logs and secrets leak through a typical agent • Keeping credentials in the execution layer, never the LLM • Hashes, split keys, handles, narrow scope and confidential compute SPEAKER Joshua Mo, Lead DevRel Engineer, Venice AI LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/joshua-mo-4146aa220/ X: https://x.com/joshmo_dev GitHub: https://github.com/joshua-mo-143 Website: https://joshmo.ooo LINKS Venice AI: https://venice.ai Venice API docs: https://docs.venice.ai Rig (Rust AI framework): https://github.com/0xPlaygrounds/rig CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:55 What Venice is 1:40 Why privacy matters 2:35 How Venice handles privacy 4:15 Not all systems are private 5:05…

items.title: Teaching Agents to Search with NVIDIA Data Designer — Dhruv Nathawani, NVIDIA
items.excerpt: 50,000 seed examples become 7,000 training records after generation and filtering. Dhruv Nathawani uses that funnel to explain how NVIDIA builds synthetic data that teaches a model to search, rather than answer from memory. The starting material is a set of walks through Wikidata: connected entities become riddles whose answers require multiple searches. Data Designer turns those seeds into questions, tool calls and responses, with Tavily providing search through MCP. The goal is a reusable pipeline for teaching a chosen behavior, with search serving as the worked example. Three notebooks build the workflow in stages. The first combines seed topics, difficulty samplers, prompt templates, structured outputs and model judges to generate question and answer pairs. The second adds tool access and captures search traces. The third creates search riddles from graph paths and produces complete trajectories for supervised finetuning. Previewing a few records before running a batch makes the process inspectable and easier to revise. Nathawani then examines the difficult part: verifying that generated answers are correct when even the source graph can become stale. Model judgments, deterministic checks and human review contribute different evidence; no single score establishes dataset quality. Questions distinguish seed generation from agent execution, explore reinforcement learning alternatives and discuss other training tasks. The closing examples use synthetic personas to preserve demographic distributions, while the broader lesson remains practical: design for diversity, inspect examples, overproduce, filter and version the recipe. Ndukwe installs repository skills, connects Qodo and walks through the planning templates in Codex. Audience questions test the boundaries: how rules are inferred and approved, how severity controls merge blocking, when verification should run again and how local checks relate to cloud review. The exercise finishes by resolving the remaining issues rather than treating a passing local run as the end of the workflow. Its reusable artifact is a structured process that keeps plans, code changes and review evidence connected. items.title: Can Your Agent Hear You Now? Building Live Voice Agents with Gemini — Thor Schaeff
items.excerpt: An agent that hears you, sees you, and answers in your language, in real time. Here's how to build one with Gemini. Thor Schaeff, who works on developer experience at Google DeepMind, runs a set of live demos of Gemini's real-time and media models. It supports 90 languages, interruptions, tool calls and Google Search grounding. He ends with a voice and vision demo in Google AI Studio. items.excerpt: A customer service agent looks up an account, checks an order, and handles a refund. The harder part is controlling what happens between those steps and keeping that control when the agent reaches production. Elizabeth Fuentes Leone and Sandhya Subramani build the workflow with Strands Agents, starting with a system prompt and three tools backed by mock customer data. They inspect messages and tool calls, add a conversational interface, then introduce a hook that limits tool invocations. Lowering the limit makes the constraint visible in a live test. An audience question separates blocking another tool call from ending the agent's turn, showing why a control needs a precise definition. The next modules add skills and steering. Markdown instructions provide account troubleshooting, order tracking, and refund procedures when they are needed, while steering handlers check workflow order and response tone. The presenters compare programmatic checks with instructions left to a probabilistic model, then move the same customer service code into Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The deployment walkthrough covers the application entry point, local testing, runtime setup, generated infrastructure, and a successful invocation. It also shows the observability configuration needed to inspect sessions, traces, and token use. The result is a path from a small notebook agent to a deployed service, with explicit places to add context, enforce constraints, and examine behavior. items.title: RAG Needs a Map: Using GraphRAG to Retrieve Connected Context — Nyah Macklin, Neo4j
items.excerpt: An agent answering questions about a course needs more than the five chunks closest to a query. It also needs the connections between lessons, concepts, and the sources behind its answer. Nyah Macklin builds that retrieval path with Neo4j, combining vector search with a knowledge graph that people can inspect and query. The workshop starts with the difference between semantic similarity and relationships, then walks through GraphAcademy, an Aura database, and a Python environment. An LLM extracts entities and relationships from course material, embeddings support similarity search, and Cypher exposes the resulting structure. Vectors remain part of the system; the graph adds connected context and a way to answer questions that require traversal or aggregation. The hands on build moves from a knowledge graph pipeline to an agent in Aura. Macklin creates a vector index, configures a lesson search tool, adds a retrieval query that returns related graph data, and enables natural language questions through text to Cypher. The agent answers a question about temperature using course content and displays its sources. A lesson count prompts a closer check of the underlying database query, showing why visible evidence matters even after the pipeline works. The final code walkthrough covers chunking, entity types, relationship types, and a schema that guides extraction rather than leaving the model to invent the graph's structure. items.title: Beyond RAG: Build a Relational Context Engine from Scratch — Peter Werry, Unblocked
items.excerpt: Ask a vector store for the PRs you merged last week and it can hand back one that is semantically perfect and three years old. Peter Werry builds context engines at Unblocked, and his thesis is that RAG, meaning similarity search, is only half of retrieval. Engineering context lives in pull requests, review comments, tickets, wikis, and chat, and all of it has structure: authors, dates, states, labels, relationships. Dumping it all in a vector store and reranking fails any question with a temporal or structural half. So the other half is turning natural language into a real database query, where the model does not answer the question, it writes the query. The workshop walks six stacked pull requests that turn a stubbed query playground into a working engine over a GitHub repository. Four pieces make the query reliable. Schema discovery samples three hundred documents and merges them into one tree, with procedural code rather than a model inferring types and enums. Identity resolution maps Peter to his GitHub login with simple fuzzy matching. Query planning passes the schema, forces a name extraction tool call, and includes the current date. Validation is deny by default: an allow list of operators keeps a function clause from running JavaScript on the server, and hidden metadata fields are wiped and reinjected for tenant isolation. A retry loop feeds validation and execution errors back to the model, which exposes the need for full text search when exact match fails. The same engine then powers a chat agent, and the Q&A covers scaling schemas with summaries, continuous ingestion, why Slack holds the why questions, MCP, and hybrid search. items.title: Latency Is a Budget. Humanlike Is the Goal. — Jesse Hall, LiveKit
items.excerpt: Your voice agent's dashboard says it's fast. Your callers say it feels robotic. They're both right. Jesse Hall, staff developer advocate at LiveKit, explains how to build voice agents that feel human. He shows why leaderboards can't pick your models (scores measure one model, but you ship a pipeline, and errors compound from speech-to-text to the LLM to text-to-speech) and why measured latency isn't what your callers hear. He covers buying time like a person does while tools run, plays a hotel-receptionist demo that handles interruptions and a caller changing his mind, explains LiveKit's audio-based turn detection (4.5% of users cut off vs 9.9% for the best alternative), and lays out the window that matters: a second and a half end to end still works, and around 600 milliseconds starts to feel human. He ends with LiveKit's open-source benchmark you can run against your own agent, a sneak peek of a voice-tuned Gemma model on LiveKit Inference, and a checklist. items.title: Dwarf Fortress uses version control now
items.excerpt: I remember hearing a while ago that Dwarf Fortress didn't use version control. That fact has been lodged in my head, because given its inherent complexity I have trouble imagining a codebase that would benefit from version control more . That's art. I went looking and I'm sad to report that the days without version control appear to have ended. Quoting Tarn Adams over time: March 2013: "I don't use version control -- I didn't like the feeling of having the code get committed into a black box thingy with no immediate upside" March 2016: "I don’t even use version control. If you don’t know what that is then you’re not gonna yell at me. If you even know what version control is you’re gonna be like, ‘You don’t use version control? You don’t use source control? What is wrong with you? How can you even work? I’m just not cut out for it, in a sense. It’s been 15 years, so the reasons have change over time, but that’s my current understanding of it." March 2023: "I've got Discord channels to check and version control stuff to use now, so the process is definitely a little more involved" That March 2023 quote comes from an interview about the release on Steam which made them millionaires . I'm a tiny bit sad that they gave in before they hit that milestone, but what an impressive run. Tags: version-control

items.text: If you want to know where all the tokens will get consumed in the future, here it is. Agent swarms will have massive implications in a number of enterprise domains like software development, cyber, life sciences research, AI research, finance, and more. The ability to parallelize agents against a unified goal where the volume of work is large, or where the search space not entirely known upfront, is going to be massive. Agents can fan out and coordinate work together on a specific mission in completely different ways from what humans are able to do. Today even in the most resource-abundant organizations, your ability to parallelize work on most projects is quite limited. Humans run into constraints on being able to communicate with one another, share status, deal with conflicts in work, keep shared context, and so on. As AI models can handle larger context without getting confused, and as they’re able to communicate effectively across their work with shared infrastructure, they can avoid many of the pitfalls that people have. You can see how this can lead to not just faster execution of tasks, but qualitatively different outcomes in medicine, research or defending against cyber attacks, scientific and math discoveries, and so on. This is why we’re going to need 1,000X more compute.

items.title: An AI Future Without the Lock-In — Remy Guercio, Tailscale
items.excerpt: The era of unlimited AI budgets is over, and most teams are locked into whichever tools they picked first. Remy Guercio, who works on Tailscale's AI gateway Aperture, looks back at a year of AI lock-in and asks how teams get out of it while proving real ROI. He breaks an internal AI deployment into four layers (the models, the data connectors like MCP, CLIs and APIs, the interface, and the sandbox) and argues an AI gateway is what keeps them swappable. He shows how Aperture uses your Tailscale network for identity instead of shared API keys, sets budgets per model (unlimited for cheap models, tight for frontier ones), works as both an LLM and MCP gateway, handles authentication for Cursor, Claude Code and Codex in one place, and keeps logs you can use to diagnose what an agent did. In this talk: • Why unlimited AI budgets are ending, and what ROI maxing means • The four layers of an AI stack and where lock-in hides • How an AI gateway ties identity, budgets and logs together • Aperture as both an LLM and MCP gateway SPEAKER Remy Guercio, Strategic Projects, Tailscale X: https://twitter.com/remyguercio GitHub: https://github.com/remyguercio LINKS Aperture docs: https://tailscale.com/docs/aperture Aperture: https://aperture.tailscale.com Tailscale: https://tailscale.com CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:45 A year of AI lock-in 2:05 The end of unlimited budgets 2:45 Wasted tokens 3:20 How do we get out? 4:44 Finance wants answers 5:14 ROI maxing 6:09 The four layers 8:09 Meet Aperture 9:24 How most AI gateways work 10:09 Identity from the tailnet 10:44 Built with tsnet 12:04 Budgets per model 12:44 LLM and MCP gateway 14:04 Auth in one place 16:49 Sandboxes 18:04 Why you need a gateway Recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 in San Francisco. items.title: How MiniMax M3 Was Built: Sparse Attention and Native Multimodality — Olive Song
items.excerpt: Most models learn text first and get vision bolted on later. MiniMax M3 learned both from the very first training step. Olive, who works on reinforcement learning research at MiniMax, goes inside MiniMax M3, an open-weight model with frontier-level coding and agentic ability, a 1 million token context window and native multimodality. She explains MSA, MiniMax's sparse attention design (about 9x faster prefill and 15x faster decoding than full attention): an index branch that picks which blocks matter and a sparse branch that attends only to those, and why existing designs like DeepSeek's DSA didn't fit grouped-query attention or GPU memory access. Then she covers training with text and vision from step zero, why adding vision later gave unstable results, what the attention maps show, and why 3D attention inside the vision transformer improves visual understanding. In this talk: • What makes MiniMax M3 different: agentic coding, 1M context, native multimodal • How MSA sparse attention works, and why DSA didn't fit • Block-level retrieval and kernels built for real GPUs • Why training on text and vision from step zero beats adding vision later SPEAKER Olive Song, RL Lead, MiniMax X: https://x.com/olive_jy_song LINKS MiniMax: https://www.minimax.io MiniMax M3 (GitHub): https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/MiniMax-M3 MiniMax M3 (Hugging Face): https://huggingface.co/MiniMaxAI/MiniMax-M3 MiniMax M3 tech report: https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13392 MSA (GitHub): https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/MSA CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 1:03 Meet MiniMax M3 1:37 1M token context 2:57 Sparse attention: index and sparse branches 4:17 Why not DeepSeek's DSA? 5:07 Problems with existing sparse attention 5:37 GPU memory access 7:01 MSA: what we changed 7:46 Block-level retrieval 8:21 Efficient kernels 9:01 Multi…

items.title: AI Agents Don't Read Your Policy Docs. They Hit Your APIs — Gravitee
items.excerpt: You can write all the rules you want in a markdown file. Your agent can still call the API. Sam, CTO at Gravity, skips the slides and runs five live scenarios against a hotel-booking agent to show why governance belongs in the infrastructure, not in the agent's instructions. Running on the Gravity Gateway with a Databricks backend, Sonnet and Groq, he shows the gateway blocking a destructive "delete all bookings" tool call, stopping an attempt to pull every guest's personal data, rate-limiting a buggy agent that fires the same request eight times, serving repeated questions from a semantic cache, and rejecting an oversized prompt before it ever reaches the LLM. He also covers telemetry across your agents, decoupling from any one hyperscaler, trimming bloated MCP tool lists, and shadow AI on employee laptops. In this talk: • Why prompts and policy docs can't enforce what agents do • Blocking destructive tool calls and data exfiltration at the gateway • Rate limits, semantic caching and token limits that cut cost • Observability, decoupling from vendors, and trimming MCP tools SPEAKER Sam, CTO, Gravity CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:52 Agents without governance 1:32 Move policy to the gateway 2:57 Demo 1: Blocking destructive tools 4:57 Demo 2: Stopping data exfiltration 6:56 Demo 3: Runaway repeat requests 8:21 Demo 4: Semantic caching 11:01 Demo 5: Blocking oversized prompts 12:21 Expensive agent habits 15:01 Avoiding vendor lock-in 15:41 Trimming MCP tools 16:16 Shadow AI 16:56 Wrap-up Recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 in San Francisco. Subscribe for more talks from the engineers building with AI. items.title: Beyond RAG: A Relational Context Engine That Cuts Token Burn — Unblocked
items.excerpt: Vector search can't answer "which PRs did I merge last week?" A relational context engine can, and it cuts token burn along the way. Peter Werry, founding engineer at Unblocked, explains what a context engine is and why coding agents need more than code search: the PRs, Slack threads and incident history that explain why the code is the way it is. He shows Claude sessions with and without that context, including one with about a 50% drop in cost and one that traced a regression to a model switch. Then he builds Unblocked's open-source document query engine step by step: automatic schema discovery, identity resolution across systems, query validation that blocks dangerous operators, retries that feed errors back to the model, and full-text search. He closes with the open-source context engine simulator for testing whether pre-gathered context helps your agents. In this talk: • What a context engine is, and how it lowers cost on real agent sessions • Why vector stores can't answer structural questions about your work • Turning plain-English questions into safe, validated database queries • Schema discovery, identity resolution, retries and full-text search SPEAKER Peter Werry, Founding Engineer, Unblocked LINKS Unblocked: https://getunblocked.com Document query engine (GitHub): https://github.com/unblocked/document-query-engine Unblocked on X: https://x.com/get_unblocked CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:52 Agenda 2:22 Demo: agents with and without context 4:17 Half the cost 4:57 Tracing a model regression 6:17 Let's build 7:11 Questions vector search can't answer 8:21 The hard part: scaffolding 9:46 The document query engine 10:31 Automatic schema discovery 12:26 Identity resolution 13:45 Validating queries 15:50 Retries 16:35 Full-text search 18:30 Context engine simulator Recorde…

items.text: Agent capabilities will soon evolve at RSI pace. Agentic security (identity, permissions, observability) will need to outpace this. The evolutionary direction of the broader agents space is capability -> trust -> autonomy The first phase has been about capability - can the combination of model + harness + tools + context reliably get work done? Capabilities have gotten pretty far, so the focus now shifts to trust…does the harness / system take the right action with right permissions? Can we observe it, audit it and establish accountability? A lot of serious work has already gone into these problems over the last couple of years. Now the challenge gets more important. and harder.

items.title: Zero Cold Starts: Serverless AI Agents on Akamai Functions — Thorsten Hans
items.excerpt: Cold starts, proprietary SDKs and one-region deployments slow AI apps down. WebAssembly at the edge removes all three. Thorsten Hans, senior developer advocate at Akamai, shows how to build and ship MCP servers and AI agents with Spin, the open-source WebAssembly framework, and run them on Akamai Functions, a globally distributed serverless platform with no cold starts. He explains why WebAssembly on the server is fast, portable and sandboxed by default, then live-codes MCP servers with wasmcp: scaffolding tools in TypeScript and Rust, composing them into a full server, testing with MCP Inspector, deploying it worldwide in about 60 seconds with one command, and calling its tools from the Zed editor. He finishes with an agent built on the Vercel AI SDK, backed by a model on a Linode GPU, and explains how memory snapshots keep apps warm. In this talk: • Why edge-native beats single-region for AI apps, and how WebAssembly kills cold starts • What Spin and Akamai Functions are • Building and composing MCP servers with wasmcp in TypeScript and Rust • Deploying an MCP server and an AI agent globally with one command SPEAKER Thorsten Hans, Senior Developer Advocate, Akamai LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/ThorstenHans/ X: https://twitter.com/ThorstenHans GitHub: https://github.com/ThorstenHans Website: https://thorsten-hans.com LINKS Spin: https://spinframework.dev Spin (GitHub): https://github.com/spinframework/spin Akamai Functions: https://www.akamai.com/products/akamai-functions wasmcp (GitHub): https://github.com/wasmcp/wasmcp CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:57 Why edge-native? 1:32 The cold start problem 2:52 WebAssembly on the server 3:37 What is Spin? 4:52 Akamai Functions 5:32 Sandboxed by default 7:32 Demo: scaffolding with wasmcp 9:41 Composing an MCP server 10:16 Testi…

items.excerpt: Most teams build an agent once, on one laptop, and never share it. Here's how to take it from local to the whole org to the CI pipeline. Jose Palafox, who has spent six and a half years at GitHub and now works with companies on Copilot adoption, walks through the path from a local custom agent to agents that run unattended in your pipeline. He explains how Copilot works under the hood, the built-in agents in the Copilot CLI, and how to generate and edit a custom agent with the agent builder. Then he shows how to share agents across an organization with a marketplace, run agents across repositories with Orchestrate, and move them into CI with GitHub Agentic Workflows: headless Copilot CLI runs in GitHub Actions, triggered by slash commands in issues, plus a repo with about 200 agents running different parts of the pipeline and agents that investigate their own cost overruns. items.subtitle: Aaron Levie · ceo @box - your business lives in content.…
items.text: Good post to start thinking through the long term safety approaches to managing intelligence in an enterprise. As agents begin to do vastly more task execution in the organization than humans, our need to secure, govern, control, and audit that work will become paramount. You’ll have agents operating against most of your most valuable data; they’ll be making decisions that will be harder and harder to reverse engineer; we’ll need to understand the liability and accountability regimes when models make decisions for us; and we need ways of containing the blast radius of accidentally or intentionally malicious agents. “Treating frontier closed and open weight models like insider risks is a way to build such a system. Not because they are necessarily malicious, but because any sufficiently capable actor with access to important systems can make mistakes or be compromised, and the architecture of containment and control must account for that” In a sense, AI will need to have its “zero trust” era that security saw. And all of this leads to needing various layers of protection and auditability of what agents are doing, what data they can work with, and controls for when things go wrong. And a huge opportunity right now for those building such systems across the enterprise.
