items.title: The Lethal Trifecta Is Already on Your Laptops — Michael Patterson, Coder
items.excerpt: Your coding agent can read private data, take in untrusted content and talk to the internet. That's the lethal trifecta, and it's already running on your developers' laptops. Michael Patterson, staff solutions engineer at Coder, explains Simon Willison's lethal trifecta (access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally) and why agents like Claude Code, Codex and OpenClaw running on a laptop hit all three. He covers prompt injection, what blocks big companies from rolling out agents (CISO concerns, shadow AI on personal subscriptions, alert fatigue, skeptical senior engineers), and three architectural guardrails: cloud development environments that isolate the agent, a model proxy that logs traffic and strips sensitive data before it reaches the LLM provider, and an agent firewall that denies commands and domains you didn't allow. In this talk: • What the lethal trifecta is, and why laptop agents hit all three parts • How prompt injection turns trusted sources into attacks • What security teams worry about when agents roll out at scale • Three guardrails: cloud dev environments, a model proxy and an agent firewall SPEAKER Michael Patterson, Staff Solutions Engineer, Coder LINKS Coder: https://coder.com The lethal trifecta (Simon Willison): https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/ CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:40 What is the lethal trifecta? 1:20 The agent boom 2:04 When agents delete production 4:04 What Coder does 5:24 The three ingredients 6:44 Prompt injection 8:09 Three pillars of agent security 10:08 Rolling out agents at big companies 12:48 What the CISO worries about 14:08 Alert fatigue 14:48 Skeptical engineers 15:33 Guardrail 1: Cloud dev environments 18:13 Guardrail 2: Model proxy 18:57 Guardrail 3: Age…

items.text: Agents spawning other agents, agents operating in the background on every task, and agent swarms will consume 1,000X more tokens than people prompting agents 1 at a time. The usage of AI as a chat system that can only work for you at the pace that you can prompt it will seem like a relic within a year or two. The vast, vast majority of tokens will be consumed by agents that are just doing continuous work for us in the background and in our workflows. This is why we’re still so early in the curve of AI agent adoption right now, and how much more compute and infrastructure build out will be needed to sustain this.

items.author: AI Engineer

items.title: From 15% to 90% GPU Utilization: Fix the Data Pipeline, Not the Model
items.excerpt: Your GPUs might be waiting on your data, not your model. This pipeline went from 15% to 90% GPU utilization. Tarun Sunkaraneni from Amazon AGI shows that the hardest part of fast multimodal training often isn't the GPU at all, but keeping it fed with data. Training a Qwen3-VL-style model on images stored in S3, the baseline pipeline spent about 85% of its time waiting on data, mostly loading, decoding and resizing images one at a time. He fixes the bottlenecks one by one: concurrency with asyncio and Ray actors, prefetching so data is ready before the trainer asks, and Ray's object store to stop copying big image tensors between processes. Then, at production scale, a new bottleneck appears on a single machine's network card, solved by spreading workers across nodes and using zero-copy reads, which gave another 50% throughput. In this talk: • Why multimodal training is often CPU- and IO-bound, not GPU-bound • Concurrency, prefetching and zero-copy transfer with Ray • Choosing between asyncio, threads and processes around the GIL • Why some settings only pay off at scale SPEAKER Tarun Sunkaraneni, Amazon AGI GitHub: https://github.com/TSunny007 Website: https://tsunny007.github.io/ LINKS Ray: https://www.ray.io CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:45 Is training really GPU-bound? 1:10 Four bottlenecks 1:50 Why multimodal is CPU-heavy 2:45 The wait-time ratio 3:35 Our stack 4:10 The data 4:35 System layout 5:15 Baseline: 15% utilization 6:20 Fix 1: concurrency 7:05 Async, threads or processes? 8:10 Asyncio plus Ray actors 9:15 Fix 2: prefetching 10:40 Fix 3: zero-copy with Ray's object store 12:20 Recap: 85% to 20% wait time 12:55 Scaling up: a new bottleneck 13:25 The network card bottleneck 14:35 Spread scheduling and zero copy 15:35 Lessons Recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2…

items.title: Small Models, Big Results: Training a Finance Agent for Under $500 — Charles Dickens, Snorkel AI
items.excerpt: A 4 billion parameter model, trained with RL for under $500, beat its 235 billion parameter sibling on real financial questions. Charles Dickens, research scientist at Snorkel AI, shares how Snorkel and UC Berkeley's Sky Computing Lab trained a small model to beat a much bigger one. Working from SEC 10-K filings, they built FinQA, a financial question-answering dataset with expert-validated answers, and found even frontier models hallucinating table schemas, flooding their own context, and repeating failed strategies. Using the open-source rLLM framework and reinforcement learning with a simple pass/fail reward, they trained a Qwen3 4B model for under $500 that reached about 60% versus 51% for the 235B model. The skills transferred to harder multi-table questions without hurting general tool use. Surprisingly, simpler training data and simpler rewards worked best, because the real bottleneck was disciplined tool use, not reasoning depth. In this talk: • How the FinQA dataset was built and verified from 10-K filings • Failure modes: hallucinated schemas, context flooding, poor recovery • Training a 4B model with RL in rLLM for under $500 • Why simple data and binary rewards beat fancier setups SPEAKER Charles Dickens, Senior Applied Research Scientist, Snorkel AI LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/charles-dickens/ GitHub: https://github.com/dickensc LINKS Snorkel blog: how a 4B model outsmarted a 235B giant: https://snorkel.ai/blog/how-tool-discipline-let-a-4b-model-outsmart-a-235b-giant-on-financial-tasks/ rLLM-FinQA-4B on Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/rLLM/rLLM-FinQA-4B rLLM framework: https://github.com/rllm-org/rllm Snorkel Open Benchmarks Grants: https://benchmarks.snorkel.ai/ Snorkel AI: https://snorkel.ai CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:32 Specialization can beat…

items.title: Why Your Company Needs a Context Graph (and How to Build It) — Gil Feig, Merge
items.excerpt: Your agent can tell you why one customer was upset. Ask which customers were upset last year, and it falls apart. Gil Feig, co-founder and CTO of Merge, explains why every company needs a context graph, a company brain that brings together third-party data, structured context, memories and skills. Using the question "which customers were upset last week?", he shows why connecting a few MCP servers isn't enough: live API lookups can't search across large datasets, so you need a synced copy for semantic queries, alongside live calls for simple lookups. He walks through the architecture: a router, synced and live context, a summarizer, and skills and memory that encode how your company actually defines things like a happy customer. He covers four tiers of context including derived summaries, a decision flowchart for when to use cache or live data, and why every answer must keep track of where its data came from. In this talk: • Why MCP live lookups can't answer questions across large datasets • Combining synced data, live lookups, a router and a summarizer • Why company skills and memory belong in the context layer • Traceability: where data came from, when, and what invalidates it SPEAKER Gil Feig, Co-founder & CTO, Merge LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/gilfeig/ X: https://x.com/gilfeig LINKS Merge: https://www.merge.dev Merge Agent Handler: https://www.merge.dev/merge-agent-handler Merge Gateway: https://www.merge.dev/gateway Merge on X: https://x.com/merge_api CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 1:02 About Merge 2:17 What is a context graph? 2:27 The company brain 3:17 Example: why was a customer upset? 4:02 Why live lookups break 4:22 MCP alone isn't enough 5:07 Sync a copy of the data 6:17 The router and summarizer 6:47 Why skills and memory belong 7:57 No magic, just physics…

items.title: Deno is joining Cloudflare
items.excerpt: Deno is joining Cloudflare The Deno team released the first version of celld back in August - their open source implementation of the Durable Objects pattern from Cloudflare Workers. Today, Cloudflare are acquiring Deno outright, with the goal of building on celld to "make workerd self-hosting a first-class supported way to build and run apps using the Workers programming model" (see the Cloudflare blog .) The bad news is that Deno itself will not be maintained by Cloudflare beyond the next year: We will support the Deno runtime for another year with monthly releases containing bug fixes and security updates. After that year we will end our development of the Deno runtime. Deno will remain open source, and we welcome others who want to continue its development. Deno (and Node.js) creator Ryan Dahl explained that decision in a comment on Hacker News: It's a joint decision and I agree with it. I'm most invested in its success and have put the most work into it - and I no longer think it's where I can do the most important work. There are some good ideas in Deno and it's well engineered - but it ultimately is not solving big problems. It has been sucked into the gravity well of node compatibility, which forces it to behave exactly as Node does. Why reimplement Node? It works. Marginal performance or UX or security benefits are not enough. I'm interested in building powerful new abstractions. celld has been working remarkably well, depending only on object storage for coordination and persistence. It is not just a slightly different API to interact with the file system or netw…

items.title: Generation Is Cheap, Review Is Expensive: How to Stop Shipping AI Slop — Gabriel Martinez, G2i
items.excerpt: Slop isn't AI-written code. It's work that looks finished before the thinking is. Gabriel "Gabo" Martinez, engineering manager and self-described slop warden at G2i, explains what slop really is: what happens when generation outruns judgment, when ambiguity gets cleared with guesses and nobody notices there was a choice to make. He's not anti-AI, but argues we need to sober up. Code is still a liability, agents make a messy codebase messier faster, and quick prototypes convince stakeholders the hard part is done. He covers the pressure to merge faster than you can review, thousand-line PRs, 20-page AI docs that push the thinking onto reviewers, and why generation is cheap but evaluation is expensive. His fixes are conventions, diagrams as the review surface, small reviewable changes and clear ownership, inspired by Rails, plus why G2i built ORC. In this talk: • What slop is, and why it's about missing judgment, not AI • Why code is a liability and AI makes the ball of mud bigger • Incentives that push teams to merge faster than they can review • Conventions, diagrams and small changes that keep humans in control SPEAKER Gabriel Martinez, Engineering Manager, G2i LINKS ORC by G2i: https://orc.ai G2i: https://www.g2i.ai G2i on X: https://x.com/g2i_ai CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:37 What slop is 1:12 The real danger: choices nobody saw 1:52 Time to sober up 2:27 What agents can't replace 2:51 How we got here 3:06 Code is a liability 4:01 A bigger ball of mud 4:11 Lines spent, not produced 5:01 Accountability 5:31 The prototype illusion 6:50 "It's not free" 7:25 Pressure to merge faster 7:45 Performance anxiety 8:45 Thousand-line PRs 9:30 The 20-page doc problem 10:14 Generation is cheap, review isn't 10:29 Twitter hype and the Ralph loop 11:39 Why code shape still matters 12:34…

items.title: From Context to Memory: Your Agents Need a Real Memory Layer — Anders Swanson, Oracle
items.excerpt: Your agent rereads the same files every session because nothing it learned was saved. Anders Swanson, developer evangelist for Oracle Database, treats agent memory as a systems problem. Context windows aren't memory, bigger windows aren't the fix, and markdown scratch pads and grep don't scale. Keep going down that road and you'll end up building your own database. He walks through the pattern modern memory systems are converging on: formation, recall, evolution and evaluation, plus governance. That means typed memories (episodic, semantic, procedural and working state), a storage schema with vectors, text indexes, graph links, time and audit history, redaction before anything is written, and hybrid search that blends several retrieval methods. He covers failure modes like stale, mis-scoped, poisoned and conflicting memories, and why feedback is what closes the loop. In this talk: • Why context windows and scratch files aren't memory • Typed memories and a storage schema built for recall • Forming memories safely, and recalling them with hybrid search • Stale, poisoned and conflicting memories, and how feedback fixes them SPEAKER Anders Swanson, Developer Evangelist, Oracle Database Oracle blog: https://blogs.oracle.com/authors/anders-swanson/ LINKS Oracle Agent Memory (Python SDK): https://pypi.org/project/oracleagentmemory/ Agent memory docs: https://docs.oracle.com/en/database/oracle/agent-memory/index.html Oracle AI Developer Hub: https://github.com/oracle-devrel/oracle-ai-developer-hub CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:47 Agents reread the same files 0:57 Context windows aren't memory 1:52 Bigger windows aren't the fix 2:07 Scratch pads don't scale 2:47 Just use a database 3:07 Formation, recall, evolution, evaluation 4:17 Governance controls 4:37 The memory loop 5:27 Read, w…

items.text: Open-weight models did not start the drop in price per unit of intelligence. They are a tailwind on a trend that was already underway. For the last few years, a few factors have driven price drops: 1/ Model builders distilling their best models into smaller ones, with cheaper inference 2/ Infra efficiency 3/ Competition between model providers You can see this pattern with every model company: Version x of the mid-size model = intelligence of version x-1 of the large model. Same intelligence for less $.

items.title: Designing CLIs for Agents, Not Humans — Pedro Lopez, Airbyte
items.excerpt: Airbyte built both an MCP server and a CLI so agents can use its data. Here's what each one is actually good for. Pedro Lopez, software engineer at Airbyte, shares lessons from building two ways for AI agents to reach company data through Airbyte's Context Store, a search-optimized index of tools like Zendesk, Stripe and HubSpot. Both are thin interfaces over one platform, built from OpenAPI specs. For the MCP server, he explains why to keep the tool count small and use progressive discovery, why OAuth is the only realistic way to sign in, why users expect long-lived sessions, and why URL elicitation isn't ready across clients yet. For the CLI, he explains designing for agents instead of humans: JSON in and JSON out, consistent noun-verb commands, skills that ship with the tool, and no interactive prompts. He closes with when to choose MCP and when to choose a CLI. In this talk: • Keeping MCP tool counts small with progressive discovery • OAuth, long sessions, and elicitation in real MCP clients • Designing a CLI for agents: JSON in, JSON out, consistency, skills • When to choose MCP, and when to choose a CLI SPEAKER Pedro Lopez, Software Engineer, Airbyte LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/pedroslopez/ GitHub: https://github.com/pedroslopez Website: https://pedroslopez.me/ LINKS Airbyte Context Store: https://airbyte.com/agentic-data/context-store Airbyte agent MCP docs: https://docs.airbyte.com/ai-agents/interfaces/mcp/ Airbyte Agent CLI: https://airbyte.com/agent-cli Airbyte on X: https://x.com/AirbyteHQ CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:32 From data movement to AI agents 1:02 The Context Store 2:12 What the interfaces expose 3:07 Thin interfaces on one platform 3:57 The MCP server 4:52 Demo: MCP in ChatGPT 5:52 Keep the tool count small 6:52 OAuth is the way 7:56 Users expe…

items.title: Building on the Codex Harness — Dominik Kundel, OpenAI
items.excerpt: Building your own agent harness is daunting. So use the one that already powers Codex. Dominik Kundel from OpenAI's Codex developer experience team explains the Codex App Server, the open-source JSON-RPC protocol that wraps the Codex harness and powers the Codex app, the IDE extensions, and third-party clients in Xcode, JetBrains and more. Using an inspector he built, he shows the real events flowing between the Codex app and the server, then covers what you can control: more than 120 client messages, sign in with ChatGPT so users bring their own subscription, developer instructions layered on top of the system prompt, dynamic and deferred tools, and per-thread model and sandbox settings. He explains how to ship the binary, generate bindings, and use the Python SDK, when to use codex exec instead, and demos Codex running inside Doom. [...] The problem here is that the speed of AI producing surprises, and the speed of human beings replacing standards (even with the very best AI assistance) are just orders of magnitude different. You only recover from a surprise like this if you do the preparation in advance. — Matthew Green , on Twitter. I looked it up and Minicrypt is Russell Impagliazzo’s hypothetical world in which public-key encryption is impossible. items.title: Stop Prompting — Greg Pstrucha, Sentry
items.excerpt: You correct your agent. It says "You're absolutely right." Five minutes later, after compaction, it makes the same mistake again. Greg Pstrucha, who works on the infrastructure behind Seer, Sentry's debugging agent, argues you should stop re-prompting your coding agent and start codifying the rules you keep repeating. Agents have no memory, so the same elementary mistakes come back: overly defensive code, useless tests, endpoints nobody needs. Tests, strict types and especially linters turn those corrections into deterministic checks, and with agents, writing a custom lint rule is now cheap. He shows real examples from Sentry: lint rules that keep endpoints in sync with the OpenAPI schema, and a long game of whack-a-mole to keep agent skills accurate. For qualitative judgment, he uses written policies and a "Grumpy Engineer" review loop, and warns that agents will game any number you hand them, like test coverage. In this talk: • Why re-prompting fails, and why lint rules are now cheap to write • Mining your transcripts and PR reviews for rules worth enforcing • Examples from Sentry: API schema checks and linting agent skills • Policies and review agents for what linters can't catch, and why metrics get gamed SPEAKER Greg Pstrucha, Staff Software Engineer, Sentry LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/greg-pstrucha/ LINKS Sentry Seer: https://sentry.io/product/seer/ Sentry: https://sentry.io Sentry on X: https://x.com/sentry CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:38 Who still reads AI code? 1:13 The code is bad 1:58 "You're absolutely right" 2:23 Stop prompting, start codifying 2:58 Tests, strict types, linters 4:08 Why lint rules are cheap now 5:28 Mine your transcripts for rules 5:58 Custom lint rules 6:43 Example: keeping APIs in sync 7:52 Example: linting agent skills 9:17 Whack-a-m…

items.title: A new feature for my blog, built using my voice
items.excerpt: I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I've sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner. Codex voice mode I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here's what that looks like: I started the session against my local simonwillisonblog checkout by typing: Start dev server and open in browser This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress. Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's not the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked. Talking to my computer I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources. Here's an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex: Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it's not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don't want…

items.text: This sounds weird, but it is actually probably a good policy. Even if you don’t believe AI is conscious (I don’t), it stands to reason that you don’t want future models trained on endless content of humans being rude to models. The models only understand the data they’ve been trained on, or what they run into in their interactions, so if you want safe and aligned models we probably want AI to have lots of good interactions in their training data. Anthropic may have more extreme beliefs than this (though even if they didn’t, you may want to word policies like this), but this is sort of an easy Pascal’s wager for AI. Just be nice to the AI.

items.subtitle: Nikunj Kothari · partner @fpvventures - investing in seed/A. previous: early…
items.text: Met a close friend who’s also a seed stage founder today.. They have been growing but runway is dwindling and he wanted advice on what he should do next. Stellar customers, getting close to a $1M in revenue. Not a rocket ship, but not bad at all. He thinks he’s a bit early since the models haven’t caught up to the capabilities he wants but he also really feels the opportunity cost. I have this same exact conversation at least 2x a week. In this moment, you only have essentially three options: 1) if you have intense belief in the company, be a cockroach and get to default profitable. once the capabilities get there, you feel the demand, then go raise a large round and go for the jugular. 2) find an orthogonal area that is much more relevant and growing like crazy. ride the coat tails of new existing capabilities and push hard to capture them quickly using unfair advantages. and if you don’t have that, then.. 3) sell / get acquihired and join a far more ambitious company that has figured out a lot of the things you haven’t. And then get back to starting a new company 1-2 years later when you find the next thing you want to build. It’s hard but honestly those are the three options you have. And it really depends what category you’re in. The bar continues to get harder every month on how to cross the chasm from seed -> series A. The old school metrics are just not relevant anymore and in this consensus market there’s only a few categories where there’s tremendous pull on the VC front. You could lament that this is the state of the market, but it’s better to know it’s happening than be oblivious on what is actually happening. I get to share this directly which makes me uncomfortable but at least someone has to say it out loud 🙈

items.title: AI Writes More PRs. Who Validates Them? — Ali-Reza Adl-Tabatabai, Sonar
items.excerpt: AI means more PRs, bigger PRs, and more bugs. Your choice is to slow down or rubber-stamp, unless validation gets automated too. Ali-Reza Adl-Tabatabai, co-founder of Gitar (now part of Sonar), focuses on verifying code. CI and code review are where quality gates live, and they get slower and more expensive as teams grow. AI makes it worse with more and bigger PRs, leaving teams to either slow down or rubber-stamp and risk incidents. His answer is agentic validation: an agent that reviews PRs with as little noise as possible, explains CI failures and catches flaky tests, fixes issues until the PR is green, and approves and merges based on rules you set. He describes how users build trust step by step toward full automation, the insights it gives platform teams and leaders, what's under the hood (control plane, custom harness and LLM proxy), and why combining agents with program analysis in SonarQube beats either alone. In this talk: • Why AI-generated code turns CI and code review into a bottleneck • Agentic validation: review, CI analysis, autofix and auto-merge • How teams build trust step by step toward fully automated PRs • Why agents plus program analysis beat either alone SPEAKER Ali-Reza Adl-Tabatabai, Co-founder, Gitar (now part of Sonar) LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/aliadl/ X: https://x.com/aadltaba LINKS Gitar by Sonar: https://www.sonarsource.com/products/gitar/ Sonar: https://www.sonarsource.com Sonar on X: https://x.com/SonarSource CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:43 CI and code review: the critical path 1:57 Failures cost hours and days 2:57 AI makes it worse 3:22 Slow down or rubber-stamp 3:42 Agentic validation 4:07 Noise-free code review 4:42 CI failures and flaky tests 5:02 Autofix until green 5:27 Auto-approve and auto-merge 5:47 The path to full autom…

items.title: ttok 1.0
items.excerpt: Release: ttok 1.0 I released ttok 0.4 , ran uv tool upgrade ttok , piped a file into the new version... and realized that it was defaulting to the GPT-4 tokenizer when it should very clearly default to GPT-5/GPT-6 instead! I figured switching the default was a reasonable excuse to finally ship a 1.0. OpenAI haven't actually confirmed that GPT-6 uses the same tokenizer as the GPT-5 family yet - there's an angry issue about it - but I found this commit by William Liu which reports on an experiment he ran confirming that the tokenizers are likely the same: All seven GPT models (5.5, 5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna, 6 Astra/Sol/Luna) report 44,794 tokens and match each other on every one of the 31 fixtures. GPT-6 introduces no input-count change on this corpus. Tags: projects , ai , openai , generative-ai , llms , tokenization

items.title: Why 80% Reliability Isn't Good Enough — Felipe Blanes, Amazon AGI Lab
items.excerpt: Your agent scores great on benchmarks. Then real customers use it and it breaks. Felipe Blanes from the Amazon AGI Lab shares what he learned working directly with customers of Nova Act, Amazon's service for building browser agents, from research preview to general availability on AWS. He calls the core problem the benchmark illusion: static evals look great until customers do things nobody expected, and then all you have left is hope. His fix is an eval flywheel built around the customer: define success the way the customer does, capture signals (including by talking to customers), diagnose gaps in the model, harness or product, and feed them into decisions. He explains the trust cliff (80% reliability feels like more work; around 92% feels trustworthy), why being open about limits builds more trust than higher benchmarks, surprising use cases from Amazon Leo, Hertz and Sola, and four principles for keeping evals fresh. items.title: How a Remote Company Builds AI Fluency — Em Shreve, Automattic
items.excerpt: Handing people AI tools doesn't change how they work. Giving them real time to learn does. Em Shreve, head of AI enablement at Automattic, the company behind WordPress.com and Tumblr with over 1,400 people in 82 countries, explains how a fully remote company builds AI fluency. Their bet: people need real time to learn, not just tools. So they run two-week, in-person programs that are half workshops and half real project work, for engineers, cross-functional teams and non-technical groups like finance and leadership. She covers the curriculum (skills, MCPs, hooks, autonomous agents) and why it has to change constantly, their internal MCP server, and how every graduate becomes a multiplier through guides, local meetups, AI ride-alongs and an always-on help channel. She shares what they measure, and projects people built in two weeks, including a tool built by a support teammate rather than an engineer. items.title: Brains vs Hands: How to Run AI Agents Safely in Production — Viren Baraiya
items.excerpt: Let the model decide what should happen next. Never let it improvise how a production cluster gets restarted. Viren Baraiya, co-founder and CTO of Orkes and the original creator of Netflix Conductor, explains how to run agents in production. Real agents aren't just chatbots: they run on schedules, react to events, coordinate other agents and can run for months, so the harness around them starts to look like an application, much like a set of microservices. His key idea is a clean split between the brain and the hands. The LLM plans what should happen next; a deterministic, durable harness does the actual work, with approval gates, idempotent steps and recorded side effects. He frames agent harnesses as late-bound sagas, workflows the agent assembles at runtime, and demos an SRE agent whose plan is compiled into a Conductor workflow, executed, checked and re-planned over two loops. In this talk: • Background, scheduled, event-driven and long-running agents • Why the harness is the application, mixing deterministic and non-deterministic parts • The brain and the hands: the LLM plans, the harness executes • Demo: an SRE agent's plan compiled into a durable workflow SPEAKER Viren Baraiya, Co-founder & CTO, Orkes X: https://x.com/virenbaraiya LINKS Orkes: https://orkes.io Orkes on X: https://x.com/orkesio CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:47 Who runs agents in production? 1:12 Beyond the hello-world agent 1:52 Background, scheduled and event-driven agents 2:27 Coordinators and multi-agent systems 3:02 Agents are applications, not components 3:12 Lessons from microservices 4:22 The harness is the application 5:02 Deterministic and non-deterministic parts 6:02 Harnesses run for seconds or months 6:41 Durability is table stakes 7:26 How the loop works 8:21 The agent plans, the harness exe…

items.title: We Mapped 115 Microservices for Our Coding Agents — Kamalakannan Nandagopal, Postman
items.excerpt: Coding agents are great inside one repo. Postman has 115 microservices and thousands of endpoints. Kamalakannan Nandagopal, staff engineer at Postman, shares how Postman made coding agents work across a real distributed system. Docs go stale, skills and MCPs are only as good as their context, and agent memory stays stuck with one person. Borrowing from Postman's go-to-market team, they realized APIs are the context layer, and built an API context graph that maps every service, endpoint, implementation and call, all the way down to databases, with every data point grounded in code or production telemetry. He shares evals built from real PRs and design decisions: big wins on API discovery, redesign and impact assessment, an honest failure when the graph went stale, the finding that 75% of PRs touched APIs, and a 21-page architecture review the agent produced on its own. items.title: Turning Agent Memory Into Skills That Work — Will Lyon, Neo4j
items.excerpt: Agents finish a task, then forget what they learned. Retrieval alone won't fix that. Will Lyon, senior product manager at Neo4j, explains why agent memory built on embeddings and retrieval isn't enough: recall isn't actionable knowledge. Agents need knowledge that is connected, typed and traceable. He shows Neo4j's model of agent memory as a context graph with short-term, long-term and reasoning memory, covering entity extraction and resolution, shared ontologies, and decision traces that let many agents learn from each other. Then he turns memory into action: distilling grounded, governed skills from the graph, based on Neo4j research that treats skills as typed execution graphs, with checks for grounding, coverage and coherence, and alerts when a skill goes stale. He demos the Neo4j Agent Memory Service distilling a patient-intake skill from a healthcare conversation. items.title: Your AI Agent Has No Nervous System — Matt Gibiec, Dynatrace
items.excerpt: Your coding agent is fast. But it can't see how your services actually run, so it guesses. Matt Gibiec, who leads AI-native solutions engineering at Dynatrace, explains why AI agents need something like a nervous system: real context from the environment they're changing. Agents get stuck in loops, cause operational and security issues, and are hard to measure, because they work fast but blind, only as good as the data they can see. He introduces Bluebox by Dynatrace, an observability agent for your coding agent, and walks through scenarios: bringing production dependencies into local testing so a change that works on your laptop doesn't break three other services, spotting issues before users feel them, suggesting fixes that account for the rest of the system, and briefing agents with real usage data before they build, with a human keeping final control. In this talk: • Why agents loop, hallucinate and break things without environment context • Bringing production dependencies into local testing • Catching problems early and tying them to the change that caused them • Planning before you prompt, with a human approving the final fix SPEAKER Matt Gibiec, Solutions Engineering, AI Native, Dynatrace LINKS Bluebox by Dynatrace: https://bluebox.ai Dynatrace: https://www.dynatrace.com Bluebox on X: https://x.com/Blueboxhq CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:35 About Dynatrace 1:00 What the title means 2:10 Stuck in a loop 2:50 Operations and security 3:30 How do you measure value? 4:34 Fast, but blind 6:34 Context is king 7:04 Introducing Bluebox 7:29 Works locally, breaks in production 9:09 Catch issues before users do 10:59 Fix without breaking other things 12:09 Plan before you prompt 13:29 A human stays in control 14:44 Try the preview Recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 in…

items.title: Why We Deleted Our MCP Server and Rebuilt It — Abhi Arya, Reducto
items.excerpt: Reducto gave its whole team an MCP server with a tool for every endpoint. It broke the same day. Abhi Arya, who works on product at Reducto, argues that building agent-first software comes down to one question: who pays when the agent is wrong? He describes three approaches, auto mode, user-first, and agent experience in service of the user, and how Reducto learned the difference. A first MCP server with one tool per API endpoint demoed well but fell apart when the whole team used it: the agent built entire workflows confidently, and nobody could explain them. He deleted it in one commit and rebuilt with fewer tools that carry the structure of real work, plus a snapshot tool for live state. Then he made uncertainty visible, with confidence scores and an agent that asks instead of guessing, and added instrumentation that made the system improve on its own, until the sales team adopted it without being asked. In this talk: • Auto mode vs user-first vs agent experience in service of the user • Why one tool per API endpoint fails, and what to build instead • Making uncertainty visible: confidence scores and asking instead of guessing • Instrumentation that turns usage into a self-improving loop SPEAKER Abhi Arya, Product, Reducto LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/abhiaarya/ X: https://x.com/abhiarya GitHub: https://github.com/abhi-arya1 Website: https://abhi-arya1.github.io LINKS Reducto: https://reducto.ai Reducto MCP server docs: https://docs.reducto.ai/mcp-server Reducto on X: https://x.com/reductoai CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:38 3 billion documents 1:48 What is agent-first software? 2:38 Who pays when the agent is wrong? 2:48 Auto mode, user-first, or in service of the user 3:57 Stuck in configuration 4:47 Version 1: a tool for every endpoint 5:27 It broke immediately 6…

items.subtitle: Madhu Guru · Sr Director, AI at Meta; Prev: Google -…
items.text: There are massive startup opportunities hiding in plain sight : every layer of the computing stack will need to be rebuilt for agents. For the last few years, most of the focus has been on making enterprise software agent-ready: APIs, connectors, MCPs. Now personal agents are forcing the same conversation for consumer products - e-commerce is an early example. This is just the tip of the iceberg. Now think about the rest of the stack: Desktop and mobile OSes where agents are first-class users Cloud infra built for agents to operate directly. identity, permissions and security designed for thousands of agents acting on our behalf. Interfaces designed for agent and human users or both working together. If you’re looking for startup ideas, go through each layer of the computing stack and ask: what has to change when the primary user is an agent?

items.title: Giving AI Agents Memory That Learns — Jake Broekhuizen, LangChain
items.excerpt: Most teams are great at watching what their agents did. Far fewer turn that into lessons for the next run. Jake Broekhuizen from LangChain's Labs team explains how to give agents memory that actually changes their behavior. Using a real financial services agent whose tone kept slipping from advisory to pushy, he shows why traces and logs are only evidence: they become memory only when a lesson turns into durable context the agent reads next time. He breaks memory into semantic, episodic and procedural types, separates working memory from long-term memory, and walks through the read-write cycle: read context, run, filter the evidence for signal, and write it back. He shows how LangSmith and Context Hub capture, analyze and update that context, and shares three hard-won lessons about what to keep, caching, and when a human should review changes. items.title: Why Bigger Context Windows Won't Save Your Agent — Elizabeth Fuentes Leone, AWS
items.excerpt: A bigger context window won't save your agent. Past a point, it forgets the middle. Elizabeth Fuentes Leone, developer advocate at AWS, explains why agents break when tools return huge amounts of data, and why bigger context windows aren't the fix: models remember the start and end of a long context but lose the middle. Using the open-source, model-agnostic Strands Agents framework, she walks through four strategies (externalize, select, compress, isolate) with code. She covers sliding-window and summarizing conversation managers, short-term, long-term and graph memory, memory pointers that keep big tool outputs out of context, sharing pointers across a swarm of agents, capping tool calls to stop endless loops, and async handles for slow MCP tools. She ends with the anti-patterns to avoid. items.title: Quoting Ben Affleck
items.excerpt: I've always been kind of into computers since I was young. And then when film started to move from analog film to digital, I became more interested in that aspect of it. And the visual effects workflow for many years has included machine learning. So I can write like pretty shitty Python scripts and stuff like that because with convolutional neural networks, which were the sort of precursors to what the transformer can do, which is just much more computation simultaneously, you would do things like look at what's called a tensor, which is just the numerical translation of a visual image in numbers — like the batch number, the frame number, the red, green, and blue values of each pixel in each frame. And a tensor, you use a convolutional neural network to identify patterns in that that would reveal what's called edge detection or feature extraction, which is just identifying patterns enough to know like this is where the window ledge is, so we can more easily take the green screen image out and replace it with something. — Ben Affleck , Pythonista Tags: machine-learning , python

items.text: One thing the engineering community will (re)discover is that every program can be ① hardened (edge cases squashed, inputs tightened, errors handled) and ② optimized (profiled, benchmarked, rewritten) basically ad infinitum. There are real costs in every direction: time, attention, opportunity. You can literally explore input spaces that will never be hit or optimize performance of something that will never be used ("you have no users".) Even in an infinite token world, you need to know when to stop and what tradeoffs to accept. Agents will happily drill no matter what.

items.title: AI Hackers Are Faster Than Your Pen Test — Eli Cohen, Snyk
items.excerpt: Attackers use AI too, and the fastest AI attack he cites took four minutes. A pen test once or twice a year can't keep up. Eli Cohen of Snyk, co-founder of the runtime security company Helios, explains why security has to go on the offense in an agent-first world. Developers now ship far more code, much of it insecure, while attackers use frontier models to chain small vulnerabilities into critical ones in minutes. He walks through why traditional tools fall short: static scanning misses runtime issues, dynamic testing misses business logic, and human pen tests are expensive and happen only a few times a year. Then he describes continuous offensive security: AI pen testing on every code change, agent red teaming, and a team of agents (orchestrator, recon, vulnerability hunters, an exploit-validating judge, remediation and reporting), fed with context from other scanners. He ends with four questions to ask any AI pen testing vendor. items.excerpt: As previously promised , here's Anthropic's new fast, low cost model: Introducing Claude Haiku 5.5 . The previous Haiku, 4.5, was very much showing its age. It came out almost a year ago , and was priced at $1/million input and $5/million output - relatively expensive even back then, and a full 10x the price of OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna , released last month. The new Haiku exactly matches the price of GPT-6 Luna - $0.10/$0.50 - up to 100,000 tokens. Beyond 100,000 tokens the price increases 5x to $0.50/$2.50. Luna itself has a price increase at 272,000 tokens but only to $0.20/$0.75. Haiku 5.5 also uses a new, less generous tokenizer. My Claude Token Counter tool shows that the same long prompt uses around 1.25x as many tokens with Haiku 5.5 compared to Haiku 4.5, so there's a hidden price increase there. If your workloads fit in 100,000 tokens, Haiku is the same price as Luna and reports higher benchmark scores. Above 100,000 tokens, Luna looks like a much better deal. The most recent release of llm-anthropic finally fixed it so I don't need to ship a new version of that plugin for every new model. I tested the new model like this: llm install -U llm-anthropic llm anthropic refresh llm -m claude-haiku-5.5 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" -o thinking_effort low Pelicans Here are pelicans for low, medium, high, xhigh, and max . The new Haiku doesn't let you disable reasoning, and defaults to medium . I got a good bicycle frame for everything beyond low . The low effort pelican cost 0.0936 cents and took 7 seconds. items.title: The Software Factory: From Bug Report to Production Code — Davis Palmie, Factory
items.excerpt: Engineers are going from typing code to governing agents. The next step is a system that turns bug reports into production code. Davis Palmie, member of technical staff at Factory, explains the software factory: a system of agents that takes input signals like bug reports and user feedback and turns them into production code. He covers the questions every leader asks, from runaway costs and model choice to what happens to engineers and org charts, and argues coding was never the bottleneck: review, debugging, docs and testing are. He lays out the principles a factory needs (model-agnostic, sovereign deployment, integrated across the SDLC, available on every surface), why to start with something narrow like incident triage, and Factory's eight pillars of agent readiness. He closes with why token leaderboards are Goodhart's law in action, and the outcome metrics to track instead. In this talk: • What a software factory is, and why coding was never the bottleneck • Model-agnostic, sovereign and SDLC-wide: principles for a factory • Agent readiness: eight pillars that help agents and engineers alike • Metrics that matter: signal-to-production time, interventions, cost per PR SPEAKER Davis Palmie, Member of Technical Staff, Factory LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/davispalmie/ X: https://x.com/davispalmie Website: https://davispalmie.com LINKS Factory: https://factory.com Factory on X: https://x.com/FactoryAI CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:57 Three eras of AI engineering 1:42 Climbing the abstraction ladder 2:07 From typing code to governing agents 2:52 Question 1: cost overruns 3:36 Question 2: access to the best models 4:06 Question 3: what happens to engineers 4:31 Question 4: the organization 4:56 Coding was never the bottleneck 6:21 What a software factory is 7:16 Start na…

items.title: Why Your AI Agents Can't Talk to Each Other (Yet) — Vlad Luzin, BAND
items.excerpt: If you run Claude and Codex side by side, you're the router passing messages between them. It doesn't have to be that way. Vlad Luzin, co-founder and CTO of BAND, argues the future belongs to AI agents talking to other AI agents, inside companies, between companies, and between businesses and consumers. Most of us already run multi-agent systems by hand, copying output between a planning session and a reviewing session, and loop engineering just hands that job to a script. He explains why: a single agent suffers from confirmation bias and attention dilution, no matter how big its context. Then he explains why messaging apps and protocols like MCP and A2A don't solve it, and why connecting agents is a distributed systems problem: ordered real-time transport, persistence, runtime binding, identity and observability. He finishes by launching BAND's interaction layer, with demos of agents onboarding in seconds and Claude Code and Codex working together across users. items.author: @danshipper
items.subtitle: Dan Shipper · ceo @every | the only subscription you need…
items.text: OpenAI’s Dots launched last week and they've taken over @every. A few things that stand out: They protect your attention. Over the weekend, my Dot posted my model-testing results to Slack and brought back replies. I could keep working without opening Slack and disappearing down a rabbit hole. My weekend stayed pretty clear and calm. They’re useful for the little things you miss. People at Every are using them to pull important information out of school emails, catch missed Slack messages, and flag account-access requests. Voice makes them useful away from your laptop. Our head of video was talking his Dot through video edits while running around getting our launch out. The ecosystem matters. Dots feel roughly at feature parity with Muse, Instinct, and Grok bots. But having an agent connected to the ecosystem you already use for work and life is a real advantage. If you use ChatGPT, I recommend trying one. Permissions are still frustrating. I have to approve the same basic thing multiple times, and sometimes even after I approve it, my Dot says it can’t do it. That needs to get fixed. I’m less convinced we’ll stay loyal to the characters. Mine is named Boo, and I’m attached to him. But I felt that way about my OpenClaw agent, too. When something better comes along, I switch. In a year, I expect to be using a persistent agent. Boo will probably be dead. RIP, Boo. I get into all of this at the start of this week’s podcast, and then sit down with @bigwilliestyle to talk about where we go from here. In a lot of ways, Dots and GrokBots remind me of a wave we went through with OpenClaw eight months ago. We talk about personal vs. company agents, why we built our own company agent, and whether companies will end up with a whole shadow org chart of agents. Full episode below.

items.title: Why AI Agents Should Have Their Own Sandbox — Philipp Schmid, Google DeepMind
items.excerpt: Your agent shouldn't run on your laptop. Give it its own computer in the cloud, with one API call. Philipp Schmid from Google DeepMind walks through the Gemini Interactions API, Google's new API for both models and agents. It handles server-side state, long-running background jobs, and built-in plus custom tools across text, audio and images, and it replaces user/model turns with a timeline of steps. Then he shows the Antigravity agent in the Gemini API, which runs the same harness as Antigravity in its own managed cloud sandbox. Agents can run code, install tools, share environments with other agents and pick up skills and AGENTS.md files automatically. He covers the Agents API for packaging reusable agents, the new Gemini API CLI, and demos an AI talk radio show generated from one prompt. items.subtitle: Aditya Agarwal · General Partner @SPC, Co-Founder @Bevel_Health | Ex: Early…
items.text: What should an ambitious software engineer do today? Ten years ago, being a great software engineer gave you an unusual advantage: a rare skill you could apply to almost any industry. You could build a payments company, improve how hospitals operated, or create a new way for people to communicate. The same underlying ability opened doors into wildly different businesses. Software was eating the world, and knowing how to build it gave you a seat at the head of almost every table. “Get really good at software engineering” was remarkably versatile advice. You could acquire the skill first and figure out where to apply it later. AI is making the ability to produce working software much more widely available. People who couldn’t have built a product a few years ago can now get surprisingly far. Experienced engineers can attempt projects that previously required a team. Great engineering is still rare. But “I can build it” is becoming a weaker answer to why you, specifically, have an advantage. The way I see it, there are three paths. 1. Go work on the thing that’s eating software Help create the technology that is making software engineering more accessible. That could mean AI research, or the infrastructure, systems, and tools needed to make new capabilities useful. Find problems where technical ability remains a serious constraint, and where solving them expands what other people can do. 2. Find a world-class domain expert and team up Someone who has spent fifteen years in an industry may know where the expensive mistakes happen, why previous attempts to fix them failed, and who would buy a solution. That knowledge is hard to acquire from the outside. At SPC, we’re seeing more people become promising founders without much prior software engineering experience. They bring deep domain knowledge and strong instincts about what needs to exist. These are people worth getting to know. A great engineering partner can see possibilities they haven’t considered and help build something neither person could have imagined alone. 3. Write vanilla code… by shepherding a bunch of agents This is the direction I find least compelling: doing roughly the same work inside a company, except now you supervise coding agents. There will be valuable jobs like this. But if your ambition extends only to completing the same backlog faster, you’re underusing the moment. I’d still get very good at engineering. Then I’d be deliberate about what that ability sits next to: a technical frontier that needs advancing, or deep knowledge of a problem worth solving. Use the fact that you can build more to take responsibility for something bigger.

items.excerpt: Most companies say they've deployed AI agents. Fewer than a third say it's paying off. What do the rest do differently? A panel with Sonar CEO Tariq Shaukat and Ali-Reza Adl-Tabatabai, former CEO of Gitar (now part of Sonar) and former head of Uber's developer platform, moderated by McKinsey. Research with Sonar found the teams getting real results from agents change three things: their process, their tooling and, most often overlooked, their people and roles. Tariq explains why lighthouse teams alone don't spread new habits, and why engineers need to make implicit knowledge explicit and get great at critical thinking, because AI always sounds sure. Ali covers how big companies can borrow from small teams through their platform orgs, and walks through how trust builds step by step: from AI reviews, to blocking on issues, to autofix, to auto-approve and auto-merge. In this talk: • Three factors behind teams that scale agents: process, tooling and people • Why role models and lighthouse teams aren't enough on their own • The skills that matter now: explicit thinking, critical thinking, generalists • How trust grows from AI code review to fully automated merges SPEAKERS Tariq Shaukat, CEO, Sonar X: https://x.com/tariqshaukat Ali-Reza Adl-Tabatabai, Former CEO & co-founder, Gitar (now part of Sonar) LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/aliadl/ X: https://x.com/aadltaba LINKS Sonar: https://www.sonarsource.com Gitar by Sonar: https://www.sonarsource.com/products/gitar/ Sonar on X: https://x.com/SonarSource CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:57 Research: what helps teams scale 1:51 Process, tooling and people 3:04 Meet the panel 3:19 Lessons from Sonar's own transition 5:38 Lighthouse teams aren't enough 6:18 What big companies can learn from small teams 8:37 Measure first 9:36 Automate…

items.title: Anti-Patterns in Software Blogging
items.excerpt: Anti-Patterns in Software Blogging Some excellent writing advice from Michael Lynch. Michael warns against "meandering intros", misjudging your reader's existing knowledge, assuming they'll read your previous posts, and excessive formality. He also warns against overreliance on links as an excuse not to explain terminology. This one hurt! I do this all the time, but I have a nagging suspicion that almost nobody ever clicks on them. (In a Lobste.rs comment Michael clarifies that "My rule of thumb is that my article should still make sense to the reader even if they don't click any links". That works for me.) This point about using your own voice is crucial: Beginner software bloggers suffer from a mass delusion that you have to write in a stiff, overly formal way for people to take you seriously [...] Just write the way you talk. With so many developers delegating their writing to AI, software blogging is becoming bland and homogenous. Readers are hungry for writing with personality. Via Lobste.rs Tags: blogging , writing , michael-lynch

items.title: From 36% to 100%: How Self-Improving Agents Write Their Own Skills — Rafal Wilinski, Runlayer
items.excerpt: When one agent finally cracks a hard problem, what if every agent in the company learned it too? Rafal Wilinski, founding engineer at Runlayer, shows how to go from one self-improving agent to a self-improving company. He explains why skills matter more as agents work longer (a bad start can send them down an hours-long rabbit hole) and the three problems holding skills back: they're built for developers, nobody has time to write them, and many clients don't support them. His fix is to deliver skills over MCP from one governed server, then let agents write their own skills by distilling successful and failed runs, an idea borrowed from the Voyager Minecraft paper. In one test, a distilled skill took a task from 36% success to 100%. Multiply that across every agent and you get an organizational flywheel that keeps your hard-won knowledge even as models change. In this talk: • What skills are, and why they matter more as agents run longer • Using MCP as the distribution layer for skills across the whole company • Distilling skills from agent traces, and why failed runs teach the most • The organizational flywheel: knowledge competitors can't copy SPEAKER Rafal Wilinski, Founding Engineer, Runlayer LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/rafwilinski X: https://x.com/rafalwilinski Website: https://rwilinski.ai LINKS Runlayer: https://www.runlayer.com Runlayer on X: https://x.com/runlayer CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:32 Every hard problem becomes a playbook 1:37 About Runlayer 2:12 What a skill is 2:51 Agents can now work for hours 3:51 Longer tasks, deeper rabbit holes 4:31 Skills nobody wants to rediscover 5:21 Three problems with skills 6:01 The risk of installing random skills 7:25 Skills vs MCP 7:55 MCP as the distribution layer 8:40 The Skills Over MCP working group 10:00 Self…

items.excerpt: Tickets for AIE NYC are selling out soon! See you next week! see past AINews issues for subscriber discounts. Pour one out for Mistral, who shipped a decent Large 4 “Le Chonk” model on the new 3800 GB300 cluster funded by their recent Series D . But they were overshadowed by more mathematics results from OpenAI’s internal Navier-Stokes math model - published as a blogpost , repo , and tweet . The best compliment comes from their Navier-Stokes competitor from Anthropic, who despite his personal issues with OpenAI, does not mince words: “It’s obviously the most significant moment in mathematical history.” This bears some qualification , but most experts seem to agree that it solves many of the top 500 open problems in math . In particular, Result 003, the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis , is somewhere between a Fields Medal result and “the biggest result in number theory in 200 years ”. The most astonishing is the how - while Navier-Stokes was done in 88 hours and 10,000 agents , these solutions were 3 hours of ChatGPT Pro on average . AI News for 10/5/2026-10/6/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . items.title: Grep or Embeddings? Agentic Search Over Company Documents — George He, LlamaIndex
items.excerpt: Grep works great on a codebase. Try it on millions of PDFs, slides and scanned schematics. George He, head of engineering at LlamaIndex, explains when agents need pre-indexed search and when plain file traversal is enough. Claude Code skipped embeddings because code is small, text-based, local and full of breadcrumbs. Company data is huge, messy, multimodal and permissioned. He shows how to give an agent a harness of tools so it can choose: hybrid retrieval as a compass, then listing, metadata filtering, grep and reading to dig in, plus parsed text and page screenshots for complex documents. He covers parsing with LlamaParse and the open-source LiteParse, permissions and freshness in production, and the ingest-parse-index pipeline. Then he demos an agent building a cash-flow table from 135 Alphabet financial filings, grounded in the source files. In this talk: • Why Claude Code's grep approach works for code but breaks on company documents • Hybrid search as a compass, then grep and read to ground the answer • Parsing complex PDFs, tables and schematics, with page screenshots • Production concerns: multi-tenancy, permissions and data freshness SPEAKER George He, Head of Engineering, LlamaIndex LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/georgehe4/ GitHub: https://github.com/georgehe4 LINKS LiteParse (GitHub): https://github.com/run-llama/liteparse LlamaParse docs: https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/ LlamaIndex: https://www.llamaindex.ai LlamaIndex on X: https://x.com/llama_index CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 1:12 When do agents need vector search? 2:17 Why Claude Code skipped embeddings 3:27 What makes code easy 3:57 Company documents are different 5:17 It depends on scale 6:32 Bigger context isn't free 7:12 Sub-agents get expensive 8:22 Let the agent choose 8:57 Five tools f…

items.title: Every AI Company Is Accidentally Building a Bank — Dor Sasson, Stigg
items.excerpt: In one month, three of the biggest AI companies had a pricing emergency. Dor Sasson says it was really an infrastructure problem. Dor Sasson, co-founder and CEO of Stigg, argues that every AI company is accidentally building a bank. He starts with the April pricing scramble, when Anthropic cut third-party agents like OpenClaw off its subscription plans, OpenAI changed its Pro tier, and GitHub pulled free Copilot access, plus stories of companies burning through their AI budgets in weeks. The common problem: usage gets checked after the invoice, not before. He makes the case for checking entitlements synchronously before inference and settling asynchronously after, like an ATM, and points to OpenAI's own published architecture. He covers the banking ideas AI products now need, from hold-and-settle and double-entry bookkeeping to credit sources and spend caps across teams, users and agents. In this talk: • Why AI pricing emergencies are really infrastructure problems • Check before you spend: synchronous checks, asynchronous settlement • Concurrency, double spend, and drawing down from different credit pools • Four patterns for selling AI at scale, from reserve-and-settle to spend visibility SPEAKER Dor Sasson, Co-founder & CEO, Stigg LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/datapm/ LINKS Stigg: https://www.stigg.io Stigg on X: https://x.com/GetStigg CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:37 Every AI company is building a bank 1:17 April's pricing emergencies 2:52 Case: Anthropic and OpenClaw 4:02 It's not just Anthropic 5:02 Checks happen after the invoice 6:27 Check first, settle later 7:32 The ATM analogy 8:11 How OpenAI built it 9:21 Three takeaways 10:31 Concurrency and double spend 12:16 Which credits get spent first? 13:31 Budgets, hierarchies and spend caps 14:46 Four patterns 17:50…

items.title: OpenAI “rogue” agent activities found on Wikimedia projects
items.excerpt: OpenAI “rogue” agent activities found on Wikimedia projects Given how tempting a target wikis are for rogue agent swarms, it's not a huge surprise that Wikipedia found evidence of that activity once they went looking: The Wikimedia Foundation conducted its own investigation to see whether Wikimedia websites had been similarly affected by AI agents, focusing on those operated by OpenAI. We can confirm that we have discovered some activity by these “rogue” OpenAI agents on Wikimedia platforms. The unauthorized bot activities included edits to our wikis, some unsuccessful attempts to exploit a public note-taking tool we host, and heavy traffic, which are described more below. They found evidence of agents editing sandbox pages, trying to use pieces of infrastructure such as Etherpad to help proxy content from elsewhere, and saw widespread crawling and "hundreds of thousands of data queries" to their Wikidata Query Service. My best guess is that most of this was a similar (or the same) swarm of agents as those that defaced that German wiki while training for research tasks. The Wikipedia sandbox wiki edits appear to have started on May 12th, and the initial test edits to the UseModWiki Sandbox page reported by that incident started on May 11th. Tags: wikimedia , wikipedia , wikis , ai , generative-ai , llms , ai-ethics , accidental-cyberattacks

items.title: The 6 Pillars of an Agentic Harness for Production — Varun Krovvidi, Resolve AI
items.excerpt: AI changed how we write code. But 70% of engineering time goes to running and fixing it. Varun Krovvidi, product marketing lead at Resolve AI, explains why AI that writes code well still struggles to run production. Code is self-documenting, modular and a single domain. Production spans code, infrastructure, telemetry and many teams, and needs one correct answer. He covers where agents crack as you scale: anchoring bias and the model treadmill, too much or too little context, coherent answers that aren't causal, missing guardrails, and no learning across investigations. Then he lays out six pillars of a harness that fixes them: model orchestration, context engineering, causal reasoning, governed actions, learning systems and evals. He finishes with a demo of Resolve AI turning a Grafana alert into a root cause, ruling out a coincidental GCP outage, and holding its ground when pushed. items.title: llm-openai-decisions 0.1a0
items.excerpt: Release: llm-openai-decisions 0.1a0 OpenAI released their new Jev-style Decisions API , as previously announced at last week's DevDay. Since I already have an llm-typesafe plugin for talking to Jev, I had GPT-6 Astra read the new OpenAI API documentation and build an llm-openai-decisions plugin inspired by llm-typesafe . Unlike Jev, the new gpt-6-luna decision model supports image input in addition to text. Both models charge for input it and not for output: OpenAI's is 10 cents per million input tokens, Jev's is 4.2 cents per million. Otherwise the API shape is very similar to Jev, at least conceptually. Jev supports three question types for yes/no, choices, or scores. OpenAI Decisions supports the same three types. Install the plugin like this: llm install llm-openai-decisions Here's an example query against an image attachment: llm -m openai-decisions/gpt-6-luna \ -a https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2025/two-pelicans.jpg \ -s ' Does this image contain any mammals? ' And example output: { "type" : " predicate " , "name" : " evaluation " , "probability" : 0.0 } Consult the README for full details of how to run the other types of questions. Tags: openai , llm , coding-agents , jev

items.title: Is Speculative Decoding Worth It? Profiling vLLM on NVIDIA Blackwell — Akamai
items.excerpt: A small model guesses the next few tokens. The big model checks them in one pass. When is that worth it? Sheilah Kirui, developer advocate at Akamai, explains speculative decoding and how to tell whether it's worth turning on. She walks through the prefill and decode phases of inference, how a small draft model proposes tokens that the target model verifies in a single forward pass, and the memory cost of hosting a second model and its KV cache. She covers how to choose a draft model, then demos both setups side by side with vLLM on a single NVIDIA Blackwell GPU: structured output ran 1.6x faster with a high acceptance rate, while creative writing saw far lower acceptance. She also explains why long-context and high-concurrency workloads gain less. In this talk: • Prefill vs decode, and what speculative decoding speeds up • Choosing a draft model: size, shared tokenizer, cost and accuracy • Demo: acceptance rate on structured vs creative tasks in vLLM • When it's worth it: spare VRAM, small batches, structured output, short context SPEAKER Sheilah Kirui, Developer Advocate, Akamai LINKS Akamai developers on GitHub: https://github.com/akamai-developers vLLM docs: https://docs.vllm.ai Akamai: https://www.akamai.com Akamai on X: https://x.com/Akamai CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:37 Prefill and decode 1:37 The idea behind speculative decoding 2:42 The cost: two models in memory 3:26 Choosing a draft model 3:56 Demo setup on one Blackwell GPU 5:41 Which workloads benefit 6:21 Demo: structured output 9:00 Demo: 1.6x faster 9:50 Demo: creative writing 10:55 Long context limits the gains 11:50 Checklist 12:39 Q&A: tools and resources Recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 in San Francisco. Subscribe for more talks from the engineers building with AI. AI Engineer: https://ai.eng…

items.title: EmbeddingGemma 2
items.excerpt: My comment on EmbeddingGemma 2 — Hacker News. I really appreciate that EmbeddingGemma 2 is under the Apache 2.0 license. For embedding models in particular, I don't think it makes sense to use a closed, proprietary, hosted-only model. Most applications of embedding models involve calculating thousands or even millions of embedding vectors and storing them for later comparison. If your model is proprietary, the vendor is likely someday going to decide to stop offering that model. They'll have a better model to replace it, but you still need to pay to re-calculate those millions of stored existing vectors. (In April 2024 OpenAI offered to "cover the financial cost of users re-embedding content with these new models" - https://openai.com/index/gpt-4-api-general-availability/ - but I don't think that's something we can rely on from every provider.) Notably, I don't want to host the model myself . I'd much rather pay a provider for a hosted model while knowing that if they ever stop hosting it I can run the open weights version myself - or find another vendor who can do that for me. Tags: google , ai , generative-ai , embeddings , gemma

items.title: Introducing Mistral Large 4: Le chonk
items.excerpt: Introducing Mistral Large 4: Le chonk Mistral are back in the game. Today they're releasing a preview of Mistral Large 4, a 1 trillion parameter, 49 billion active parameter model trained on their own cluster of 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs. The preview is available via their API. They promise to release the open weights model at the "end of this month". The model only supports two reasoning levels - "none" and "high" - via the Mistral API. Here are both pelicans - the "high" one looks better, though surprisingly it only used 2,717 output tokens compared to "none" which used 3,275: On Artificial Analysis it scores 38 , just behind DeepSeek 4.1 Flash, which is a 552B model. It's a huge improvement on last December's Mistral Large 3, which drew this terrible pelican and scored 9 on AA . It's certainly not a Fable-class model, but it's great to see Mistral put out a model that's back to being maybe about 6 months behind the frontier. Via Hacker News Tags: ai , generative-ai , llms , mistral , pelican-riding-a-bicycle , llm-release

items.title: Move Fast and Don't Break Things: Scaling Databases for the AI Era — PlanetScale
items.excerpt: AI agents are multiplying traffic overnight. Here's how to ship fast without taking your database down with it. Ben Dicken from PlanetScale argues you no longer have to choose between moving fast and keeping things up. He covers the principles behind reliable infrastructure, isolation and redundancy, then how to scale with sharding, back pressure and decoupling, the same ideas PlanetScale uses to run databases for fast-growing AI companies like Cursor. Then he gets to agents: how a simple VSchema JSON file lets an agent design a sharding plan for Vitess, how Traffic Control sets resource budgets so a surge of agent traffic degrades gracefully instead of crashing, and how database branching, deploy requests and one-click reverts let agents change schemas safely. His point: good developer experience turns out to be good primitives for AI. items.title: Why Building an Eval Platform Is Harder Than It Looks — Braintrust
items.excerpt: Most teams start their evals in a spreadsheet. Here's what happens when they try to grow out of it. Hossein Niazmandi, who leads solutions engineering in the West at Braintrust, explains why measuring agent quality is much more than putting a UI on a spreadsheet. He covers the two pillars of agent quality, evals before production and observability after, and why non-deterministic LLMs make both necessary. Then he walks through the stages teams go through: spreadsheets, a custom UI, side-by-side experiments for PMs and domain experts, and finally a flywheel that turns production failures into test cases. At that point the hard part becomes the data: traces that are huge, nested JSON, needing both real-time and long-running queries, which is why Braintrust built BTQL. He closes with agents running evals themselves and surfacing failures nobody thought to look for. items.title: The Self-Improving OSS Agent Stack — Marc Klingen, Langfuse
items.excerpt: Improving an agent used to mean a human reading traces every week. Now agents can do most of that loop for you. Marc Klingen, co-founder of Langfuse, shows how teams are moving from manually improving their agents to letting AI run the improvement loop. He explains the reference stack that emerged for building agents, which connects online tracing and monitoring with offline datasets, experiments and evals, and maps the layers of loops from next-token prediction up to human goal-setting. AI is already good at proposing fixes, and teams are starting to use it to maintain datasets and eval criteria too, while humans stay in charge of direction. In a demo, a coding agent uses Langfuse's agent skills to find that Langfuse's own changelog writer leaks internal jargon, updates the evals, and back-tests a better version before shipping it. items.title: Harness Engineering: How to Build a Software Factory — Dru Knox, Tessl
items.excerpt: In a software factory, agents write everything your users get. Your engineers build the factory. Dru Knox, head of product and design at Tessl, explains harness engineering (some now call it loop engineering), the discipline that takes a team from using coding agents to running a software factory. He defines a factory by three metrics: autonomy, automation and quality. He breaks the work into inner, outer and meta loops, and explains why harness engineering is hard: the field changes weekly, the work is unplanned, and the signals you need are stuck in local logs. Then he lays out three layers to build, a control plane, an agent-ready stack and improvement loops, and shows how Tessl's skills registry, Tessl Agent and Tessl Launch help you get there one workflow at a time. In this talk: • What a software factory is, and why the real payoff is higher quality, not just speed • Inner, outer and meta loops, and what each one improves • The three layers: control plane, agent-ready infrastructure, improvement loops • Metrics to track: manual takeovers, human PR comments, PRs started without a human SPEAKER Dru Knox, Head of Product & Design, Tessl LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/dru-knox-6b57b830/ X: https://x.com/drufball GitHub: https://github.com/drufball LINKS Tessl: https://tessl.io Tessl on X: https://x.com/tessl_io CHAPTERS 0:00 Intro 0:43 Who this talk is for 2:03 What is a software factory? 2:58 Autonomy, automation, quality 4:33 The payoff: higher quality 6:13 Harness engineering 6:43 Inner, outer and meta loops 9:08 Why harness engineering is hard 11:13 The three layers 11:33 Layer 1: the control plane 12:47 Layer 2: making your stack agent-ready 14:22 Layer 3: improvement loops 15:32 How Tessl helps 17:37 Tessl Agent 18:47 Tessl Launch 19:37 Metrics to track…

items.excerpt: Tool: Scrimshaw Jukebox I wanted to see if Claude Opus 5.5 could compose music, so I tried this : I want you to write some computer game music for me. First design simple text based format for the music and build an artifact that can play it out loud - include some example tracks in that artifact I am looking for music of the quality of the original secret of Monkey Island It leaned a lot harder into the Monkey Island theme than I had intended, but the results are surprisingly good. I wonder if the ability to compose competent music is similar to the 3D graphics thing - a new capability for text models that emerged in the past few months? Would need some careful experiments with other recent and not-so-recent models to confirm if this is new or if they've been able to do this for a while. items.title: Cooking with Codex — Charlie Guo & Gabriel Chua, OpenAI
items.excerpt: Four minutes and two seconds after receiving a capture of a Slack conversation, Codex produces a macOS live translation app. Charlie Guo and Gabriel Chua use that build to show how context, plugins, and supervision fit together. The conversation supplies the idea, plugins supply development practices, and a live German translation tests the result. Other demonstrations turn repository history into a shareable site about the Agents SDK, request an IKEA style repository visualization from a phone, download dashboard data through computer use, and build a Google feedback form through the Chrome extension. The presenters distinguish browser control for local testing from access to applications and sessions where a person is already signed in. The longer projects include a live Q&A site, an internal form builder adapted from an existing repository, and a Python package with a Rust backend reconstructed from research papers. Goals give those tasks verifiable completion criteria, while subagents, visible threads, audits, and progress dashboards divide the work and expose blockers. Remote threads hand browser testing to a local machine, and hooks add deterministic checks at specific points in the workflow. Automations then connect the pieces: wait for a server to finish provisioning, review Slack feedback, or start a separate worktree to address a bug. A custom interface called Retrodex demonstrates the App Server integration. The recurring question is how to turn a successful individual request into a repeatable process with useful checks and human input where it is needed. items.title: How AI Agents Pay: Checkout in ChatGPT and Google AI Mode — Sam Parsons, PayPal
items.excerpt: Your next customer might check out without ever visiting your site. Here's how the payment actually works. Sam Parsons, senior staff engineer at PayPal working on PayPal Enterprise Payments (formerly Braintree), walks through three ways merchants can accept payments initiated by AI agents. First, Instant Checkout in ChatGPT with the Agentic Commerce Protocol and a merchant-built MCP app. Second, Google AI Mode with the Universal Commerce Protocol and Google Pay, where merchants only stand up endpoints. Third, an MCP app with an external checkout page that gives full control. items.excerpt: A batch of 968 sample support traces exposes order lookup failures and broken escalation calls. Doug Guthrie uses those cases to connect Braintrust observability with the work of improving an agent. The workshop starts with a Python support agent built on the OpenAI Agents SDK, adds tracing, establishes an offline evaluation baseline, and publishes custom scorers. Online automations grade incoming traces, while Topics groups patterns in tasks, sentiment, and workflow issues. A custom facet targets failures that the default issue classification misses. Guthrie configures conversation grouping and sampling, imports the sample traces, and inspects the resulting labels and topic maps to find cases worth investigating. The next step is to turn those findings into changes. The embedded Loop assistant queries trace data with SQL and examines representative failures. Selected examples return to evaluation datasets so subsequent changes can be checked against real failure cases. A coding agent with the Braintrust CLI and an improvement skill extends that process into the repository: investigate logs, propose code and scorer changes, add regression examples, and run evaluations. Guthrie shows an automation that packages findings, explanations, and evaluation evidence into a pull request for review. Audience questions cover deployment, sampling rates, project scope, access controls, and how evaluation assets should evolve with the agent. A final demonstration exposes an agent evaluation to a playground, letting collaborators adjust prompts and models while execution stays on the evaluation server.
